speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In accordance with the decision of this House to have a simultaneous debate on both Motions, I will now call on Members to make their speeches.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Members are allowed to consider both Motions in a single speech.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: By "negativing", the term is to mean the effect of qualifying, transposing, contradicting and nullifying the other Motion.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Any Member who wishes to vote against either Motion can do so directly.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Leong has said that CECA is not the PSP's main concern, but it has been thrust upon them by the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Motion today, would you not agree, shows what he says to be untrue?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, your post on 22 June 2021, I quote, "the most important economic policies that have affected the jobs and livelihoods of Singaporeans relate to foreign PMETs and free trade agreements, in particular, the Comprehensive Economic Cooperation Agreement with India." But today, we heard you say that you are in favour of free trade agreements.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, is it that you are in favour of free trade agreements, but specifically oppose CECA?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is what it looks like, based on what you have said so far.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Your comments have troubled your own PSP members.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They have said that your statements in Parliament on CECA were targeting the Indian community.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You protested here that you are not a racist and that these statements and sentiments ascribed to you are a diversion and a distraction.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But your party members are quoted as saying, that you are targeting the Indian community and they say it is totally a racial undertone.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Leong, your statements have been interpreted by your own party members, as being racist.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: People in your party think your statements are racist.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I do not expect that you will accept that you are racist, but would you accept that people in your party think that your statements are racist and have said so?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We are supportive of FTAs and even CECA in general, but we need more information about all these FTAs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: If we do not have more information, we cannot say we are wholeheartedly supporting them.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It has to be evaluated on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Two, the Minister commented on I having commented on CECA on many occasions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Can the Minister give me the examples of occasions that I have spoken about CECA?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Other than starting from my Facebook post on 22 June, can the Minister give me instances that I have spoken about CECA before?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Even for the 22 June Facebook post, it was after I had accepted the challenge from the Minister.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, I had started to comment a bit, to put things into perspective.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In this second point, the Minister also mentioned that Dr Tan Cheng Bock had mentioned at the party launch about CECA in August 2019.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But he was responding to the feedback from Singaporeans and the phrases "free movement" and "free flow" are not phrases owned by PSP.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The Government Ministers had been talking about "free flow" way before Dr Tan Cheng Bock had said it.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I do not think I need to quote George Yeo or about what the Prime Minister had said and all that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We allow them to express their views and sometimes, there are one or two members or a minority of members who have different opinions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We have told them that they cannot make their views that public.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But some of them chose to do that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We cannot stop them because we are a liberal party.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We are not a party which will prevent all our members from having their own opinions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, one or two party members mentioned that what I am doing in Parliament today is racist but that does not mean I am racist.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Leong, so, your party members, you say some of them, think you are racist based on your statements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, second, Mr Leong says, now, they have got nothing to object to CECA and other FTAs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think it is an important statement and I would like that recorded.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think we all need to note that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But assuming that, then, we have over 20 FTAs —

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I say I am supporting FTAs and, in general, including CECA, but I did not say that I am supporting CECA wholeheartedly.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We do not have enough information to support.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If you do not have enough information, are you supporting or not supporting?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, you are not supporting CECA or FTAs, is that right?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The FTAs, we need more information as well on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I am trying to understand what your position is.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, you are not supportiing FTAs, including CECA, is that right?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, for each FTA, we want to look into the details.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, may I ask, Sir, through you, to Mr Leong, one, just tell us does he and does PSP support FTAs?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us then have that recorded as he and PSP support CECA and FTAs in general.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Before we know more information about that, we cannot shut down discussion on FTAs and CECA, which the Government is trying to do.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The day after the Ministerial Statement on 6 July, the next day, in The Straits Times, the Government straightaway said CECA has no effect on our ability to regulate immigration.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But the data provided by the Government is not conclusive.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The Government did not provide the data to prove its point.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: As a result, although the Government may say, yes, we have told you many, many times and we have discussed this again and again, each time the disclosure is incomplete.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: That is why we have to continue discussing.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because sometimes, the time allowed for the discussion and the debate is also not sufficient.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Of course, in the Ministerial Statement on 6 July, because we are going to file this Motion, we are also holding back some of the things we wanted to discuss.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is simply that if you look at the Motion which I read out, it highlights CECA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am just trying to understand whether CECA has a special place in Mr Leong's affection and mind, or is it treated the same as all the other FTAs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If it is the same as all the other FTAs, why is CECA getting special mention?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The focus of the debate today is on the impact of our foreign talent policy on jobs and livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, we are focused on all the work pass holders and not one particular nationality.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, if you can answer the Minister's question, which is a straightforward one.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Because if it was just FTAs in general, then why is CECA being flagged out specifically?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But you do want to know more data about all the other FTAs, right, from what you were alluding to earlier?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, why no mention of the other FTAs but CECA, in particular?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: No, but in our Motion, we said FTAs and CECA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think Mr Leong does not know his own Motion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, there are some FTAs which do not concern him and there are some FTAs which concern him.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, these are the FTAs, including CECA —

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Including the Australian FTA, the China FTA, the US FTA, for example.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: For the China FTA, we are looking at the China FTA to compare with CECA, because both countries have very big populations.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, some of these FTAs, as I have said, we have to look at it on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If I may just have that confirmation before I move on?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Moreover, we have, I think, Sir, Mr Leong's confirmation that he supports FTAs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I then ask, Sir, through you, does Mr Leong accept that his and his party's statements on CECA having been interpreted by some of PSP members as being racist, may well be interpreted by Singaporeans as racist as well?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The reason why I stated our position at the beginning of my speech is exactly in anticipation of what the Minister is going to ask on this.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: CECA is an economic agreement, trade agreement that we want to have more information on.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because the perception is that there are certain terms on the Movement of Natural Persons that are not beneficial to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, we want more information, not necessarily directed at just CECA as an FTA —

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That has nothing to do with what I asked.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Okay, in that case, Minister, sorry, can you repeat the question again?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some of Mr Leong's party members interpreted his statements as being racist and I quoted.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One of the quotes is "You are targeting the Indian community and it is totally a racial undertone".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: My question was, if his own party members can think like that, it is entirely possible for other Singaporeans to take a similar view.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But CECA is an economic agreement that is the concern of many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Do you have a response specifically to the Minister's question?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I want the Minister to repeat the question again.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Leong, it is commonsensical, is it not, that those PSP members will not be the only ones who think that your statements are racist?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If they can think like that, your own party members, then, other Singaporeans can reasonably think that your statements are racist too.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Yes, okay, actually just now my answer was going to that point.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But it does not mean that if someone accused somebody who is trying to find out more and discuss about an economic agreement thinks that the person is racist, then we need to shut out the whole discussion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, we are having a long debate, we are going to be here for very long.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And it will be even longer if we do not get answers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: There will be some people who will think that there is racial undertone, yes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: With that, Sir, I want to go back to some of the questions that were raised and not answered the last time in July.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is clearly set out in two clauses.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are standard clauses commonly found in all FTAs." And then, he refers to Chapter 9.1.2 and 9.1.3.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He then says, "There is a strong immigration carve-out and National Treatment is not found in Chapter 9 of CECA, nor any other corresponding Chapter in the FTAs that Singapore has entered into", "...nothing in this agreement implies that Singapore must unconditionally let in PMEs from India.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is false because, as I explained earlier, all foreign PMEs have to meet our work pass conditions in order to come and work here", "The second common criticism is that intra-corporate transferees from India can also freely enter Singapore to work.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Based on my explanation on how the Chapter works, this is again not true.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Intra-corporate transferees also have to meet our work pass qualifying criteria." Then, he said, "Mr Speaker, Sir,	I hope we can put a stop to all this misinformation about our FTAs in general, and CECA, in particular." So, bearing that in mind, Sir, can I ask, through you, for Mr Leong to respond to questions posed by Mr Ong Ye Kung that CECA does not allow a free flow of Indians into Singapore?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It has been used by the Government as well.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, let us focus on what exactly — we are just talking about the numbers of foreign nationals that have come into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, will you be coming to an answer to that question?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: If you do not give us the numbers, how are we going to answer to Singaporeans that, really, CECA has no influence over our immigration policies?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We asked for ICT numbers but only one year's number is given.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: If you give all the numbers from 2005 to 2020, and the number of ICTs who have later on become PRs and new citizens, and obtained new work passes —

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One, what does CECA or the other FTAs allow?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is a matter of interpretation of the agreement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is what we had been debating in July and Minister Ong said there is nothing in CECA that allows for free flow.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The second is, within the framework of CECA or any other FTA, and I note that Mr Leong only wants to know CECA and not any other FTAs, how many have come in?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Those are matters of numbers and details, and we can deal with that separately.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Hopefully, we will not take another hour for that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But, first, as a matter of interpretation, the Minister who, as a civil servant, was negotiating this agreement, referred chapter and verse, and had explained how the Government applies that policy, that it is subject to our work pass rules.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that is how it has been applied for the last 15 years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, unless Mr Leong says that Minister Ong Ye Kung lied or that the Government policies are other than what it says it is, let us just get an answer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Do you accept that there is nothing in CECA that allows for free movement of PMETs?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is just untrue, based on what Minister Ong has said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are arguing about your Motion which refers to the provisions of CECA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second question: will he now, in the context of his Motion, agree that we are debating the provisions of CECA?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And will he accept that there is nothing in CECA that allows for free movement of Indians into Singapore?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The provisions that we put in the Motion is actually pertaining to the economic effect of the provisions.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, the provisions are the legal agreement, as explained by the Minister.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And what are your views about those provisions?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: They are written in black and white and we covered that quite extensively at previous Sittings.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: My view is that we are not arguing about a legal document today.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The legal documents dictate how these interactions take place with the other countries.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, unless you are doubting the validity of the agreement, or you are doubting the way in which it is implemented, I think we are seeking a view on that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We do not think that we can interpret, I mean, we can draw a conclusion from just the explanation given by the Minister.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Maybe if I can help to paraphrase that.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Minister has explained what the terms are.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Do you agree that those are the terms of the free trade agreement as agreed between the two countries?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: No, as I have said, I am not arguing about a legal document.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: What I am arguing about is, there is a legal document, but the way you implement the legal document and the economic effect can be different.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I wanted to get, Sir, through you, to Mr Leong, because Minister Ong specifically raised this and Mr Leong said they need more time to study this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have had August and September to study it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, first of all, the English meaning, unless some other language may be different, but the English meaning of "the provisions on Movement of Natural Persons in some free trade agreements like CECA" means what they say, which is the legal provisions in CECA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, let us not try and wriggle out of that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, before we talk about implementation, first, in terms of the legal provisions, I have read out what the Minister said, what these provisions are, does Mr Leong have any basis to contradict that or challenge that, or does he accept it?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If he does not know the answer, he can say he does not know the answer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I am not sure the answer is going to be found in the phone.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can I suggest that we leave it here for now and we can discuss again after —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: No, I think Mr Leong can answer them.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I think they are pertinent to the issues that are at hand presently.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You may raise it later or you can pass your speech to Mr Leong.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We went back to consider the points put up by —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, before we proceed, can we just answer the questions rather than cover the same ground again?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: What does that mean, exactly, when you say that you do not agree with the legal documents?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You do not agree that that is how it was phrased or you do not agree with how it is being phrased?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So that we can proceed with the argument, so that we can develop the debate further.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because we are looking at the economic effects of the —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We are talking about the provisions that are provided under the FTAs, in this case, CECA.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: What exactly is it about the agreements that you disagree with or whatever that might be?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Okay, then if it is not the legal opinion, what is your opinion on them?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: My non-legal opinion would include my interpretation of the economic effect.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, it will be a bit different from what the Minister is asking.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Minister has said that there is no free movement allowed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We apply and we are entitled to apply our workforce rules and that this is how it has been operated since CECA has come into force and, likewise, for the other FTAs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Which part of that statement does he disagree with, Sir?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Yes, maybe he can look at these statements and say which part of it he disagrees with.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Does he disagree that we have applied it this way?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Does he say that the Minister was lying in Parliament?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Or does he say that the interpretation that the Minister has given is inaccurate and that we should, in fact, or are obliged to give free movement of all Indians into Singapore?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And looking at the economic effects, there are some initial doubts whether the movement is easier than what the Government has represented or not.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But we still cannot come to a conclusion yet because we need more data from the Government.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I do not think we are going to get any further clarity on this.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We will just have to agree to disagree and register both points.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will take it, Sir, based on the answers that Mr Leong really does not know about these legal provisions, despite the wording of his Motion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And he has no understanding of the provisions of CECA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I assume that he has the same concerns about the provisions in the US FTA, the China FTA, and the Australian FTA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, if so, I hope to see those FTAs being referenced in future rather than CECA being singled out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have another clarification to seek, Sir: the PSP's claim that CECA allows the 127 categories of Indian professionals to come here freely to work.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When I finish, if there are clarifications, Mr Leong can ask me, just like I am asking him.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Can I, Sir, ask through you, and I think I heard the answer in Mr Leong's speech, confirm that Mr Leong accepts that we need some foreign PMETs for our economy?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, that we cannot have zero PMETs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Can I, Sir, through you, have him confirm that?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, the number of PMET job vacancies have been around 30,000 over the past five years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Third, the size of our PR population has remained stable in the last five years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: From 2016 to 2020, it is at about 520,000.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, it has been stable even before that, but we will just take five years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, with these numbers in mind – local PMETs increased by 300,000; foreign PMETs increased by 110,000, Employment Pass and S Pass holders; PR population, stable and Mr Leong agrees that we need some foreign PMETs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If that is too much, then can he tell us what is the right number?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Okay, the number of rebalancing that we need to do depends on the Government's estimate of what is the number of Singaporeans that are being displaced, which is something that I will push during the debate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, can I take it, Sir, through you, that Mr Leong can confirm that he does not really know how many, what should the number be?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The Government is always controlling the numbers, controlling the data.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I will have to refer to the Government to give me some data to come up with an accurate answer.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I got some numbers in mind, but I would prefer to wait for the data.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Yes, at this moment, I will need more data from the Government before I can come up with an accurate number.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, therefore, it follows, logically, Sir, that Mr Leong is not able to assert here or anywhere else that we have too many foreign PMETs in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You were saying that you see many unemployed Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Underemployed Singaporeans have come forward to reflect to us, feedback to us.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We have also seen in statistics, the number of gig workers, they are increasing.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And also the number of self-employed Singaporeans is also increasing.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, there are Singaporeans that are being displaced.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, we got some rough numbers, but we want the Government to give us more accurate numbers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Leong agreed earlier that he does not know if 350,000 is too many or too little.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it is a natural conclusion that he does not really know if there are too many foreign PMETs here.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is basically based on what he says.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Not that I do not have an idea of how many Singaporeans are being displaced.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Perhaps Mr Leong can give us an explanation as to why there are so many vacancies which are unfilled in Singapore and have been unfilled for the last five years?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Okay, but if all these vacancies and numbers are being presented in a proper time series dataset, then, we will be able to analyse the numbers better.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, at the moment, I cannot give him an answer on that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because you always come up with single data and ask me for answers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, Mr Leong had said that he will study it carefully.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I think what this House is witnessing is a Motion that has been put up and Mr Leong does not know the meaning of the Motion that he has put up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because he says "the provisions on Movement of Natural Persons in some free trade agreements like CECA".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He has given no credible explanation on why CECA is singled out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He has no credible explanation as to why he refers to the provisions, which means legal provisions, the clauses in CECA, in his Motion and then asserts here that he does not know anything about the provisions in CECA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then, he should not have referred to that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it is meaningless, the Motion; does not make any sense to him, let alone to us.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And he says, there are too many foreign PMETs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But now he says, he does not know if there are too many and he does not know what the number ought to be.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He does not tell us what further data he needs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the point is to find the right solutions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And then come to Parliament and say, I do not know anything about the terms of CECA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is not the way Members should behave, I am sorry to say.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You got to know what your own Motion says.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am a lawyer, but you do not need to be a lawyer to know that this term, "provisions on Movement of Natural Persons in some free trade agreements", has got only one meaning.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You will have a chance to respond, Mr Leong.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Minister, you have made a lot of accusations there.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: One is that we go back to square one again about my Motion statement.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I bring the Motion statement to this Parliament about the economic effect of the provisions in the FTAs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I am not bringing to Parliament the legal interpretation of the provision.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But if you have a legal interpretation, I am fine.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I am just telling you that I am concentrating on the economic effect of the provisions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Second point, you say you provided the data but I asked for a lot of data that is not provided.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Three, the displacement in Singapore and that is a key point that we are debating today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The Government says it is due to global forces.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I say, or PSP says, a large part of it is not due to global forces.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, that is what we are debating about.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, do not jump the gun and come and make the conclusion now.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, before we get all heated up, let me refer to what was discussed here the last time around.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Minister Ong pointed out, on 7 July, the same; that Dr Tan said "...CECA is an agreement between Singapore and India to bring in to allow, I think, 127 categories of professionals to come to Singapore and be given that free hand, practically free hand to come and work here".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that is what the Motion says, "the provisions on Movement of Natural Persons in some free trade agreements".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I mean one has got to be both honest and accurate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If Mr Leong does not know what the Motion means, if it has been drafted by someone and he has put his name to it, he can say so.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I disagree with what the Minister said about his interpretation of the Motion and that I do not understand the Motion and all that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I already said again and again, that the Motion statement that I put up is about the economic effects of the provisions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I do not expect this Parliament to just argue about legal interpretation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: This Parliament is about jobs and livelihoods of our people, about the economy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, what we are arguing, actually is a larger part of, should be about economics, social, economic issues.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We are not going to stand here and keep arguing about a legal interpretation of a clause.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, if I may, the provisions are the first step, is it not?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Because if the legal provisions do not provide for that, then it provides a basis for us to discuss about the economic effect.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It does not preclude discussing that part because your Motion addresses that.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, that is the issue at hand and we are trying to understand what is your understanding of the provision.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Because it is in black and white, so, what are your views on that?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We can subsequently discuss about economic effect, you can take all day if you wish.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But what are your views on the legal provisions?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It was spelt out in black and white, as illustrated by Minister Ong previously.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Do you agree that those are the provisions that were spelt out in the agreement?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Yes, but then, in order to have a legal interpretation of provisions, you must look at other parts of the agreement and then you must look at other practices.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But since Mr Leong has no opinion, it must logically follow that as far as he is concerned, there are no provisions in CECA that he is concerned about.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You may, but I think we know the answer.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: My answer is, at the moment, in terms of the legal interpretation that this agreement does not have further implementation, implications and all that, I do not have an opinion.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But you do have a negative view about it?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Despite the fact that you do not have a legal or otherwise opinion of it?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I am trying to get a view, if the Government is prepared to release more data, about ICTs and about all that, then I will have an economic view.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister, I suggest we move, because I do not think we are going to make much progress here.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He professed his deep disappointment that "DBS is still without a homegrown CEO".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Can I ask, Sir, whether Mr Leong still believes what he said, that naturalised Singapore Citizens should not hold top positions?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: When you are citizens, naturalised or homegrown, you are citizens.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I have raised the issue during my maiden speech because I was talking about the succession plan, about skills transfer, which is part of what we are going to discuss today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: About DBS, when he was appointed the current CEO, he was to still a foreigner.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Why was the chance not given to a homegrown Singaporean?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The bank should have had a succession plan that grooms Singaporeans to take over the job.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: That was what I was trying to drive at.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: None of that answers the point I made.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am quoting Mr Leong, he professed his deep disappointment when Mr Piyush Gupta was and is DBS CEO, during his maiden speech, that DBS is still without a homegrown CEO.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Meaning he was disappointed that it was Mr Gupta and not a homegrown CEO.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, let us not beat about the bush.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are not talking about succession plans here.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am just asking for an interpretation of Mr Leong's words: "DBS is still without a homegrown CEO".

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: What I was referring to was actually referring to the point he was appointed, not at this moment.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Okay, what I was referring to was at the point of appointment, the year of appointment, the point when he was appointed, he was still a foreigner.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But anyway, when I made that statement, I was not in any way, having Mr Piyush Gupta in mind.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I was just talking about the many CEOs that DBS had got; they never had a succession plan.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Being one of the top lawyers in Singapore, maybe the Law Minister could make some interpretations and ask me in that way.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Sorry, Sir, can I ask that the natural interpretation of a statement that "I have deep disappointment that DBS is still without a homegrown CEO".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At a time that a naturalised Singaporean is a CEO, the normal interpretation, whatever may be the workings of Mr Leong's mind, the normal interpretation would be that he is disappointed that it is Mr Gupta and not a homegrown Singaporean.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Would that not be the natural interpretation, Sir?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, would that be a fair interpretation of what you have said?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I did expressly say we leave aside whatever Mr Leong may have intended.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am simply asking whether what I have said is a fair interpretation, natural interpretation of what he said.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: How it is interpreted, I think, depends on who is listening to it.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I think the question is, whether it is fair for anyone in public to interpret it the way as Minister has put across.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Because that was what was said, I remembered, I think many of us would remember that.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: A few of us raised our eyebrows, because we were wondering what exactly you meant.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, would it be fair that that is how people would interpret it, notwithstanding whatever your intent might be?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Because what we say in Parliament matters, because that is how the public will perceive it.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Which is why the choice of words and phrases is important.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Would that be interpreted the way it has been put across by the Minister?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I would say some minority of the people might interpret it that way.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: All these issues that the Minister has raised are not related to the Motion today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Now he is going into the statements I made at my maiden speech.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, can I ask that we go back to the debate proper?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He meant 2020 and Mr Gupta was appointed in 2009.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think we can at least be honest with each other when the words are in black and white.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that is what the words of this Motion suggest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: None of this is to deny the legitimate concerns of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: None of this is to deny that there are people who have lost jobs, that there are people in their 40s and 50s, in particular, who are very concerned and that we have to do everything we can to help them and we have to stand by with them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I think race-baiting, nationality-baiting, putting down Motions and then coming to Parliament and saying, "well, I don't know, I don't have a view on the legal provisions", when your party has made it a point from day one to attack the legal provisions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Based on his speech, Sir, Mr Leong has painted such a dark picture of what is going on in Singapore, which really bears little resemblance to reality.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think we ought to do better by the people who have lost their jobs or who are underemployed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Is it that our Universities have produced graduates who cannot get jobs?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Over the past 10 years, nine in 10 graduates have been employed within six months after graduation, with starting salaries rising steadily.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think it is demeaning and dismissive of all the good people in our Universities and Polytechnics working hard to train our students, to say that they are producing people who cannot get employed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Would Singapore be consistently ranked highly on the UN's Human Development Index if Singaporean were oppressed in the labour market, if incomes have not risen and productivity stalled?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not perfect anywhere in the world and we have to consistently work to improve.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it is not the picture that Mr Leong is describing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I would say Mr Leong's views have been so completely distorted by his lack of understanding of CECA and his eagerness to attack Indians and CECA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I would say what his party and Mr Leong are doing is one of the worst types of political opportunism – using race as a bait.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The reason why we raised this Motion has nothing to do with race or xenophobia.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We will continue to debate on why we think the situation in Singapore is far worse than what the Government has presented to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At their core, both Motions concern the employability of the Singapore worker and PMETs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On this lived reality, fundamental questions that have come up in the last two decades include: where does the Singapore worker stand and what are his or her job prospects in our hub economy?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These questions will continue to come up more regularly than ever, as we move into a post-COVID-19 future.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My colleagues, Members He Ting Ru, Leon Perera, Gerald Giam and Jamus Lim, will also participate in this debate, with perspectives on both Motions and suggestions on the way forward.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, I will set out the Workers' Party's stand on free trade agreements (FTAs) and the India-Singapore Comprehensive Economic Cooperation Agreement (CECA).

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Second, I will iterate the public sentiments on job insecurity felt by Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Third, I will make a few suggestions on what should be done to alleviate the concerns of Singaporeans and ensure that the local/foreigner employment divide does not become a permanent fault line.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I note that the Minister for Manpower recently announced that anti-discrimination legislation will be introduced.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is one of the things that the Workers' Party has called for in its manifesto.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We believe that, for a few groups, such as the sandwiched class, workers who lack skills and lower-income Singaporeans, the opposite may well occur.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These groups may see depressed wages and fewer good job opportunities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government must ensure that Singaporeans are not discriminated against during their job search or at the workplace; that our education and training systems provide skills that are workplace-ready; and that skills are transferred to Singaporeans by foreign talent.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party also notes that there have been some elements in our society or perhaps from abroad that have used CECA as a dog-whistle, masquerading racism for genuine economic concerns.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party accepts that genuine economic concerns exist and that it is fair to raise concerns about them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, we abhor and denounce the racism and xenophobia that have become a part of the public narrative in some quarters.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some have gotten carried away resorting to loose and vile language online as an outlet for their frustration, something they would not do in person, or worse, extended this behaviour to the real world.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This can never be right, and must also be rejected and condemned.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I now move to the second part of my speech: public perceptions on job insecurity.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some of this has resulted in highly-charged conversations and incidents, both online and offline, even without the PSP's focus on this subject.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Immigration and the job prospects of locals are not only issues for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Globalisation has meant that the local populations of many countries, particularly advanced economies, share such concerns.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As a young nation, these feelings of insecurity and dislocation can shake our national cohesion, with the country being unrecognisable to the one many of us grew up in.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Job displacement is very emotionally jarring, especially when your HR department tells you that your role has been made redundant, only for you to later find out that your job has been rejigged and filled by a foreigner.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is also upsetting for Singaporeans when they learn that a foreigner has filled a job position for which a Singaporean is suitably qualified.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The emotions that we see today, while directed differently – towards Indians in some cases – have been directed at other communities in the past.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As noted by Minister for Manpower in his Ministerial Statement in July and I quote, "In the 2000s, we experienced a similar situation when the share of PRCs in our foreign workforce increased significantly, before tapering as China's growth took off.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Both then and now, the large numbers did not go unnoticed and created frictions within our communities." An important distinction between the vitriol directed against the PRC workers was that many of them were employed in low- to middle-income sectors, while there has been an acute focus on Indian professional workers today.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Today, the influx of employees of Indian ethnicity – not all of whom are from India, some are from the US and elsewhere – taking up competitively paying jobs has also activated emotions in a not small number of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some ask, "why can’t our people do those jobs?" After all, our students score so well on standardised tests.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Our much-vaunted education system should have put our workforce in a much better position.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is a subject Member Gerald Giam will speak more about in his speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Our sense of home is also affected when some EP and S Pass holders struggle to speak, let alone communicate in our workplace lingua franca – English – which represents a fundamental basis around which we organise public affairs in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When this happens, some Singaporeans stop feeling that we are one Singapore, all rowing in the same direction.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Those Singaporeans who ride on the opportunities created by a growing economy, or who are new immigrants doing well economically, can more readily accept the new status quo.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is a small price to pay and one can interpret the new reality as the price of progress and economic growth.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But for those who lose their jobs, see their incomes stagnate and fear for their children's prospects in a competitive Singapore – and these are commonly the sandwiched class and low-income Singaporeans – strong feelings are aroused, with many feeling that the playing field is uneven and the Government is slow to protect Singaporeans in their own land.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Ordinary Singaporeans do not delve into the intricacies of FTAs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Instead, they look around and come to conclusions based on what they perceive and experience.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If Singaporeans have not for years been seeing foreigners occupying well-paying jobs while qualified Singaporeans are unemployed or underemployed, we would not be talking about this today.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Over the last two decades, the effect of the Government's immigration and foreign talent policies has been so pervasive that former Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong covered the subject in his autobiography released only a few months ago, the second part of his autobiography, and I quote, “….take PRs, for example.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the years before, the numbers rose to 50,000, then 70,000 a year.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Since then, we have kept the numbers to around 30,000 PRs every year.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But even then, when you add the numbers up over the years, you will begin to feel the cumulative effects within the society and in daily living…" Then he goes on, " ...as a government, we needed to monitor the inflows of PRs and foreign workers as well as demographic changes more closely.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: No surprise that the people reacted in the way they did….the negative ground sentiment went beyond crowdedness.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It also encompassed perceived job competition from foreigners and preference of some companies for foreigners over Singaporeans.” Unquote.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I make five suggestions which I will elaborate on in turn.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The first suggestion: promoting and tracking the transfer of skills to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My first suggestion is that the Government should double down on how it monitors the success of skills transfer initiatives which are generously funded with taxpayers’ money.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Do skills transfer initiatives work and to what extent?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There has to be a reckoning, a balance sheet drawn up, where the successes and shortcomings of such initiatives to transfer skills to Singaporeans are properly accounted for and assessed across sectors and industries.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As each industry is tracked, reasons should be given why skills can or cannot be transferred.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It should also be clearly stated how these gaps are being plugged.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To ease the insecurity felt by the Singaporean worker or PMET, Mr Speaker, I restate a proposal raised by my colleague Member of Parliament Leon Perera, at the Committee of Supply debates in March.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: He suggested fixed-term EPs that are tied to the training of, or skills transfer to Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Currently, employers expect the EP of foreigners to be routinely renewed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This new category of work pass can be piloted in newer, disruptive industries, such as autonomous vehicles and AI, where there should be no reason why Singaporeans should not be the candidates of choice.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I hope MOM can look into such alternative proposals to secure tangible and positive outcomes for the Singapore worker or PMET by tracking skills transfer to our people.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government needs to track and solve underemployment.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Workers' Party Chair Ms Sylvia Lim, in her Committee of Supply speech in 2016, suggested that underemployment should be measured.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: She said that the Government was working closely with the ILO to develop suitable methodologies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We have yet to hear of the result of this work with the ILO.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Skill-related underemployment appears to be a reality affecting some of our workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These workers are not undertaking work for which they were trained, for example, engineers working as private hire drivers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some reskilling initiatives for these workers may be necessary to better align their foundational capabilities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Yet others may have made the transition out of choice.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Better measurement and regularly reporting of such underemployment would also enable Singaporeans to assess the Government’s efforts in this regard.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: An accurate understanding of skills-based underemployment would also have the knock-on effect of ensuring that the selection criteria for work pass applicants would be more accurately scoped.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This high level of accountability would do two things.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, such a committee would closely monitor the Government’s efforts by tracking unemployment and underemployment and job-related data, in addition to calling witnesses to give evidence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such a committee could also ensure that Singaporeans are getting a fair shake at the workplace and address concerns on job security and employment prospects of Singaporeans, including where training and skills upgrading opportunities lie.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Second, such a committee, by virtue of increased transparency and signature, compared to the current status quo, would minimise mischievous attempts at stoking xenophobia and unreasonable expectations of job protection regardless of competence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In other parliamentary standing democracies, such permanent Parliamentary Standing Select Committees on fundamental national matters that are appropriately resourced and supported by a strong secretariat, are par for the course.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is about time we had such a committee.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My fifth suggestion is that the Government needs to communicate more and much better than it has been doing till now on foreign employment.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And by this, I mean giving factual information so that public debate can be better informed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And this calls for a change of culture.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government should have started doing this years ago.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Quite clearly, this feeling of displacement and heightened sensitivity was the order of the day well before CECA entered the public lexicon in the way it has done over the last few months.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As early as August 2015, the Government fact-checking website, Factually, put out an article titled "Does CECA allow firms to hire Indian professionals in Singapore without valid work passes, or without adhering to fair employment guidelines?" The fact that such an article was needed and put out there suggests that the Government was fully aware that CECA was in danger of becoming a fault line many years ago.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In July, when Minister Ong Ye Kung and Minister Tan See Leng made their Ministerial Statements, I shared with this House that more than five years prior in 2016, my Parliamentary colleague, Workers' Party Member of Parliament Leon Perera, asked the then Minister for Manpower a straightforward Parliamentary Question on the number of Intra-Corporate Transferees (ICTs) through CECA.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Specifically, Mr Leon Perera asked how many ICTs from India had been approved under CECA from its first year to the latest year for which data was available.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Then Manpower Minister, Mr Lim Swee Say, replied, and I quote: “ICTs from any country, including India, would need to meet the Ministry’s work pass qualifying criteria to work in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The only difference is that ICTs from all countries are exempted from the advertisement requirement in our Jobs Bank.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government simply refused to answer a question of national relevance for which data was readily available.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can Singaporeans be blamed for assuming that the numbers must have been so huge that the Government saw fit not to reveal them?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To say that no other government reveals information to the granularity requested ignores the fact that Singapore is sui generis – of its own class.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How many other multi-racial hub-economies, immigrant-needy and in our unique geographical and demographic situation can we name?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government’s position on revealing ICT information seemed to change with Minister Tan See Leng’s speech in Parliament in July.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I quote: “We recognise that if misconceptions continue to spread, in spite of all our attempts to address them in so many other ways, even more damage will be done.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, I will share some numbers to address the misconceptions and allow for a meaningful engagement of the issue.” Unquote.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But I should point out that this was a number after the onset of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Quite obviously, there must have been a reduction of Indian nationals entering Singapore in 2020 compared to the previous years.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The ICT numbers that Mr Leon Perera asked for in 2016 would allow us to make a better assessment of the impact of ICTs under CECA compared to other FTAs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Revealing the numbers would promote a fact-based conversation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government’s initiative to release only the ICT figures for 2020, instead of placating CECA detractors, may actually have the opposite effect: it begs the question of what the figures for the earlier years were.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As far as the release of information from the Government is concerned, may I add that I read Minister Tan See Leng’s speech with an implicit caveat that the Government’s release of information on such matters would likely continue to be reactive and when it suits the Government, rather than proactive and when it suits the people.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would be delighted to stand corrected on this, but if I am right that the Government prefers to remain reactive, I would suggest to the Government that this approach can no longer hold water, nor should it, a point Member of Parliament He Ting Ru will make in her speech as well.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This desire to interrogate facts communicated by the Government will only increase, a point that I have shared previously in this House.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government must share detailed facts that matter to the public and not only consolidated facts that broadly support the Government’s position.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, since July, the Government has been using the digital notice boards located at every ground floor lift lobby in HDB blocks to launch an aggressive campaign to address the concerns surrounding CECA.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But where should Singaporeans go when they want more details?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, at what wage levels were these jobs?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This also invites the question of correlation and causation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is it possible that these are net jobs created by firms since 2005 that are in India through CECA?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If so, that does not necessarily mean that the advantages afforded by CECA created those jobs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such information is not provided in the displays.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I do not believe such additional information is a bridge too far, if the Government wants to clear the air.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Surely, it would not be too difficult to incorporate additional detailed information or have it available by way of a QR code in the digital notice display.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As intimated earlier, particularly for an issue as sensitive as this, the default position of the Government should be to release more information and explain the situation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government needs to reflect on its own omissions and resistance when it comes to providing data and information, and how it ought to take some responsibility for the groundswell of misinformation about CECA.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Many Singaporeans receive news and information through social media.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Much of the racist vitriol and xenophobia directed at Indians over CECA can be found online and from anonymous posts.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such realities make it more important to be forthcoming and aggressive in releasing information.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Separately, the foreigner-local issue is a fault line that can be exploited by external parties to compromise and destroy Singapore's psychological defences.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some bad actors, knowing that we rely on foreigners to address our fertility numbers and to ensure an economically vibrant and successful Singapore and are equally aware of how nation building is more challenging as a result for us, would have their own reasons, no doubt, to see Singapore fail.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Pitting one racial community against another is an easy way to do this.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is in our nation's interest that the Government anticipate, change tack and drive an active, not passive, conversation informed by facts rather than misinformation on jobs and the employment situation in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But the Government can bring this all together with key principals, such as MOM, SkillsFuture Singapore, Workforce Singapore and MTI, in an open and accountable manner.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In August last year, I said in this House, "Foreigners are important to Singapore and they help power our economy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Their presence gives Singapore a vitality that keeps us economically relevant and also provides jobs and opportunities to our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In my estimation, Sir, a more open and accountable approach by the Government to the dynamic employment situation is likely to alleviate the anxieties of foreign businesses.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They may well devote their intellectual capital to being a dedicated part of the solution, providing greater emphasis on in-house skills upgrading for all their workers, including Singaporeans, and become more conscious of their need to hire and train more locals.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Clerk will examine your proposed amendment for compliance with the Standing Orders, but meanwhile, please continue with your speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Under limb (c), to delete the words "supports" at the start of the sentence and to replace it with "calls for stronger".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Under limb (d), to delete the word "and".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Under limb (e), to include the word "and" at the end of the sentence after the semi-colon.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: My colleague, Member of Parliament He Ting Ru will propose an amendment to the Motion by Mr Leong Mun Wai in her speech.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It has been proposed as an amendment to the Motion standing in the name of the Minister for Finance as articulated by the Leader of the Opposition: At paragraph (c), to delete the word "supports" at the start of the sentence and to replace it with "calls for stronger".

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In comparison, the proportion of EP holders from China has remained stable, therefore, implying that the number of EP holders from China grew in tandem with the increase in the total number of EP holders, that is, an increase of 172% from 2005 to 2020 or an average growth rate of 7% per year.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister explained that the increase in migrant workers from India is a global trend.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Based on the figures provided in the Ministerial Statement, the number of international migrants from India increased from 10 million in 2000 to 18 million in 2020 or an average growth rate of 3% per year.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we assume a stable growth rate, then, for comparison purposes, the global growth of migrants from India over the period 2005 to 2020 would be 55%.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To summarise, the percentage growth of EP holders from India to Singapore is nearly seven times that of the global trend.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What then is the basis for claiming that the growth rate in Singapore is a reflection of global trend?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Minister provide examples of other countries that experienced similar growth to Singapore's?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans who experienced such changes in their daily lives naturally searched for answers, thus, putting CECA in the spotlight for it seems to offer an explanation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Ministers have explained that the clauses on manpower are still subject to our manpower policies and also pointed out that Japan and South Korea have similar agreements with India.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Japan and South Korea have natural barriers in the form of language, thereby making them less accessible as compared to Singapore.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Other English-speaking countries are presumably more cautious about signing such an agreement.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are all familiar with the effect of messaging in a commercial context.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two identical products, one with a good advertising campaign with a strong message and another with a weak message can have very different sales outcomes.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The same applies to other areas of life as well.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This clause on the movement of 127 professionals in an agreement signed by the governments of two countries sends a strong message of welcome to Indian professionals.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To ignore this effect and conclude that the presence or absence of this clause does not change anything since it is still subject to our manpower policies and criteria is being blinded to reality by technicalities.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Consider two different countries, one with whom we signed an agreement on the movement of labour and another without.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The agreement imposes an obligation to grant work permissions to nationals from the first country, provided our manpower policy requirements are met, but no such obligations exist with respect to nationals from the latter country.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, the agreement forms the first gate and our manpower policies form the second gate.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To address the concerns of Singaporeans, we need to go beyond CECA to our foreign manpower policies in general.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we impose only a minimum salary requirement and open up all jobs beyond that salary to fair competition globally, then, when our small population competes fairly with the huge global population for those jobs, mathematically speaking, we can expect a significant proportion of the jobs to go to foreigners.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As the world becomes more integrated, it will only get more so.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, while fair competition sounds ideal, it is neither tenable nor practical.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is especially so when many other developed countries impose a tighter level of control on foreign manpower, making it an unlevel playing field for Singaporeans competing for jobs globally.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is our view that tighter controls on foreign manpower are necessary.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government maintained that by opening up to global labour supply, we bring in more jobs for Singaporeans and that the foreign workforce provides a buffer for job losses for locals in times of an economic downturn, as in the recent pandemic.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My colleague Mr Leong Mun Wai has raised doubts over claims that our foreign manpower policies have created more jobs for locals and queried this number.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A portion of the 380,000 jobs could be due to reclassification, a result of Permanent Residents (PRs) becoming citizens and foreigners becoming PRs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, suppose 1,000 foreigners holding PME jobs applied for and became PRs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Then, these 1,000 jobs previously classified as foreign PME jobs became local PME jobs when they became PR.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is no increase in jobs but there is an increase of 1,000 local PME jobs and a decrease of 1,000 foreign PME jobs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Each year, we have about 20,000 new citizens on average.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Over 15 years, that is an increase of about 300,000.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The number of PRs has been stable in recent years.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, the total number of residents, comprising both citizens and PRs have increased by about 300,000.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As for the point on foreign labour providing a buffer for job losses in an economic downturn, our foreign workforce is large enough that even if we were to cut the foreign workforce significantly, the same buffer would still exist.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In addition, what is not addressed is underemployment, an area my colleague Mr Leong Mun Wai has spoken on earlier.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans who were displaced from their jobs may subsequently find employment that do not commensurate with their qualifications, skills or experience.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does the labour survey contain questions to identify and measure underemployment, apart from hours of work?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Economic theory tells us that when supply of labour increases, all else being equal, the price of labour, or wages, in other words, decreases.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: There are, of course, other factors affecting wages, with the supply of labour being one factor.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: But looking at the labour force growth and the real wage growth from 2009 to 2019, we see that in years of higher labour force growth, we tend to have lower real wage growth and vice versa.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: When labour force growth is lower, real wage growth is higher.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: The handout contains a scatter diagram showing the correlation and the regression line between labour force growth in Singapore and the real wage growth.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: The regression line is negatively sloped, which means that these two move in opposite directions.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: In other words, when labour supply growth goes up, real wage growth goes down.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: As we pursue economic growth, we should always bear in mind that economic growth is a means, not an end.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: A means to improve the lives of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: If our priority is economic growth, then, indeed, we should welcome all foreign direct investments, or FDIs, even if they should require a huge influx of foreign manpower.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: But if our priority is wage growth, then we would be more selective and focused in bringing in FDIs that benefit primarily the local workforce and does not require a high proportion of foreign manpower.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Trading economic growth for wage growth is a worthwhile exchange.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: My colleague Mr Leong Mun Wai has spoken extensively on manpower policies and proposals.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I will now touch on another area of concern and that is enforcement.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: There is a Chinese saying, "上有政策、下有对策", which, translated, means that while the government has policies, those who are governed have ways to deal with it or have counter measures.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: There have been several widely publicised cases of underpayment by employers.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: This is when employers make inflated claims of staff salaries to MOM or staff are paid full salaries but told to return a portion to the company in cash.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: This practice effectively circumvents minimum salary requirements for S Passes and EPs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: The reality is that this practice has been going on for years.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Mainly, because money is returned in cash, it is difficult to trace unless a thorough investigation is conducted or the employee reports the matter to MOM.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Recent calls by a Labour Member of Parliament and a Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP) Member of Parliament asking for greater teeth to be given to TAFEP for enforcement are also an indication that the current level of enforcement is not meeting our needs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Recently, a business executive who is tendering for various projects highlighted to me that this practice has created an uneven playing field.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: He is aggrieved that while he does the right thing to employ Singaporeans wherever possible and to report to authorities actual salaries paid, his competitors would use such tactics to lower their costs, and therefore, offer much lower prices to win tenders, with salary being a huge proportion of the cost for projects.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Organisations calling for tenders do not have incentives nor reasons to care whether or not such practices are going on in the company winning the tender.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: While we are trying to build a Singaporean Core in companies, should we not strengthen our policing of such practices?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: It would be ironic if companies that break the rules are rewarded over law-abiding ones.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: The increasingly common practice of subcontracting can also dilute the effectiveness of enforcement.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Separate companies can be set up to take over certain business functions and "take the fall" should they be discovered to have violated any manpower policies and regulations.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: There are also various other ways of circumventing the rules, for example, the use of phantom employees to meet quota requirements.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: We would, therefore, like to suggest two ways of strengthening enforcement.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: For example, to include audit requirements on successful tenderers to ensure compliance with manpower policies.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: This will provide incentives for companies to comply and also make evasion via subcontracting more difficult.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Currently, we license certain professions, for example, doctors, lawyers and real estate agents, amongst others.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: We impose on them certain standards of service and code of conduct.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Those who fail the standards can have their licence taken away.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: We can similarly license HRMs and task them to ensure compliance with manpower policies in their companies.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: A high turnover of HRMs will also be a tell-tale sign of trouble.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: To what extent do we take in foreign manpower?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Increasing labour supply leads to GDP growth, which increases Ministerial Salaries.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: However, the same labour supply increase depresses median wage growth.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Our current model can lead to a divergence in the movement of the salaries of political leaders and those of average Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: This is not a good basis on which to build trust.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: On the other hand, if Ministerial Salaries are pegged to the median wage, it sends convincingly the message that the political leaders and Singaporeans at large are on the same boat, more so than any words can.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Today, representatives from various parties talk about the importance of a Singaporean Core.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: As the saying goes, what gets measured gets done.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I would also like to take this opportunity to respond to some of the points that were raised earlier by Minister Lawrence Wong and Minister K Shanmugam.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: On the issue of spreading misinformation about CECA, from what has been said, it seems that attempts to spread misinformation hinge on the use of words like "free flow of labour".

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: For most laypeople, such words are not taken so literally but merely seeks to imply easy access rather than the total absence of criteria.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: In our opinion, asserting that Singaporeans are not ready for a non-Chinese Prime Minister does greater damage to our decades of efforts to eradicate racism.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
