text: There are other quotes we can delve into if we wish to discuss this matter further but we would rather not open up old wounds and prefer to look forward and engage in a constructive debate on how to make things better.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: It is an area that deserves attention and a fuller discussion in the right spirit, one which is empathetic and cooperative, not adversarial.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Minister Lawrence Wong gave an example of an Indian Singaporean who feels that debating about CECA is affecting his job search.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: If foreign manpower is tightened, he will find his employment prospects much improved.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I am an employer myself and I have been reading resumes for 20 years.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Recently, I have seen the trend of Singapore Citizenship status gaining greater prominence in resumes, not just in the resumes of Indian Singaporeans but also Chinese Singaporeans and Malay Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: If more Singaporeans feel that their citizenship improves their job chances, is that not a good development?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 5.35 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 5.16 pm until 5.35 pm.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am concerned about some of the points and assertions made by hon Member Mr Leong Mun Wai earlier.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am not sure whether Mr Leong is aware of the ground sentiments on this both from employers and workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: My union leaders have shared with me, to handle this raising in a carefully considered manner.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Each time the S Pass rates, which apply to foreigners, are raised, Singaporeans who are working alongside these pass holders and doing the same job, may not always get the immediate percentage increases at the same time, which is why it has to be done incrementally and carefully in a considered manner.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Second, let me also state that we also have a significant number of S Pass and EP holders in the healthcare and essential services sectors, looking after all of us and fighting alongside us in this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Many of them are my fellow union members as well.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: A suggested sharp curb of S Passes and EPs in these sectors as well as in many of these essential services must also be handled with care.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I hope Mr Leong is aware Singaporeans also marry foreigners and apply permanent residency for them.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Member Ms Hazel Poa earlier suggested that we should squeeze out more foreigners, create an even tighter labour market, and this will result in median wages going up.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I think this may be a too simplistic analysis.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Tighter labour market alone, by removing all foreign PMETs, does not necessarily result in higher median wages.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We agree and support our national operating philosophy to grow the cake so that we have a bigger slice and piece all around.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In the same vein, we value and support tripartism, inclusive growth and working together with the Government to ensure we continue to strengthen the Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I have been a strong advocate of strengthening the Singaporean Core and robust policies in this space since 2011, just like many of my fellow Labour Members of Parliament and PAP Members of Parliament in this House.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: And I am heartened that in my past 10 years of lobbying, many of these measures from advisories, guidelines, policies, programmes, regulations, have been put in place by MOM, with strong support of our tripartite partners and even our economic agencies such as the Monetary Authority of Singapore and the Economic Development Board to better protect and support our Singaporean workforce and provide them with a fair and level playing field in the job market.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I, therefore, disagree with hon Member Mr Leong Mun Wai's Motion, which suggests no concrete action has been taken.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: PMEs are most concerned with the lack of job security amidst this outlook, and their need for more support in employment and training opportunities.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is especially so as the Singapore economy continues to experience ripple effects and challenges of the COVID-19 situation and other factors like technological advances and digitalisation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: These challenges seem to impact our mature PMEs aged between 40 and 60 more, as they attributed their age as the key reason for their plight.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Mature PMEs have voiced concerns about displacement, disruption and the issue of competition in a globalised and fast-changing economy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In the converse, I also hear of positive sharing of human resource (HR) practitioners and employers taking great pains and significant efforts to convince their overseas headquarters to consider and recruit Singaporeans for positions in the region and in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I sincerely thank these HR practitioners and enlightened employers for believing in Singaporeans and doing their part to ensure that Singaporeans have a fair chance and shot at job opportunities.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In our engagements, our PMEs understand the need for a foreign workforce to complement the local workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They do not advocate the closing of borders to foreigners, but they want resolute actions taken against employers who are recalcitrant in their hiring policies, to protect our locals from discrimination.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They also hope to pick up the in-demand skills to take on the new jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The reason why some of our workers experience discrimination is not due to foreign competition, but due to a small proportion of egregious companies and employers who are out to exploit the system.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: While we take cognisance that many measures and policies, including the Tripartite Guidelines on Fair Employment Practices (TGFEP), the Fair Consideration Framework (FCF), Triple Weak Scrutiny, tightening of requirements for S Pass and EPs, including the formation of the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP) and so on, had been put in place over the years to minimise unfair hiring and workplace practices.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am glad to know that we are constantly asking ourselves what more needs to be done to weed out the small proportion of egregious companies out to exploit the system.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We need to look at ways to ensure that local PMEs receive fair opportunities and treatment while maintaining competitiveness in the economy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: These are big and bold moves, and I think it is important for us to spend time engaging the tripartite partners and stakeholders before implementation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Many union members, workers and PMEs I have spoken to are heartened by the announcements and acknowledged that these are the right steps taken to punish those errant employers and correct discriminative hiring policies and practices.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They are positive that this will send a clear message against workplace discrimination and eradicate unfair hiring practices.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Beyond legislation, we will need to continuously raise HR standards, to further enhance our HR practices and capabilities so that practices and processes are more transparent.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: HR practitioners, especially those in the recruitment functions, play a vital role in ensuring that the companies adhere to the employment legislation and regulations to improve compliance with fair employment practices.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They are also the advocates for the recruitment of Singaporeans in positions within their companies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: These are suggestions we have raised in the past many years and I am glad the Leader of the Opposition has also weighed in on this; and third, strengthening TAFEP to take decisive action against errant employers who pay lip service to the Fair Consideration Framework (FCF).

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: For a start, employers and businesses can partner NTUC and the Labour Movement in this journey.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In this age of disruption, digitalisation, transformation and the next normal, the tripartite partners need to stand even more united together to support, enable and ensure our workers stay ready, relevant and resilient: ready with the new skills, relevant to the new jobs and resilient to the new changes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is so that we can better weather any storms and pivot and transform when curved balls are hurled at us.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This will ensure Singaporeans stay employed and employable and their lives and likelihoods are secure and improved.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Immigration is a topic that is complex and sensitive, and we must, as a society – together with the Government – learn to have difficult conversations with each other without vilifying those who may have a different opinion from ours.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Too often do we hear cries of "xenophobia" and "racism" being thrown at those of us who may raise, often legitimate, concerns about the changing nature of our social fabric or the strain on our labour markets.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And on the other hand, those who try to speak up in defence of greater international movement of labour and trade are labelled as sell-outs and as "opening the floodgates" at the expense of hardworking Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This polarising approach is neither healthy nor productive, and I believe all of us must take a more nuanced and open-minded approach.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And immigration has been a fundamental part of our story for a very long time, from our founding as a free port in the 1800s to our transformation into a modern city in the 1980s.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Immigrants have and will always continue to shape our story.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We are the country we are today only because of our embrace of diversity and different histories, and this has to continue.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, for most of our pre-Independence history, immigration exceeded natural births.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After Independence, the Government first tightened immigration, then implemented a policy that uses migrants to fulfil a certain role in our labour force as one of the economic tools to drive the growth of our economy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I do not think that many will deny that this is a complex and difficult balance to get right.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is because the consequences of immigration are often felt very personally by individuals.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These changes in the make-up of our society cut at our very daily experience: who we see in our communities every day, the languages we hear around us and the sheer numbers of "others" we have to share our already crowded public spaces with.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Above all, the perception of the impact of immigration on jobs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is especially against the backdrop of unprecedented disruption caused by the shift to, amongst others, digitalisation, Industry 4.0 and a re-balanced normal, all of which have been exacerbated by COVID-19.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: On the other hand, the promise is that immigrants bring skills and a diversity of experiences, and often take up the slack in our labour markets.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, these benefits brought about by our foreign manpower policy tend to accrue more generally and are less directly experienced by individuals.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The argument that more trade, more foreign workers and more enterprise equals better and more jobs for Singaporeans is less visible and is not always immediately evident.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Tensions are felt when this "grand bargain" is not one that all Singaporeans have bought into.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This could be especially hard to bridge because many come to the debate with views that are seen through a personal lens, one that could bring biases due to personal life experiences, which would, in turn, lead to a very generalised view over our foreign manpower and immigration policies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And citizens may thus approach the matter without the required nuance or balance that academics or policymakers have the luxury to adopt.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our citizens are, after all, still feeling our way through how to respectfully debate such sensitive topics.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is hardly right then that we dismiss all these views and concerns as narrow-minded and xenophobic.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The challenge to citizens to accept and accommodate more people into our communities, with the different histories, languages, accents, ways of life and cultures they bring is not always an easy one for a society to accept and it is imperative on all of us to play an active role to manage and mitigate any potential fall-out.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, we have seen how our public debate around immigration and foreign manpower has changed over the last decade.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, we must be mindful of how world events can shape the conversation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It has also been pointed out that the current era we are living in has been an unprecedented one which became hyper-globalised, with its roots in the 1980s, when Reaganism and Thatcherism took off.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Too easily have immigration and migrants become convenient bogeymen, just like CECA and our FTAs appear to have done, often against all data that suggest otherwise.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Singapore is vulnerable to such dangerous sentiments, and the shocks caused by COVID-19 and the anxieties wrought by a changed world only add to the fears of our people and need to be addressed through more sensitive policies and engagement with the populace.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Now, more than ever, there needs to be humility in the approach taken by our leaders to such matters, and the listening ear of the Government needs to be attuned to and prod at the genuine concerns behind why some of us feel the way we do so strongly; sometimes, in the face of endless explanations that our assumptions or understanding of these policies and FTAs are flawed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Rather than immediately take issue with the speaker, we could understand that lived realities on the ground could be very different to ours and we should pay attention to whether these views and experiences could reveal potential blind spots in the implementation of our policies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must also remember that widening inequality is as dangerous as any threats to our economy, as this only drives fears relating to the quality and quantity of the jobs available to Singaporeans, and can lead to anger and resentment against any incomers who are perceived to be better off and to have taken our rice bowls.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Widening inequality thus leads to increasingly polarised politics, which has a certain irony, as data suggest that it is technological advances, which are, in turn, exacerbated by the failure of politics and Government policies to address these trends, rather than globalisation trends, that drive how equal a society is.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Having said all of this, what else can we do to address the concerns and tensions highlighted above?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In order to better understand one another, much effort needs to be expended by both groups, immigrants and citizens alike, in order to have these immigrants properly integrated and accepted into society.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There needs to be mutual understanding, tolerance and, finally, meaningful relationships between these two groups to minimise the pitfalls associated with "the other" and also make real the benefits and increased richness to community life that our migrants can bring to our country.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I think this approach needs to equally apply to incomers who choose to sink roots and take up a pink IC, and those who may be here on a more temporary basis.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Judging by the recent episodes that have come to our national consciousness, both online and off, towards foreigners, this would suggest that we need to redouble our efforts in bridging any gaps that remain between the groups.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How can we, together, in a way that is accepted by both sides, come up with a common core set of values that each of us respects, that would bind us together, to lessen any mistrust and negative feelings that may be currently amplified by uncertain economic times and the fear for one’s livelihoods?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I do not think this is something that Government leaders and associated bodies, such as the People’s Association, should ram down the throats of a skeptical populace.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps what is lacking is the buy-in from both sides that it is not only important for Singaporeans to adapt to having "foreigners" in our midst, but that our foreign friends must also play their part in wanting to integrate into the communities they are in.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Efforts need to be made to learn the norms within Singapore society, whether it is how we "chope" our tables or the inclination to queue wherever we go.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This does not mean losing the richness of the culture or practices that come with one’s history; Singapore will continue to embrace diversity as being at our centre.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, I do see examples of some immigrants reaching out to us as we conduct our ground work and expressing their desire to volunteer, to work with us and give back to the communities that they live in.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is heartening, especially when we note that they do not do so because they are after priority queue numbers for school places for their children or some other benefit, but because they truly believe in doing something to further the communal spirit that should overcome differences in our backgrounds.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Just as the law comes down hard against those who make offensive and aggressive gestures against foreigners or those from different backgrounds, we also need to ensure that Singaporeans do not face discrimination at the workplace and I hope that the welcomed but long overdue anti-discrimination legislation announced will be strong and robust enough to achieve this.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While the Government may have reasons for doing so, the best medicine against misinformation, cynicism and resentment is cold, hard data, and to build a transparent culture around the data relating to our policies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We also need to understand that residents who are married to foreigners or who have foreign family members are often left wondering and speculating about why their family member's application for Long-Term Visit Pass (LTVP), permanent residency or citizenship was rejected and what they could do to change the outcome.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: They would naturally compare this against the number of immigrants moving into the neighbourhood who are granted the immigrant status that they have been applying for – some for decades – sometimes without any ostensible familial ties to Singapore Citizens.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Is it any wonder that resentment would build up?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A proactive, transparent and data-driven approach to the conversation around foreigners might not convince every cynic but it would go a long way to quieten any unfounded claims, leave less room for conspiracy theories to flourish and give short shrift to those who seek to sow discord amongst us and seek bogeyman, a prime example of which would be CECA and FTAs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: (In Mandarin):  :  Mr Speaker, Sir, while the Motion today is about jobs for Singaporeans, this issue cannot be divorced from immigration and foreign workers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Such discussions will inevitably stir up strong reactions in today’s Singapore society.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Real concerns from some Singaporeans may well be seen as xenophobic or even discriminatory.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I think a few points can serve as starting points for the discussions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, we must acknowledge that with globalisation, Singapore, like many other countries, faces the problems of widening income gap and rising social tensions in tandem.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Second, these phenomena have, indeed, intensified the friction between the local and foreign workers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The key lies in whether Singaporeans, foreign workers and even the authorities are making an effort to integrate them into the society.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Faced with challenges brought about by globalisation, we must cast aside our prejudices and discrimination, especially in the workplace.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If we do not face these negative sentiments squarely, misunderstandings may well become deeper.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In addition, the authorities and decision-makers should be more proactive in information disclosure, based on the principle of information transparency, so that we can engage in realistic discussions, avoid misunderstandings from happening or deepening and prevent social tensions from escalating unnecessarily.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: (In English): To conclude, immigration and foreign manpower have been heated issues in Singapore for many, many years.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: CECA and FTAs are but the latest iterations of the debate.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is a difficult, complicated topic and an issue that many other nations continue to struggle with.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must, therefore, create a strong ecosystem for conversation, interaction and disagreement on the topics at hand.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must say no to a continued top-down approach to immigration where we are told what is good for us.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The danger is that, over time, resentment continues to build, and anti-immigrant sentiment spills over into nasty incidents where there is a heavy element of racism and xenophobia that also affect our Singaporeans as well, such as the unfortunate events that we have seen in recent months.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I hope the Government will take this as an opportunity to rethink the way these topics have been managed and discussed so far and, instead, lean more into enabling conversations on the ground to change hearts and minds rather than continue to debate what is best for Singaporeans and dictate our story for us.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As in any negotiation, we give something away to get something back.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Singapore has import duties on hardly any categories of physical goods.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, it is vital that the Government engages our SMEs when negotiating FTAs and FTA reviews.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I raised this at MTI's Committee of Supply (COS) in March 2020 and through a Parliamentary Question in March 2017.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The reply stated that there were roundtables and engagements conducted but numbers were not given.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Anecdotally, some SMEs on the ground do not feel that their views factor substantially into FTA negotiations, which, they perceive, may be conducted more from the perspective of creating incentives for MNCs to hub in Singapore to invest abroad.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I believe more can be done to gather feedback from SMEs to bring into FTA negotiations, something countries like New Zealand, when defending its dairy industry in the TPP negotiations, for example, seem adept at.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many SMEs do not fully utilise FTAs when they go abroad, for reasons that range from lack of awareness to lack of administrative bandwidth.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: More can be done to make these FTA benefits visible and usable by our local firms, for instance, the idea of a one-stop whole-of-Government portal, which could allow SMEs to transact with the Government and utilise Government schemes that I have spoken about in this House in the past.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such a portal could be used to allow SMEs to gain visibility on FTA benefits in different countries and enable them to transact to realise those benefits online.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: At this stage, Sir, I declare my interest as the CEO of an international research consultancy that conducts studies related to FTAs and SME development, among other topics.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It was widely recognised that they play a useful role.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The same is not true of every country in the world.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Singapore's attitude towards the presence of foreigners and fixed-term stays and those who choose to make Singapore their permanent home used to be more liberal to my mind than that you see in some Asian countries I can think of.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: That culture was shaped perhaps by around 200 years of history as a free port and open trading economy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The sense then was that the rising tide of liberal economics would lift all boats.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There is widespread anxiety, frustration and angst about the role of foreigners in the economy, as all the Motions put forth in this House today acknowledge to some degree.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I want to share, Sir, two stories about how these things came home to me.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, she is frustrated at the curbs on foreign manpower and, asked that if I knew of Singaporeans who wanted to do such jobs, could I give her a list of their names.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This current mood is very different from the sense people had in the 1970s and 1980s, with foreign investments from the US, Europe and Japan.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To my mind, back then, there was a palpable sense that skills and know-how were being transferred by foreign companies and foreigners to locals through in-house training and foreign-Singapore joint training institutes, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, a deficit in transparency, the third T; there is angst about why foreigners seemed to leapfrog Singaporeans in some contexts in spite of our much-vaunted education system, even though those foreigners sometimes come from countries with less recognised education systems.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I should say that a transparency deficit is also felt by another group – local business owners.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: They wrestle with the issue of hiring talent and often say that Singaporeans do not want to do trades jobs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, why is the supply of foreigners for those jobs being curbed?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I am glad that the Government is now moving in this direction.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This differs from the current EP system, where many employees assume that they can renew their EPs and there is no assumption that the EPs would definitely not be renewed as a default.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As for the antidote to the transparency deficit, the key is not just more public dialogues and communication between Government and citizens, vital though that is; the key is to set out long-term goals and clear policies to advance those goals.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One major area where this angst is being felt is when it comes to education.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans do not understand why the Government keeps praising our education system but, in some employment contexts, foreigners seem to dominate or have a large share of the better-paying jobs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Has our education system groomed us with the wrong skills and attributes?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My parliamentary colleague, Mr Gerald Giam, will elaborate on what needs to be done on that front.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For the remainder of my speech, I will speak about two areas of Government employment policy where the public, I sense, feels angst from a lack of transparency and whether the system is working in their best interests.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And these two areas actually map onto the two anecdotes that I shared earlier.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I shall call this the numerical multiplier argument.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I will call this the trades jobs problem.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If I were to summarise it at the risk of oversimplification, it is the view that we do not have enough Singaporeans and not of the right skills and talent to do all the cutting-edge economic activities we want to do as a global hub city.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, we need to import foreign talent and, if we do that well, this creates good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But if foreigners account for a large share of the better-paid jobs, it is still okay because Singaporeans are in good jobs that they might not have if the foreigners were not here.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, Singaporeans are absolutely better off, even if, sometimes, they may feel relatively worse off in the employment hierarchy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Or to put it another way, this argument is saying if Singaporeans want to always hog all the better-paying jobs, we will end up poorer in purchasing power terms.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This argument stands, by the way, on solid ground in the field of political philosophy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It reminds me of the Rawlsian theory of justice I studied as an undergraduate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: According to the philosopher, John Rawls, in a seminal work "A Theory of Justice", inequality could be justified if that inequality causes the least well-off person in a society to become better off in absolute terms.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Honestly, Sir, there is much to be said for the numerical multiplier thesis and it can be found as the subtext to employment policies in many countries and cities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But to delve deeper into the empirical reality, what is of concern to many Singaporeans about this argument are a few things.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One is the pathway to skills transfer, another is fair employment practices in a foreigner-heavy workplace.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But there are deeper and more subtle problems with the numerical multiplier argument.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Or I should not say problems; maybe questions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Initial endowments of resources, like skills, do weigh heavily on ultimate outcomes downstream.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Being very reliant on foreign labour also means that we are vulnerable to global events that may make these foreigners less willing to come and work here one day.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And that day may not come so soon, but it could come in our children's time, in our grandchildren's time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, how do we get our workforce profile towards a ratio of foreigners and locals that would better address these issues?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: By "ahead of demand", I mean to attract Singaporeans to train for skills in industries that are nascent, that are newly emerging, confident that the Government is working with investors to groom and build those industries using all the tools in the toolkit.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: JTC and EDB building physical infrastructure ahead of demand was a key factor in our industrial success in the 1960s.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The key to our Industry 4.0 success in the 21st century would be catalysing soft infrastructure, that is, skills, ahead of demand.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, Mr Speaker, Sir, I want to speak about trades jobs, that it is said, Singaporeans do not want.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: By "trades jobs", I mean carpenters, plumbers, highly-skilled construction workmen and supervisors, air-conditioner technicians and so on and so forth.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There is a huge transparency deficit here with our local business owners.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In the decades after Independence, many of these trades jobs were done by Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But now, many SME owners believe that Singaporeans simply do not want such jobs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If this is true, it could be due to the overall growth of the economy and population base coupled with our low total fertility rate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It could also be due to the expansion of other more attractive jobs in other sectors.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There is also the fact that many of our Polytechnic and ITE graduates as well as older PMETs are going into gig work rather than a trade.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many SME owners are adamant that even if they paid more for these jobs, Singaporeans do not want to do them.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One of them told me that when he attends construction training courses as a guest speaker, the only Singaporean trainees there are those with white hair.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Yet, on the other hand, from a totally opposite perspective, another older gentleman I met on a market walkabout said that he was gainfully employed in the construction industry as a supervisor in his 20s and 30s.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But now, all the jobs in this line have gone to foreigners.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And even though he is willing to take a 50% pay cut from his last drawn construction industry pay, he cannot get a job.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, he became a private hire car driver.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To move more Singaporeans into trades job sustainably needs us to go beyond quotas to tackle a few things deeply.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I am not saying that these ideas are not already being looked at or have not been attempted.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But, clearly, the results are not yet there and we are far away from success in outcomes rather than just success in efforts.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We do need to accept that prices have to rise as a result to ensure that businesses can survive.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, Workers' Party has argued before, with the right policies, there is no reason why we cannot attain developed country productivity in trades jobs to justify higher pay for those jobs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, investigate and fix negative non-wage characteristics of these trades shops.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, do employers provide adequate equipment to ameliorate the physical downsides of such jobs, like proper gloves, boots, tools?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Are trades jobs persons given proper break times and reasonable expectations on hours and working at short notice?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As I argued in this House a few months ago, no Singaporean will take a trades job at high pay if he or she knows that they will be treated with disrespect and have to put up with awful conditions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: They may prefer to do gig work or a lowly-paid office job that attracts less pay with all the attendant dangers of obsolescence from technology that those kinds of jobs bring.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Fourthly, we need to enhance the prestige and standing of trades jobs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I do not have the luxury of time to elaborate on this particular point during this speech, but more can be done to try to shift expectations and attitudes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is worth bearing in mind that trades jobs are highly respected in many countries around the world.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I think continental European countries and Japan are examples that spring to mind.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This was a theme of a speech made by my party Chair Ms Sylvia Lim some years ago.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some gig jobs face long-term risk from technology.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Can we shift local Singaporeans from some of these at-risk gig jobs to redesigned, revamped trades jobs?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In other developed countries, one often finds a more relaxed and liberal attitude towards foreign talent in big cities like London and New York, where even those in relatively lower-income trades jobs, like taxi drivers and restaurant staff, have often benefited from the rising tide that foreigners contribute to.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But go to the towns and cities where living standards have stagnated or nosedived, like some of the opioid-ravaged midwestern towns in the US, and you sometimes find bitterness towards foreigners and the cancer of racism, together with the far-right, nativist politics that go along with that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: With the right policies, goals and mindsets, Sir, I believe Singapore can return to what it was in a previous era: a country of citizens who are confident enough about their present and their future to welcome foreign talent that genuinely complements our strengths and adds value to our lives.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The success, livelihoods and well-being of millions of our fellow Singaporeans are at stake.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I had hoped that the PSP would share this understanding.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: First, the PSP continues to equivocate about FTAs, claiming it does not have enough information.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have explained that all foreigners have to meet the same work pass criteria.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The PSP has asked for data on ICTs over the years because the data cited was for 2020 – a crisis year.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We did not go into these details further because the trends were similar.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But since the PSP persists in this line of inquiry, here are the numbers over the last five years.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, I would ask the PSP again, what further information does it need?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Given the racial undertones on this issue, and this is acknowledged by all Members of the House, the PSP's equivocation is not only misleading but is also dangerous.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Second, the PSP has fielded a slew of data requests via Parliamentary Questions (PQs) and it has made a sweeping statement that there is no credibility in any of our statements because we have not released all of the data it has asked for.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It has equivocated that it cannot provide answers because it has no information.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: When it comes to data on our local workforce, we publish it regularly at a high level of granularity and this is in line with international standards.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But it seems the PSP is not aware of this.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In the 26 July Parliamentary sitting, the PSP filed a PQ asking for the annual breakdown numbers of local PMEs from 2005 to 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Parliamentary rules made it clear that a PQ should not ask for information that is already publicly available.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Notably, I have not heard the PSP use any of the data we have provided in its arguments.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And instead of being bogged down by these unhelpful distractions, I want to speak about the anxieties of Singaporeans, workers and business owners alike.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The way to address Singaporeans’ anxieties about jobs and competition in a fast-changing economy, is to continue to invest heavily in developing our local workforce and ensure that foreigners complement, rather than displace, our locals.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Minister Lawrence Wong has already shared some important perspectives on our strategy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I will share some of the facts and data that are relevant.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The PSP fixates on the increase in the number of foreign PMETs to argue that locals have been displaced and lost out.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It has painted a picture of widespread displacement based on the anecdotes it has heard.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: MOM publishes this data regularly at fine granularity but the PSP has not made any mention of this.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, let me walk you through the numbers.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The PSP harps on the number of foreign PMETs.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But the number of local PMET jobs, which is depicted by the blue bars, is significantly higher.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This is the case even if you look at some of the sub-sectors that hire more EPs – Finance, Infocomm and Professional Services.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This goes to show that competition between locals and foreigners is not a zero-sum game.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The PSP has asked whether most of the local job creation went to PRs rather than Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Some other data points we published should make it clear that Singaporeans have benefited.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: First, MOM regularly publishes unemployment rates for PRs and citizens.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The unemployment rate of citizens has remained stable and low.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, it cannot be the case that most of the employment growth went to PRs.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But, more fundamentally, as a society, I do not think we should be drawing lines between Singapore Citizens and PRs.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Many of our PRs either share family ties with Singaporeans or have studied, worked or lived here for some time.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: They contribute to our strengths as a society and our economy.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Singapore is an immigrant nation and openness is one of our society's core strengths that have defined who we are.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Looking at the chart shown, outside of crises, it has generally remained at 3% or lower.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Few countries have achieved unemployment rates as low as this.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I think we are one of the lowest in the world, one of the bottom three lowest in terms of these statistics in the world.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Long-term unemployment rate, referring to those who were looking for a job for at least 25 weeks, or about six months, is even lower at below 1%.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The increase in foreign PMETs has not caused our unemployment rate to rise.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If every additional foreigner results in one less opportunity for a local, why are there still so many unfilled vacancies?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Surely, these vacancies should have long been filled.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It has risen from $4,600 in 2010 to $6,300 in 2020.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In real terms, it translates to a 21% increase.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In fact, the proportion of our workforce in PMET jobs is amongst the highest in the world at almost 60%, doubling up from 30% in the early 1990s.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This is a very different picture from the dire situation that the PSP has portrayed.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If you hear Mr Leong Mun Wai, you would have thought that it has been midnight in Singapore for the past 30 years.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Nevertheless, while the vast majority of local PMETs have experienced positive outcomes, we must not neglect the lived experiences of the minority who have not.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It is not just the PSP who talks to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I meet them, too, and I hear their concerns, and I feel their angst.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: One group, in particular, concerns me – our older local PMETs.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: They have contributed to society and they are still able and willing to work.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Yet, some amongst them have lost their jobs.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It feels like a part of their identity is lost.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Even for those who are still employed, seeing others around their age lose their jobs may cause them to be demoralised and feel anxious.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But I must point out that this is happening not because of increased competition from foreigners, but also from deeper, structural trends.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If you look at this chart, the unemployment rate amongst older local PMETs started diverging from the overall rate, from 2015 onwards.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I remember this year particularly well because it was the year I attended the World Economic Forum.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: At that time, big data was top of the agenda.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: That was the year that big data and machine learning hit the mass market very rapidly.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Companies were racing to build up digital teams.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It created new roles which required new skills sets, while disrupting some existing roles and skills.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Against this backdrop, our older PMETs faced competition, not so much from foreigners, but from technology and, possibly, also from younger Singaporeans who had the necessary skills.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We saw these trends happening and we rolled out SkillsFuture in January 2016.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We knew that lifelong learning had to become the norm, so that Singaporeans could pivot to new opportunities.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And we built on this foundation year after year.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But the Government's efforts are only half the story.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: What really makes the difference is the spirit of older Singaporeans, their willingness to remain open to new possibilities.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Take Mr Arnold Lim, who spent 25 years in the banking industry and was retrenched at the age of 50.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: After a year of effort to return to the banking industry, he decided to join PulseSecure, an IT firm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The learning curve was steep for him, given his lack of IT experience.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: PulseSecure hired him through the Web Developer Career Conversion Programme (CCP), which allowed him to pick up new technical skills and gain relevant on-the-job experience.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Lim subsequently took on additional IT certifications on his own accord.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In his own words, "After 50 is a new start for me." I have spoken at length about unemployment.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But various Members of the House have pointed out that this may not reveal the full picture of underemployment and asked if the Government is monitoring this.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: One is time-related, where the worker would like to work for longer hours but is unable to find a job that allows him to do so.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This is well-defined and, internationally, there are ways to measure this.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: MOM regularly tracks and publishes resident time-related underemployment and this can be found in MOM's Labour Force Survey.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The other type of underemployment is skills-related, when the worker believes that his current job does not fully utilise his skills.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This is more subjective and this is what I think a few Members have alluded to earlier on.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But this is more subjective as there is, as yet, no internationally accepted standard for measuring this.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: MOM is part of a working group led by the International Labour Organization, or ILO, to develop suitable methodologies to relate an individual's occupation to their skill and educational level.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: These are discussions involving professional labour market statisticians.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, while I appreciate the interest of Members for MOM to magically provide a KPI for skills-related underemployment, the fact that there is at the ILO a working group of statisticians studying how this should be measured, should highlight that this is not a simple matter.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In the meantime, we regularly track and publish the number of self-employed persons, or SEPs.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The graph here shows the share of our local workforce who are SEPs since 2010.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: They include private hire car drivers, taxi drivers, real estate agents and hawkers, who are not employed by a company.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Gig workers are defined as SEPs who use online matching platforms.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The top occupation of gig workers is private hire car drivers on online matching platforms like Grab or Gojek.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In response to a survey by MOM, 70% of them said they do this on a preferred basis because they would like the flexibility and also the freedom of time.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: More than 70% of their private hire car drivers have chosen to take up work via Grab because of the flexibility of time.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: For the 30% who wish to transit to regular employment, they can tap on our skills training and employment facilitation services, including career advisory counselling offered by WSG and e2i.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: As mentioned by Prime Minister Lee during the 2021 National Day Rally, MOM will form an advisory committee to propose recommendations to improve protection for this group.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Ultimately, the best thing we can do for our locals is to continually invest in them to help them adapt and compete.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But it seems the PSP would want us to take a more effortless route and simply target the 400,000 foreign PMETs they say are here.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In fact, as Mr Leong Mun Wai noted, the number of EP and S Pass holders has fallen to 350,000.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: How much lower does he want it to go?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Ms Hazel Poa has painted a simple narrative that if we keep labour supply tight, it will contribute to productivity improvements and a higher wage growth for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But at a certain point, a tight labour market can also lose us opportunities and the ability to internationalise.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This can cost us jobs and wage growth in the long run.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It is not such a simple linear relationship.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Let us focus instead on the PSP's policy suggestions.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Can the PSP explain how all of this will not dampen Singapore's attractiveness to foreign investors and cause poorer outcomes for the vast majority?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: As a small country that is devoid of any natural resources, there are severe consequences if we turn inwards, lose our lustre as a regional hub and cause companies to leave our shores and take the jobs with them.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I speak to many businesses, trade associations and chambers.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: A common thread in their feedback is the difficulty of finding enough locals with the right skills and this has hampered their expansion plans.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Some of them are giving up and turning to hiring foreigners based in their home country.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: After all, people can now work from anywhere.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If they decide to leave, we would not be talking about recouping tens of thousands of jobs but about losing more of them instead.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Members might also know that Singapore has already fallen from first to fifth in the Institute for Management Development's, or IMD's, 2021 World Competitiveness Ranking.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This was partly due to COVID-19 as our small economy was more affected by the global slowdown than larger ones.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In particular, we have slid in our openness towards global trade and talent in rankings regarding "attitudes towards globalisation", "availability of skilled labour" and "immigration laws preventing companies from hiring foreign labour".

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will say this plainly to Mr Leong Mun Wai.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: What he and his party spew, attacking CECA and FTAs and foreigners in general, has had an effect on IMD's assessment and on business sentiments, both here and overseas.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Investors watch and wonder how many other Singaporeans feel this way.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Has Singapore become less welcoming of foreign investments and of global talent?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Why do you think we are taking this issue so seriously?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In July, Minister Ong Ye Kung and I made Ministerial Statements.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We decided to confront Mr Leong Mun Wai openly.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In August, the Prime Minister addressed the issue again in his National Day Rally speech.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And now, in this debate, three Ministers have spoken thus far, myself for the second time.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Do Mr Leong Mun Wai and his party think Singapore will forever be attractive to investors?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Is there some magic in our water that draws global multinationals here and that all this happens spontaneously?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You have heard Minister Lawrence Wong recall how Mr Lee Kuan Yew went so far as to pay special attention to how the road leading from Changi Airport to the city looked.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Day in, day out, many Government agencies continue to work hard to make sure that we remain safe and attractive to investors so that they come here, they sink billions here, erect plants, labs, studios, facilities here, create jobs and livelihoods for Singaporeans, including our children, so that they can do jobs of the future and not of the past.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: As a result of this unremitting work over the last 60 years, Singapore remains a competitive economy, as proven by our pipeline of investments even during the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We cannot afford to take our economic competitiveness for granted.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The attitudes that PSP is promoting are detrimental to how others perceive our openness.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai, please, have a care.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I know that, by and large, Singaporeans are pragmatic and they understand that we need to remain open to global talents and stay connected.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Some of them feel frustrated when they see a foreigner being hired, though he may not be able to do the job as well as a Singaporean, or simply because he has links with the hiring manager.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: That is why when it comes to our foreign workforce policies, we constantly adjust them to ensure that foreigners complement, and not displace, our locals.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Yet, in spite of our work, the PSP continues to criticise our foreign workforce policies as being too lax.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: They characterised our "foreign talent policy" as a conduit for quick immigration and a source of cheap labour and claimed that the qualifying salaries of S Passes and EPs are too low.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai also laments that we do not have enough Singaporeans in leadership positions and elsewhere, he has suggested greater protection for top leadership roles.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: First, on Mr Leong Mun Wai's claim that our qualifying salaries are too low and that there is unfair wage competition.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I wonder whether Mr Leong is aware that the numbers he cited are the minimum qualifying salaries for EP and S Pass holders at the youngest ages.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Does he know that our qualifying salaries rise with age to maintain a level playing field for our mature PMETs?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Many businesses, including SMEs, are already crying out that they are not able to access the foreign PMETs that they need.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We listen to them, we engage them, we help them transform and we help them find suitable Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But, ultimately, we explain to them why we have to hold the line.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai has also repeated the point that foreign EP holders are cheaper to hire than locals because their employers do not make CPF contributions.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I have already clarified this point on 6 July but let me do so again.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The CPF is set aside for our retirement needs and it can also be used for housing.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Foreign PMETs are not working in Singapore on a permanent basis and we are not responsible for their retirement adequacy or their home ownership needs.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It does not make sense for us to extend the CPF coverage and benefits to them.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I think everyone in this House knows the interest rate that we pay on our CPF contributions.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Fundamentally, our CPF system is designed to benefit our resident workers, not to help attract or deter foreigners.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, how do we maintain a level playing field?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: When reviewing the qualifying salary to maintain a level playing field, we take into account the CPF contributions as part of the cost to employers.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Ms Hazel Poa also highlighted the issue of false salary declarations and kickbacks as ways for employers to get around our work pass framework.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: MOM takes firm measures to safeguard the integrity of the work pass framework.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The fact that Ms Hazel Poa is aware of this means she is also aware that MOM has been enforcing this and publicising our efforts to stamp out these illegal practices.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: At the same time, the PSP's solution is to raise the salary criteria for EP and S Pass holders significantly.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Does the PSP think that this underlying problem will get better with their suggestion?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This is easy enough for the Government to do.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, why do we not go down this route?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Because at the EP level, our primary focus is on regulating quality.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Suppose an employer has set aside $10,000 a month for a new EP hire, a levy of $1,200 effectively reduces his budget to $8,800.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This immediately narrows the pool of EP candidates from those willing to consider a salary of $10,000 and below to those willing to consider a salary of $8,800 and below.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: How would this benefit the employer or his Singaporean employees if the intention is to seek the best talents available?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We would also be sending contradictory signals if we say that we welcome high-calibre global professionals to Singapore on the one hand and impose a levy on them on the other.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, instead of a levy, we focus on regulating quality through the EP salary criterion and this sets a high bar that EP holders must reach to work in Singapore and it raises their quality over time.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The services sector is currently at 10%, down from 25%, and there are ongoing cuts still taking place in all the other sectors.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I have also explained why we do not set quotas at the EP level because there is fierce competition for global talent and worldwide shortages in areas, such as technology and digital skills.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And doing so would send the wrong signal that we are not welcoming to such talent.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Since the 2000s, MAS has been promoting this because there is a huge infrastructure opportunity in Asia in the yawning financing gap.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: However, working in this area requires significant expertise, given the complex risk profile of infrastructure projects.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In the early days, we did not have enough local talent to work in this area.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Global banks, especially Japanese and European Banks, were the most active players in the initial phase and had the talent and the expertise.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mizuho Bank was one such bank that chose to set up a project financing team in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Now, Singaporeans occupy 70% of a much larger office.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If we have imposed the quotas up front, I doubt this would have happened.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If PSP insists on the 30% quota, then I would like to ask, would you turn away a company that creates 69 high-end jobs for locals because it needs 31 foreigners from abroad?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If PSP's prevailing assumption is that less foreigners means more jobs for locals, what would stop it from lowering this quota further to 20% or 10% or 0%?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai had previously suggested that it is not good enough for Singaporeans to make up 70% of the workforce in the financial sector, but that it should be even higher at 80% or 90%.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In which case, how do we remain and maintain our status as an International Financial Centre?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Fourth, imposing a hard nationality cap of 10% within each firm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Once you stack up a 30% cap on top of another 10% cap, it becomes clear that Mr Leong Mun Wai's policy can only make the environment so hostile that very few foreign investors will consider Singapore when building any business.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: To use the example of Mizuho Bank, the effect of Mr Leong's proposal is to tell a Japanese bank that only 10% of their workers can be Japanese nationals.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Nevertheless, as I have shared in my 6 July Ministerial Statement, we understand the tensions that can arise when a foreign nationality dominates and we have levers today to address this.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Their work pass applications are scrutinised for potential discriminatory hiring and the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP) engages them.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And as I had also shared, we are exploring further refinements to our EP framework to help us achieve our objectives of a strong Singaporean Core complemented by a diverse foreign workforce.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Many companies have programmes in place to groom talent for leadership positions.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Their staff can participate in their Management Team and Beyond Fast Track programme, be rotated into positions globally and expand their skill sets.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: When companies first set up here, it is understandable that they will need to bring in many of their senior management to oversee the business here.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If we protect the top management jobs for Singaporeans alone and companies decide not to invest here because of that, we would lose good jobs for our locals and the opportunity for them to take on the higher level positions in the future would also diminish.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I worry that the PSP is calling for policies that are not only short-sighted but protectionist and this will do grave harm to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I would also like to address Mr Pritam Singh's idea of a time-limited EP to facilitate skills transfer.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I should point out to Mr Singh that no work pass is issued indefinitely.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: At the point of renewal, employers must meet our prevailing criteria.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The idea of a skills transfer requirement sounds good in theory but, in practice, it is not as straightforward to implement.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The process of skills transfer is rarely linear or one-to-one.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, I do not think it makes sense for MOM to be the judge to set a fixed duration and force employers to let go of experienced work pass holders once their fixed term is up.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I want to finally address our efforts to stamp out discrimination.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister Lawrence Wong touched on the anti-discrimination legislation earlier, but I would like to address the PSP's claim that because FCF was introduced in 2014, fair consideration for our locals was not a priority before that.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In 2002, we added the Code of Responsible Employment Practices.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In 2007, we issued the Tripartite Guidelines on Fair Employment Practices (TGFEP).

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In 2011, we enhanced the TGFEP to include guidelines on hiring and developing a Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We introduced the FCF watchlist in 2016, as a systematic framework for engaging firms, with outlier, workforce profiles and scrutinising them for potential discrimination.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In 2020, we strengthened the penalties against firms found to have discriminatory hiring practices.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Ensuring responsible and fair employment practices has always been our priority.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Members of the House, this is a major step, both philosophically and legally.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This will cover discrimination on the grounds of nationality, in addition to other kinds of discrimination covered by the TGFEP and it sends a clear signal that discrimination of any kind is not tolerated.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: When you consider all the policies we have put in place, it is quite clear that we are providing strong support for the employment of local PMETs.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Even Ms He Ting Ru has noticed and acknowledged our plans to legislate TAFEP guidelines.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Indeed, many companies tell us that they prefer to hire locals over foreigners, so long as they can find the skill sets here.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Even if there is initially a shortage of skills, many are willing to develop local talent to fill these roles.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: When it first started, it had to rely more heavily on global talent for specialised technical skills and more senior roles that required managing regional teams.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: However, PayPal committed to hire and train 150 Singaporeans across tech and business roles over three years.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I acknowledge: there will always be more work to be done.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I have said before in my past Statements that we are always a work-in-progress because we continue to refine and tweak and improve.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We will always continuously refine our policies to secure the well-being and the livelihoods of Singaporeans in a post-pandemic world.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But, Members of the House, we must not discard the principles that have worked well for us.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: (In Mandarin):   Recently, the President of the Singapore Chinese Chamber of Commerce and Industry, Mr Roland Ng, wrote in a Lianhe Zaobao column that, “The business community agrees with the Government that it is important to secure good employment opportunities and outcomes for locals.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: However, we also recognise the value of having high-quality foreign workers who can complement the local workforce, help boost the economy, and create a win-win situation.” I fully agree with Mr Roland Ng.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The key objective of Singapore's economic policy is to create good job opportunities for our people, thereby improving and uplifting the overall standard of living.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Government’s objective has not changed: we want to help Singaporeans fulfil their potential, seize opportunities, and improve productivity.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: As our economy grows and transforms, many businesses have brought in foreign professionals to complement the local workforce.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This has resulted in stiffer competition for local workers.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Some groups of workers would inevitably feel the pressure, particularly the mature PMETs.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: For example, the digitalisation and technological shifts have led to structural changes to the global economy.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Companies require their employees to be equipped with related skill sets, but these could be different from what our mature PMETs were trained in.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In addition, mature PMETs face competition not only from foreign workers in Singapore, but also younger Singaporeans who have received higher education.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: How should we face the challenges in today’s evolving and highly competitive world?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Confucius once said, "At the age of 50, you know what fate has in store for you".

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: As one approaches middle age, one would have gone through many ups and downs in life and acquired precious experiences along the way.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: At this age, one should be more adaptable to circumstances and not rigidly follow the rules, or be unwilling to consider new ideas.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Therefore, I urge everybody to continually upskill and reskill to adapt to new working environments.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Only then, can we build a better future for ourselves and our families.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Besides mature PMETs, Self-employed Persons (SEPs) also face tough challenges.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Famous Hong Kong singer Sam Hui has a classic song called, “Life is like chess”.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: A memorable line in the lyrics goes, "Looking ahead, life is like a game of chess.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I hope that our chess skills are comparable, and that we understand life through the art of the game." Indeed, life is like a chess game.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: When you are faced with an ever-changing situation, you will miss out on many good opportunities if you are indecisive.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: As for the economy and employment, the Government is actively driving business transformation, creating more jobs that are attractive to Singaporeans to ensure that we emerge stronger in the coming endemic phase.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: To become a winner, the key lies in everyone working together, laying a strong foundation, and seizing the opportunities.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Only by doing so can we achieve good outcomes for all.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The PSP has fielded a slew of data requests.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We have given you the number of foreign PMETs.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We have given you the number of ICTs over the past few years.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We have given you the number of local PMETs.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Data is regularly published on unemployment and time-related underemployment.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, the debate today is on whether CECA and other FTAs allow complete free flow.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And second, how do these impact on local employment?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This suggestion that you are not being given data is really a red herring.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Based on what I have shared today, I think reasonable Members would agree that our strategies have worked for the vast majority of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I have not based this argument on anecdotes or perceptions alone but on hard data and facts.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Nevertheless, the concerns of the minority are just as important to all of us.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We cannot assure today to every Singaporean that their jobs will always be protected.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We will work very, very, very hard to protect every Singaporean and ensure your employability.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai has presented us with one bleak and biased view: that of an anxious and fearful Singapore, whose instinctive reaction to challenges is to withdraw from the world.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I reject this view of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It does not define us and is not us.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And we are determined to fight any party wedded to racism and xenophobia, and a small-minded vision of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: With that, I support Minister Lawrence Wong’s Motion.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: One is PSP has never said we want a closed society or economy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We have just suggested policies that you disagreed with.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But today, we are happy that we are here, that all of us recognise that there is a problem.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But, of course, before I come to this debate, I know the problem is we cannot agree on the causes of the problem and the severity of the problem.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: As a result, our solutions will be very different.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, what the Minister has said just now, I would like to one, clarify that we have not said that we want a closed economy or society.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: How we maintain an open society, how we send the message to foreigners, it depends on how we Singaporeans get united and speak with one voice.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Now, we have two voices: one from the Government, one from PSP; and maybe the other alternative parties as well because we got the feedback from the ground.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, what we want, whatever you said, today we come here to realise that there is a problem and that means the past policies have some problems.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: You cannot just say, "Oh, we just continue with those policies".

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, that is why we are asking for a rebalance and I would want to explain to you a little bit more what rebalancing we are talking about.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, are you seeking clarifications or making another speech?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You will have a chance to round up later.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If you have clarifications for the Minister, please raise them.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Okay, then, I will direct one question first.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: First of all, you mentioned about the number of PMEs that were — jobs that were increased from 2005 to 2020.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Minister, what I have said is that the policies have actually produced some problems.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, we are here to discuss how to solve the problems.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I did not say I agree with your policies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
