text: In fact, one of the reasons why we differ on our assessment of the situation is because I think for some of the basic assumptions, there is a big difference.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Leong has said that PSP has never said that it wants a closed economy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But our point in all of our speeches, I do not think the PAP has ever suggested that we want an economy that is open to every and any foreigner.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have always maintained that we want to select the right talent to complement us.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, I said, let us not talk in abstractions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: What I had debated were your concrete suggestions and why it would not lead to the re-balancing that you asked for.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To your point on the differences in data cited, it is a matter of differences in timeframe.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Anyway, all of this data is published, Mr Leong.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And, again, if you cannot find it, we are happy to point you to it, just as we have pointed Ms Hazel Poa, to where to look for that information.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Sorry, Speaker, Sir, I still have one response.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And it is about PMETs and the EPs and S Passes.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is different time horizon and also different categorisation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: So, can I request for it to be made available to us in a different form?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: The Minister is still quoting 300,000 increase in local PME jobs, but you have not quite answered my question whether those figures include changes resulting from reclassification, as I have mentioned in my speech earlier.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: To clarify on my PQs asking for data that is already published, when I communicated with the Parliament Staff, I made it clear that I wanted to compare with some of the statistics that the Government has released; sometimes, as PMETs, sometimes as PMEs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: So, I said that they could either tell us which are the finer classifications that come under PMEs or PMETs or, alternatively, give me the total number of PMETs and PMEs because what is published goes into finer classifications.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For the first point, in terms of the reclassification, I do not have all the statistics here with me now.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But the majority, I think I have shared that on 6 July in my Ministerial Statement.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, I would urge Ms Hazel Poa not to drive this kind of separation and segregation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Because I really do not think it is healthy for all of us, particularly when at some stage in our not too distant past, all of us, our parents, maybe our grandparents were immigrants.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Okay, I would like to clarify that my intention is not to separate between those who are born in Singapore and those who are naturalised, but merely to understand which are really jobs created and which are really just, due to technicalities, they result in an increase in job but is actually not a real increase; it is just that the job holder's status is reclassified.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The majority of the jobs created went to Singaporeans who are born and bred here.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Ms Hazel Poa, do you want to pursue that?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Okay, you are unable to give a number?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Ms Hazel Poa, are you asking about Singaporeans, naturalised, born here or are you talking about —

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Actually, my intention is just to net off the effect of that job increase which is due to reclassification so that we get a better idea what really is the number of new jobs created.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Would you like to elaborate what do you mean by "reclassification of jobs"?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Okay, I have mentioned this in my speech earlier.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: So, let us say, for example, you have 1,000 PME jobs held by foreigners.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: And when these foreigners become PRs, because of the change in status, these 1,000 jobs are now classified under local PMEs —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, it is still the issue of Singaporean born, others and so on.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The unemployment rate of citizens has remained stable and low.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So it is not, and it cannot be the case that most of the employment growth went to PRs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: So, there is a drop in the PRs and then the new foreigners go in to fill up the PR numbers.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: So, as a whole, the number of citizens plus PRs actually increases.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: That base increases, and, therefore, leading to an increase in the number of local PME jobs purely due to reclassification, not job creation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I am not really even making a difference between citizens and PRs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I am just talking about local citizens plus PR.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, it is not like as if these PRs became naturalised Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This majority is Singaporeans who are born and bred here.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, for that majority under that category, the statistics do not include those who are not born here.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: The majority of the job increase or majority of the PME jobs are held by those born and bred in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I am quite surprised that Mr Leong maintains this position despite the clarifications that had been provided in the last Sitting about how free trade agreements like CECA work.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is common ground that Singaporeans have anxieties about jobs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As advisor to the Metal Industries Workers' Union, I have seen retrenchments take place and I have seen how businesses cope with difficulties.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The usual cause of retrenchments is usually business difficulties or restructuring.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This has nothing to do with free trade agreements.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the course of COVID-19, many industries have suffered as well, sectors like retail, F&B and tourism.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Even well-known names like Robinsons have folded during this period.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The sufferings of all these businesses have nothing to do with free trade agreements.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Global businesses are such that business cycles have become much smaller, there is a lot more volatility and people may need to change jobs because the world changes.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Typically, in situations where redundancies take place, the reality is that it is usually the foreigners who lose their jobs first as work passes are not renewed.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For those Singaporeans who need to be redeployed or reskilled, where industries are unionised, the unions come in to help.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, this is how we try to work with Singaporeans with job anxieties.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And right now, the job anxieties are only going to get more.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For those who retain jobs, especially in this current climate, there are many people who feel pressured working from home as well, because they fear potential redundancies.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Maybe the bosses do not know that they are working, so they work longer hours.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And I think all of this adds to Singaporeans' anxieties about jobs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As Members of this House, we have to be very clear what are the causes of anxieties.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What happens if there are situations where foreigners take Singaporeans' jobs?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And we have all heard anecdotal evidence of this.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: MOM has many levers that it does pull in these situations.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As a lawyer, I have dealt with many companies which have been on the wrong side of this and which have been investigated by MOM and against whom MOM takes actions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What do free trade agreements have to do with all this?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think it would help if people understood free trade agreements.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And it is clear that Mr Leong Mun Wai may not even have read the relevant provisions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The primary aim of free trade agreements is the removal of tariffs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Tariffs are taxes imposed on goods being traded.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Generally, the higher the tariffs, the less trade takes place as the cost of trading goes up.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Reduction of tariffs encourages trade by reducing transaction costs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Free trade agreements also usually have provisions to facilitate the transfer of services to flow freely between countries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Consumers and businesses will, therefore, have choices to purchase goods and services from all over the world while producers of services can, likewise, look at more countries for a potential market place.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Related to the aim of improving businesses between countries, there are also bilateral and multilateral investment agreements.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Typically, these are a different species of agreements.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These agreements usually permit countries to invest in each other and the host country would provide protections for such investments such as not to expropriate them.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For those of you who have read about a more tumultuous past, there are many situations where foreign investors go into a country, and, because of political turmoil, those investments may get expropriated.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So multilateral investment treaties provide that kind of minimum protection.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: They have clauses that provide Most-Favoured Nation (MFN) status, which means that we will give this country the same provisions it gives to any other trading country.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It has some clauses that protect investments and these include protections against expropriation in Chapter 6.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Let us come to Chapter 9 of CECA.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is where Mr Leong Mun Wai, I think, has found the language on free movement of persons.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is primarily to facilitate people wishing to visit one country or another for business purposes.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I am part of Rajah and Tann’s South Asia Desk and I have a number of clients from India.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Generally, if any of them wishes to visit Singapore, they will need a sponsor from Singapore to indicate they are visiting for business purposes when they apply for a visa.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And on this basis, they may be granted a visa to visit.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The same applies for people who wish to visit for investments and the same thing applies to Singaporeans who wish to visit India.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, this facilitates the free movement of people to do business.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Because more people are coming here to do business.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: More businesses service other parts of the world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The drivers for our long-term employment policies are our needs, as Dr Tan See Leng has explained very clearly in his Ministerial Statement.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If it is felt we do not need that many people in a particular sector, or that Singaporeans can do the jobs, it is already within our power to do this and CECA does not change this.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, what really is Mr Leong Mun Wai trying to achieve with this Motion?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: CECA is just one out of 26 free trade agreements that we have.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Is it simply to target Indian nationals or, worse, people of Indian ethnicity?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is clear that the anxieties about jobs relate to structural issues that have nothing to do with CECA.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, CECA potentially helps to create jobs for people by facilitating investments and trade.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If people in this House who have the ability and should research and look into things before coming, do their homework, I think we will probably be in a situation where we have clarity on these issues.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I have heard feedback from many people in the Indian community about the discomfort they are feeling with the current anti-CECA stance being perpetuated, which is a thinly-veiled attack against Indians.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Even the Leader of the Opposition has acknowledged it is a dog-whistle in some corners.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Many in Singapore’s Indian community also get caught up and mistaken in this anti-foreigner torrent.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In some ways, I can understand why members of the public may have mistaken beliefs that treaties like CECA are causing foreigners to take their jobs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Essentially, they may be feeling job pressures and job losses, particularly during the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, they may see many foreigners, including Indian nationals, having jobs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But these jobs are in different sectors and these jobs, if the Singaporeans are eligible for them, they should apply for them.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And if they are not given fair consideration, they can report to MOM and MOM will take action against the employers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, I think it is important for us to help solve misunderstandings and make it clear that even though there are foreigners who have jobs, they are not getting it by virtue of free trade agreements like CECA.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But Mr Leong Mun Wai also talked about the Population White Paper and said that this was a White Paper that proposed allowing foreigners to come into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We do not want to be overwhelmed by more foreign workers than we can absorb or to expand our total population beyond what our island is able to accommodate.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, if you look at the White Paper properly, it is really a very balanced Paper that looks at Singapore's long-term needs and how many foreigners we can accommodate within that framework.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Against this backdrop, I think, to me, it is very clear that CECA and free trade agreements really have nothing to do with the anxieties Singaporeans face about jobs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are very real anxieties Singaporeans face and the way to address those is to make sure we continue to create new jobs and be an attractive place for investments to come in.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I am also one of those who agree that we should have protection for Singaporeans and I was also one of those who spoke in favour of the anti-discrimination laws, which I am glad are coming into force.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What potential anti-discrimination laws would do is also give the aggrieved individual a personal right, a personal remedy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, to me, this is one more additional measure to prevent employers from exercising discrimination.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I am glad that the Workers' Party does seem to have a lot of common ground with us.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: They have stated expressly that they agree free trade agreements are important for Singapore's future and he has also acknowledged that CECA has been used as a dog-whistle in some corners for racist behaviour.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But I will have to stop short of supporting the amendments.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The main reason I am objecting to the amendments is firstly, they change the substance of the Motion.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai's Motion claims that Singaporeans' job anxieties are caused by free trade agreements like CECA.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It focuses on the measures we need to take to deal with Singaporeans' anxieties and denounces the link to CECA and free trade agreements.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think what Mr Pritam Singh is really trying to do is to include one of his pet topics – a request for more information – into this debate, which is really quite different from what the core of this debate is.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The first amendment, of course, where he is changing the word "supports Government action" to "calls for stronger Government action" also has an insinuation that the Government is not doing enough.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I personally do not think this is fair to the hard work done by people in MOM who I know are bending over backwards to enforce and take measures to support local employment.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, I do not agree with that amendment.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There is quarterly labour market data, advanced market data coming out with breakdowns of Singaporeans and foreigners employed.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, I think an insinuation that there is not adequate information out there is something I cannot support.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I have spent 37 years in the ICT industry and I was a foreign worker myself: three years in Japan and eight years in China.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, thank you, Mr Speaker, for the privilege to join in the debate on the subject of jobs, livelihoods and foreign talent.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I have shared previously in this Chamber my views of the imperative of free trade agreements (FTAs) for Singapore businesses.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The FTA network which Singapore has established, including the more recent Digital Economic Agreements, offer a key tool for businesses to expand into new markets, enhancing accessibility to different markets.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I quote Mr Lam Yi Young, CEO of SBF who wrote in a July article, "Trade is Singapore's lifeline, and it is imperative that we remain open and connected to the world." We are a country built by immigrants.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: But Singapore has gone from third world to the first by recognising that though we are an island, it is imperative that we cannot behave like one.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We need to be relevant to the global economy.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: When I did research of all the rankings that are out there, in almost every competitiveness ranking report for the most innovative cities in the world, the world's best global cities, the world's most competitive economy, this is what I found.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: A city's ability to attract talented human capital, generate economic growth, increase competitiveness and ensure stability and security are key factors that make the difference.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore, though just a little red dot, is ranked amongst the top 10 in many of these lists.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The concentration of quality talent is invariably a key factor for outperformers, whether they are companies or cities.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's highly- educated workforce, enabled by world-class University communities here, coupled with our ability to attract diversity of global talent, has helped us maintain our competitiveness and attracted large multinational companies to expand in Singapore and startups to plant their seeds of innovation here.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: They demonstrated their commitment with a pledge in January earlier this year and Mr Per Magnusson tells me that the Singapore International Chamber of Commerce has focused on operationalising the intent of the pledge by doing a pilot of orientation programmes for newcomers to Singapore.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: But, of course, alas, industry-wide, it is still work in progress.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We might think that foreign talents are needed only by the MNCs but that is not true.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Dr T Chandroo, Chairman of the Singapore Indian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (SICCI) shared with me an example in the built environment industry.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The foreign talent was proficient in visualising building information models (BIMs) and AutoCAD.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Likewise, in the engineering domain, there is an increasing need for employees to have multidisciplinary, interdisciplinary skill sets.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses that have secured contracts from clients cannot wait for a critical mass of Singaporeans to be trained before they can service the contracts.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Foreign talent, hence, provides a good complement as our Singaporean Core upskill and reskill for the changing demands.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding that I am a National University of Singapore (NUS) alumni, I must say that NUS' bold move in transforming curriculum structures – for example, setting up the new College of Design and Engineering – to prepare the future Singaporean workforce who will be interdisciplinary, broad-based critical thinkers and problem solvers in a VUCA world – VUCA being volatile, uncertain, complex and ambiguous – is exactly what the industry expects of our world-class Universities: to lead the way of change and to secure our workforce's relevance in the new normal.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Roland Ng, President of the Singapore Chinese Chamber of Commerce, recently wrote an opinion piece in Zaobao; and I am very happy that Minister Tan See Leng actually referred to it in Chinese just now.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There are certain deep-seated negative stereotypes of jobs which Singaporeans seem to not want to take on or, perhaps, I should say, that Singaporean parents do not want their kids to take on.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: These jobs, however, are critical and essential to our economy.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Such jobs can be found in both the domestic sector like the built environment and construction as well as the export sector.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Without continued access to foreign workers, companies in these essential sectors will not be able to function, stay viable and thrive, and, hence, even the jobs of the locals in those companies will be threatened and, by extension, impact the wider economy.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Without access to foreign workers to take on work that locals do not want to do, it will affect the export readiness and competitiveness of Singapore brands.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I spoke to Dr Hsien Hsien Lei, CEO of AmCham Singapore and she shared with me a preview of the soon-to-be released 2021 AmCham Manpower Survey of member companies.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Meanwhile, in order to fill these gaps, companies need to bring in qualified foreign talent who can do the job and also support the training and development of high-potential local talent, especially in areas, such as technical knowledge and global markets.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This feedback is pretty consistent with the other TACs.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Critical for Singapore is to understand what are the relevant skills and work experience that employers are looking for and to be willing to step up to learn and to reskill as well as to lean in to express our interest in picking up the new skills and our readiness to pick up the relevant work experiences.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: If we do not unleash our voice to compete for the job, we have no one else to blame.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Asking "who has moved my cheese?" will not help.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Be humble and learn from the foreign talent coach and do not hesitate to ask the boss for that job when you are done learning.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Because you are always ready to learn and will do the job even better than your foreign talent coach.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Your foreign talent coach may get promoted in the headquarters and bring you along as he or she rises in his or her career.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There are many such heartwarming stories during the 30 years of my career.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Everything starts, in my opinion, with the right frame of mind and attitude.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: That said, during the Committee of Supply, I did highlight that in engaging with the MNCs, in particular, I hope that MTI and EDB, which are the ones the MNCs work with upfront, will lean in on them to really recognise the value of the Singapore talent as the foundation of their business success.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: While it is very good to have MOM come in to police and to check, when it is at the policing end, it is always not so much fun.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: When we start it right, that is always the best.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, if Singapore hopes to continue to secure good jobs and livelihoods for Singaporeans into the future, we need to continue to be amongst the best of global cities in the world.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The alternative is to fall off to the wayside.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For a moment, consider what that alternative might look like.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We no longer are a hub for human capital and, therefore, lose our edge in attracting Foreign Direct Investments (FDI).

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Without a melting pot of talents, innovations will likely be dry and, without innovation, the investments into the best-in-class infrastructure will not be funded.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses no longer find Singapore attractive for their hub activities and the list continues to spiral downward.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: At that point, we will not be debating as to whether having foreign talent in our workforce is a good thing or not.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The debate would shift to how do we stop the brain drain of our younger Singaporeans who, in the absence of good jobs and good opportunities in a Singapore that has become unplugged from the global network, will need to leave their country in pursuit of better opportunities for themselves and their families, elsewhere.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Let us make sure that we do not ever come close to this alternate state being a reality.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: As the Prime Minister said in his National Day Rally closing speech, "We have done it before, we can do it again".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Please allow me to speak in Mandarin, Mr Speaker.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: (In Mandarin):  :  Mr Speaker, thank you for letting me join the debate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The impact of foreign manpower on our economy and on Singaporeans is once again a hot topic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It is quite normal to have objective discussions about the advantages and disadvantages associated with foreign manpower.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: However, the focus seems to have shifted over the last one to two years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It is not hard to notice PSP’s enthusiasm for such claims.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Today, the PSP is moving a Motion on Singaporeans’ anxiety on jobs and livelihoods, making specific mention of CECA again, as though the discussion on 6 July never took place.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Clearly, PSP remains unmoved by what the two Ministers had shared.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The PSP has been using guerrilla-style tactics, raising piecemeal questions in Parliament and on social media on the nationalities of foreign workers and the structure of our labour force.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: When asked point-blank, they have expressed agreement with the Government’s economic strategy, only to change tune again.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Hearing their speeches today, I feel even more confused.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai said in his speech that CECA is not his main focus today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Then why put it in the title of the Motion?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: When he could not answer Minister Shanmugam’s questions, his response was to ask for more data.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We may never find out what is the PSP’s real stance on the issue, but that does not really matter.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I do not believe most Singaporeans would support discrediting the whole of the Government’s economic strategy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But it is true that employment is a sensitive topic to many people, especially because of the impact of digitalisation and automation, as well as COVID-19 on our livelihoods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I doubt the public would care particularly about our specific responses to Mr Leong Mun Wai and Ms Hazel Poa, but they would want to know whether the Government is aware of some reasonable doubts they might harbour and what the Government is going to do about them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I believe we can group these into four main doubts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: If the Government truly prioritises the interests of Singaporeans, why allow in so many foreign PMETs to compete with Singaporeans?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: If I am treated unfairly by my foreign boss or colleagues, how would the Government help me?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Is the Government truly aware of the struggles of Singaporean PMETs, especially those who are middle-aged and facing stiff competition and fears of being replaced?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Surely, MNCs will continue to invest here even if we further restrict hiring of foreign manpower.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Is the Government simply unwilling to do so?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Does the Singapore Government have some kind of special affinity for India and Indian PMETs?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The first doubt to be addressed: why does the Government allow in so many foreign PMETs to compete with Singaporeans?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: If I am treated unfairly by my foreign boss or colleagues, how would the Government help me?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Government has focused heavily on developing the economy over the years to secure better jobs and better lives for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We have to run to stay in the same place.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We must not depend only on our existing competitive advantages but must also capture new growth areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Singaporeans are very familiar with this set of economic strategies, particularly our drive to gain hub status for various industries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We seek to attract MNCs to invest in Singapore, particularly to set up their Southeast Asia, Asia-Pacific or even global HQs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This brings better jobs and a wider range of employment choices for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: For these strategies to work, it is not enough to have a well-trained and diligent local workforce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We have to let companies recruit foreign manpower to overcome the shortage of local workers and staff the positions available in regional and global HQs, which require familiarity with different countries and regions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: So, this foreign manpower would complement local manpower, but also compete to some extent.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Our economy has been growing but the local-born Singapore population has not been able to keep pace.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: So, we see more foreigners in our economy, and locals feel that competition has intensified.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Government wants good job opportunities and careers for local employees.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Even if a company satisfies the above requirements, the Government would take seriously any claim of discrimination against Singaporeans working there, for instance, a foreign boss favouring employees from his country and passing over deserving local employees.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Local employees would naturally feel particularly aggrieved if they were being treated unfairly by foreigners, on our own land.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Since the whole rationale of allowing foreign manpower in is to help make good jobs available to Singaporeans, the Government will certainly not condone this.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: If MOM were to receive such reports, it would commence investigations in line with the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Although such interventions are not public, companies operating in Singapore know they do occur.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: As Prime Minister Lee has said during the National Day Rally, MNC leaders do pay attention to whether their operations in Singapore have reason to cause concern to the Government.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It is the Government’s duty to keep reasonable tabs on enterprise behaviour.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Government pursues an open economic policy for the benefit of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Although we cannot do without some foreign manpower, the Government will not allow unlimited importation of foreign manpower and will not stand for discrimination against local workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Subsidies in skills upgrading are largely limited to local workers; support schemes for individuals and families to mitigate the impact of COVID-19 are also focused on locals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In other words, foreign manpower bore the brunt of the impact of COVID-19 on the Singapore economy, cushioning the locals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It is clear that the Government puts the interests of Singaporean workers first.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The second doubt: has the Government truly taken to heart the struggles of middle-aged PMETs?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Chinese phrase “人到中年” is often quoted in reference to all the pressures and frustrations that people experience once they become middle-aged.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In 1982, a Chinese movie of the same title was released.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I was very young then and did not fully understand the content.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But I recall that the protagonist was long-suffering and that middle-age seemed to be a troubled life stage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Middle-aged is usually defined as 45-65 years of age.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I am now middle-aged, and so are my friends and many of the constituents I serve.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I dare say most Members of Parliament also belong to this age group.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: So, we are most familiar with everything that is associated with this life stage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Middle-aged people have to look after aged parents and, often, young children.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: At work, aside from dealing with the demands of their bosses and customers, they need to upgrade and keep up with ever-changing technology and face up to intense global competition.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We are not as fit and spry as we once were.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: At the very least, we need new reading glasses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Some among us will also have health worries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Government pays particular attention to middle-aged workers, especially middle-aged PMETs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: PMETs used to be in the minority within our workforce, but our economic structure has changed significantly; we are now a knowledge-based economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Knowledge enterprises have grown, and PMETs now form more than half of the workforce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It is normal for companies to restructure and close, and for new companies to be formed all the time in a market economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: So, more PMETs will experience displacement, and more will find themselves changing firms or even professions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This is a structural trend which reflects the impact of digitalisation and the rapid changes in skills that the market seeks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The jobs held by some middle-aged PMETs were replaced through digitalisation and automation, but new jobs have also emerged, including those related to digital tech.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We need a structural solution, and not simply curb the entry of foreign manpower.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We use a multi-pronged approach to help middle-aged PMETs master new skills and regain employment as soon as possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: SkillsFuture, established in 2015, is, by design, tilted towards supporting middle-aged workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Unlike fresh graduates, they have been out of school for a longer time and need to reconnect with lifelong learning.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Workforce SG also focuses its career counselling and job-matching efforts on those who are middle-aged and above.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It is also a focus of the National Jobs Council led by Senior Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Middle-aged PMETs face other pressures, aside from those related to the workplace.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Other policies launched by the Government help to relieve such pressures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Older middle-agers can also be direct beneficiaries of some of these schemes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The third doubt: will enterprises really be driven away if we further restrict the entry of foreign manpower?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Building an international trade and finance hub is an arduous task.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: While Singapore has some competitive advantages, there are also obvious drawbacks, such as our limited manpower pool and high manpower costs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We have strong rivals ahead of us, and competitors nipping at our heels.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: If not for the fact that we have expended so much effort to build our economy up to a certain scale, we would not be in a position to even talk about curbing foreign manpower.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Of course, we seek to uphold the interests of local jobseekers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This was a carefully considered decision after taking in views from Labour Movement representatives and NTUC Members of Parliament.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I am glad to hear that Ms He Ting Ru has noticed this, too.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: However, we must go about this carefully and strike the right balance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Just now, Ms Janet Ang gave a vivid description of the dire consequences if we do not get the balance right.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We have a saying in Chinese: "it is easy to invite a deity into your home but hard to send it away".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It is the opposite when it comes to developing the economy and attracting MNCs: it is hard work to attract them, but only too easy to send them away.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It is not only MNCs, but local companies, too, who constantly appeal to the Government to relax curbs on foreign manpower so that they may have more breathing room.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Government understands their challenges, but we have to put the interests of Singaporean workers first.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Still a good result, but it goes to show that international competition is stiff.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Losing companies to other economies will result in the worst possible outcome for Singaporean workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It is necessary to regulate foreign manpower, but we have to do so cautiously and not in abrupt ways.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This would affect Singapore’s competitiveness and threaten Singaporeans’ prospects.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The exchange between Ms Hazel Poa and Minister Tan See Leng worries me, because the line of questioning was about local-born Singaporean Citizens.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I would be especially happy to see fellow born-and-bred Singaporeans do well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: First, local born Singaporeans share many collective memories and feel a bond with one another.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It is only natural that we cheer for one another.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Second, Singapore is such a small country, with a small population.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: To achieve international acclaim in the economic sector or in entrepreneurship, innovation, sports and the arts is no easy feat.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But if we were to question a successful person’s citizenship and ask if he is a local-born Singaporean, instead of first congratulating him or being happy for him, then something is changing in our society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: A few days ago, I was invited to a concert co-organised by the Singapore Symphony Orchestra and Lianhe Zaobao, featuring Mr Jin Ta, SSO’s Principal Flute.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: He played beautifully, but my mind was occupied with today’s debate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: There he was, such an outstanding musician performing for the audience, and all I could think about was wondering whether everyone would sincerely enjoy his music, or judge his contributions based on his birthplace.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: After the concert, the CEO of SSO, Mr Chng Hak Peng, asked for my views, and I shared my thoughts with him candidly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The question I get asked most often is what proportion of the SSO is Singaporean.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I would reply that the majority of our musicians are Singapore Citizens.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But I would get asked further: how many of them are local-born?” So, it can be seen that some people do draw such lines in our society – whether in the commercial, arts or sports fields.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: There is an ancient Chinese saying: “Judge not a hero by where he came from.” If we do the opposite, we end up going down a path of no return, which is not even logical.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We are happy with local-born Singaporeans doing well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But when someone wishes to make Singapore their home, and fight alongside us, should we not be happy, too?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This person could be working here, serving Singaporean customers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: He could head a listed company and make money for Singaporean shareholders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: He could be providing healthcare for our elderly or educating our young.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Talent from around the world have many options.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: If the person chooses to come to Singapore and not elsewhere, is that not also a form of success for Singapore?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: If we keep drawing lines between the local-born and naturalised citizens, we would have defeated ourselves, even before we face competition from others.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Let us not forget that the pandemic has accelerated the trend of working from home.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: For companies that need foreign manpower, this brings about many advantages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It also means a new challenge for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We should be upholding, not undermining, our competitiveness at such a critical juncture.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Minister Ong Ye Kung and Minister Tan See Leng had, on 6 July, clearly explained why the Movement of Natural Persons provisions in CECA have very little impact on the actual entry of Indian professionals into Singapore and that there had not been many intra-corporate transferees under CECA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai had acknowledged during the debate that he and Ms Hazel Poa are for FTAs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: He expressed understanding that the interests of Singaporeans had not been used as bargaining chips in FTA negotiations and that Singaporeans’ interests had been taken into account.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Nonetheless, the Motion standing in their names today once again mentions “widespread anxiety among Singaporeans on jobs and livelihoods caused by the foreign talent policy and the provisions on Movement of Natural Persons in some free trade agreements like the CECA”.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Even if we leave aside the question of their motivation for bringing up CECA repeatedly, I doubt it would do much good to painstakingly repeat our answers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Let us cut straight to the chase and address the fourth doubt: has the Singapore Government got some special affinity for India and Indians, so much so that we welcome ever-increasing numbers of Indian nationals to live and work in Singapore, in competition with local PMETs?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: PMETs from India have, indeed, increased in numbers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Many Indian nationals can be found in some professions, especially finance and IT, and there are concentrations of residents from India in some private estates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Some locals find this hard to get used to.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Indian PMETs are here to make a living.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It makes no sense for them to cause offence, but some might take longer to blend in, in terms of lifestyles, work habits and the way they interact.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: A handful of Indian PMETs have been caught on social media misbehaving, which has caused those who are already uneasy with the change to feel more offended.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We have been emphasising racial harmony in Singapore over the years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Hence, most people would refrain from public discussion about race and nationality.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: However, we cannot rule out some people wondering quietly: why is the Government so welcoming of Indians?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: A letter by Mr Tay Ping Hui was published in Lianhe Zaobao in May this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Entitled “I give my heart to the moon, but does the moon care?”, the letter expresses this sentiment in a subtle manner.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The main gist of his piece: is it worthwhile for Singapore to be so generous towards India and Indians, when the goodwill is not reciprocated?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The letter referred to some circumstances relating to the COVID-19 pandemic and alluded to bad behaviour by some Indian PMETs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Not everyone can write as well as Mr Tay.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Some are fearful of crossing red lines and causing unnecessary misunderstandings, and choose to keep their doubts to themselves.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This creates space for those who peddle critiques of CECA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Most people might not know or care about the details in CECA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: They only know that it is an FTA with India and assume that it could explain why more Indian PMETs have appeared in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Hence, critiques of CECA have found a ready audience.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Soon, CECA became a code word for Indians, and a cover for some racially-charged commentary.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The answer: Singapore has no special affinity for workers from any country, including India.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: What we want is to become a finance and digital/ICT hub, to create better jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: India happens to be a major exporter of skilled manpower for both industries, especially when it comes to ICT.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: India and China produce the largest number of skilled manpower in the world for the IT industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Indian ICT professionals are not only numerous, but also well-versed in English.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: China’s own ICT industry has been developing at a rapid pace.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: With a huge domestic market, the demand for their homegrown talent is robust.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: So, relatively fewer ICT professionals are available to come to places like Singapore now.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: You will find large numbers of Indian professionals in any English-speaking economy that seeks to build finance or ICT hubs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It is the case in Silicon Valley, New York and London.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: As mentioned previously, intra-corporate transferees under CECA had been few.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Most Indian PMETs entered Singapore on EPs applied for by their employers, via normal channels.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Singapore, too, has been grooming our own finance and IT talent, so that they can do well in these fast-growing sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Then, do our companies really need to hire so many Indian PMETs?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: If we restrict enterprises in their hiring of Indian professionals, they will feel constrained.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It has to do with our economic strategy to grow as a financial hub and an IT hub, which we have no reason to abandon.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: These are among the world’s fastest growing industries and can bring good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: While there is no special affinity, we certainly have nothing against Indian PMETs either.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Approval of EPs should be based primarily on the needs of companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We pay attention to overall numbers and whether Singaporeans are treated fairly, rather than focus on any particular nationality.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Government will also continue to pursue integration efforts, and encourage foreign professionals working and living here to respect local culture and integrate well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: However, becoming Permanent Residents (PRs) or Singapore Citizens (SC) is quite a different matter altogether.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: When it comes to PRs, we are careful not to cause major shifts in ethnic proportions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I hope that this debate would have dispelled some doubts in people’s minds and help them to see that: we have a comprehensive approach towards boosting the competitiveness of local PMETs and ensuring their fair treatment; the Government values middle-aged PMETs and seeks to relieve the pressures they experience; the Government has been regulating the entry of foreign PMETs and will tighten if necessary, but we must not drive away enterprises or that will harm the interests of Singaporeans; and the Government has no special affinity for workers from any country, including India.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We exist to serve the interests of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Moreover, it is the duty of the Government to consider the needs of Singaporeans at every life stage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: However, old age comes after middle-age, which means significant expenses for both the individual and society in terms of retirement adequacy and healthcare needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: If our economy does not do well, our people will have little purchasing power and the state cannot afford more subsidies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Who could possibly retire in peace in such a scenario?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Minister Lawrence Wong’s Motion contains a phrase “supports Government actions to manage the population of foreign manpower”.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Workers’ Party has proposed replacing “supports” with “calls for stronger”.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In addressing the third doubt, I have mentioned that the Government will continue to be judicious in balancing the needs of managing foreign manpower and maintaining our economic vitality to safeguard Singaporeans’ interests.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: That is well captured in the original Motion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Workers’ Party has asked to include another paragraph calling on the Government to release more information.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I do not think we lack information for this debate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This was a delaying tactic employed by the PSP when they could not answer questions posed to them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: So, let us adopt a more objective attitude in addressing the challenges that we will inevitably face when developing our economy and creating jobs for Singaporeans, and not be swayed by seductive arguments or waver in our commitment towards an open economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Most importantly, we must not allow trust between the people and the Government to be eroded.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Let us work hand in hand to overcome immediate challenges and build a stronger foundation for our future and that of our next generation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I support the Motion standing in the name of the Finance Minister.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: It was the Minister for Manpower who had given the statistics, and more than once.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: In her ensuing speech, Ms Sim Ann has expressed disdain for this attitude.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: (In Mandarin):  :  If Ms Hazel Poa had not mentioned this, I would not even want to bring it up.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: I think we have already had a clear discussion on the matter.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: I suggest that PSP need not undermine itself by reminding us of what they have said.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Motion by the Minister for Finance, who actually has elaborated on how FTAs and the efforts by the Government to help raise livelihoods have created many quality jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A very stark contrast to PSP's Motion by Mr Leong Mun Wai, which casts doubts in some way, on our various FTAs and the various FTAs he mentioned earlier on.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I will also talk about how Singaporeans, especially mid-career employees aged 40 to 60 and PMETs in sectors perceived to be affected by foreign talents and students who hope to join the workforce and how they should take advantage of the new opportunities in spite of the current economic environment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, we have benefited from globalisation in many ways in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singapore and other countries in the region have reaped substantial dividends from pursuing an export-oriented development strategy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: By opening up our economy via multilateral and bilateral free trade agreements and participating in global value chains, we were able to industrialise and grow rapidly for long periods and, in the process, transform into middle or high-income countries.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Inadvertently, Singapore has built a reputation as a key hub in Southeast Asia and, in some cases globally, for finance, transhipment activities, business services, transportation and logistics.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We should do our utmost to keep it that way.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We also have a robust manufacturing base, which is a key node in the complex value chains that wrap around East Asia.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a global financial centre, Singapore is ranked fourth, behind only London, New York and Hong Kong and ahead of Tokyo, in the 2018 Global Financial Centres Index.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I was a bit confused when Mr Leong Mun Wai mentioned that over the past 10 to 20 years, opportunities for Singaporeans and in various sectors have not improved.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have many Singaporeans working in these MNCs, some of whom are also in this Chamber now.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Despite these core strengths, Singapore's economy needs to continue growing.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: By how much is a matter of debate.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Arguably, to remain an attractive and vibrant economic hub, Singapore's economy needs to grow at around 2% to 3% a year, which is feasible for a high-income country, such as Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The challenge, however, is finding where this growth will come from to continue creating jobs for Singaporeans without coming up with changes to measures or policies that may unravel our long-term growth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the meantime, for small and open economies, continued engagement with world markets in various ways, including FTAs across many countries, including the US, Australia, China and even India.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is not a choice but an economic imperative.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is because of our persistent belief in free trade and our active engagement with countries that are willing to be equal partners, in areas of trade, travel, services and so on.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In spite of some adjustments to our trade policies over the years, we remain one of the most market-oriented and open economies in the world.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: By participating actively in the global economy, we have made it easier to move internationally and this, in turn, accelerates the factors for labour mobility, enabling Singaporeans to seek more opportunities and experiences overseas.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The discussion so far, from the start, has been mostly about domestic jobs created for Singaporeans in Singapore which is valid and which is really something that we should discuss.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But we should also discuss about opportunities for Singaporeans going abroad and the fact that our discussion today, talking about these two Motions – in my view and also in talking to the markets – is very closely watched by the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In particular, concerns about our principles of free trade and our view on foreign talent have an impact on how we are perceived by the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We are sought after in regions of growth, such as China, India, the Middle East, Malaysia, Vietnam and Indonesia and many more countries, I am sure, because of our skills and bilingualism.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That is also because our Government has invested in some of these regions and has kept a relatively comfortable stance on foreign talent as a key hub for many sectors.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have to be mindful that any change in stance to foreign talent or signs of xenophobia creeping into our policies will signal to other countries this shift in the markets and, inevitably, in the long run, also have an impact on our future Singaporean workers venturing abroad.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With the pandemic, more Singaporean talent abroad have decided to come home.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But they have brought back with them highly-valued international insights on innovation and culture.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As representatives of Singapore, they shared the Singaporean work ethic of high efficiency and reliability to the rest of the world, so that Singaporeans would remain sought-after employees.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our policies in Singapore have contributed to that, eventually with them coming back home.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Globalisation allows for different cultures and economic systems around the world to become connected and to integrate with one another because of the influence of large multinational companies and of global communication.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Yet it takes a certain type of person to truly comprehend this and turn this into an advantage.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I met a resident whose experience I thought was interesting.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Singapore resident works in an international petroleum trading company in Singapore which trades across Asia, Australia and the Middle East.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: She said that when the pandemic broke out, the Singapore office was literally the only office that was getting things done.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And because of Singapore's multicultural and multilingual characteristics, the multinational staff here were able to help fill the gaps in communications between the other offices.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One example she gave was being good with understanding accents and another was being cognisant of the needs of some international colleagues who needed time off for religious activities and having an adequate support system in place.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Consequently, she also noted the threat of remote working from anywhere in the world casting a shadow of instability on jobs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While it is important to stay vigilant and humble, Singaporeans have little to fear because we have good international reputation and unique ability to contribute a global mindset to the employer.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But what is clear is that there other more pertinent and major challenges to our Singaporean jobs in MNCs, such as disruptive technology and digital labour markets or remote working.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Globalisation is not only seen in economic activities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It also includes the proliferation of technologies where communications and distribution networks are becoming very significant in people's life.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This brings me to my next point, on digitalisation of the economy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In Singapore, technological adoption is even more urgent in view of the country's ageing population and compositional shifts of the labour force over the next decade.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, for Singapore to sustain healthy growth and living standards to continue rising, it must keep leveraging technology to drive productivity growth and new growth areas, such as, for example, in smart energy, healthcare and technology-related sectors.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That will constitute part of where the opportunities will lie.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Government has taken the lead to create a nationwide movement dedicated to this.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Under SG Digital, there is a plethora of programmes and grants to help businesses, individuals looking to get into the relevant sectors and the community of people who rely on it for their daily life.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With the increase in digitalisation of more industries, this is already creating a global demand for ICT talents and relevant roles in maintaining the security and functionality of these digital systems.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This has contributed to the increase in the number of ICT talents working in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The benefits of globalisation for small open economies, such as Singapore, are there, but there are challenges associated with globalisation and Minister Lawrence Wong has highlighted that and a few other Members here as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We need to take stock of the current tensions arising from the uneven distributional effects of globalisation, we know that and the potential dislocations posed by new technology.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Government has, over the past decades, taken practical policy measures to mitigate the side effects of globalisation and achieve inclusive growth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We should enhance these efforts, as mentioned in the Motion by Minister Lawrence Wong.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But at the same time, we need to also be cognisant that we are an economy in transition facing a demographic shrinking population issue, rising inequalities and competitiveness issues as we become a more mature economy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In Malay):  :  One segment of Singaporeans who are facing the effects of globalisation daily are mid-career jobseekers and employees in the age range of 40 to 60 years, who are worried about the current employment situation and the inclination towards digitalisation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is not because they do not want to pick up new skills.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In fact, most Singaporeans recognise that learning digital skills is the only way forward.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope to call on the Government to share on future long-term plans for the programme and enhance it further with updates or a review, and whether we will see a greater variety of jobs and roles.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With the Tech Skills Accelerator programme (TeSA), which was launched in 2016, there are courses for mid-career jobseekers without relevant experience to train them to be software developers, data analysts and UX designers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: International big tech companies like Google and IBM, as well as local employers, had joined in to provide courses and traineeships.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
