text: I believe this would help to alleviate some of the manpower crunch for the tech sector, while helping more mid-career job seekers to land skills and jobs in a rapidly growing industry.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, for those who are in this age group, there are ample opportunities to upgrade your skills set, acquire new skills and help you rise up to meet the challenges.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Globalisation and digitalisation open up new chapters in our life.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We see many who were able to switch careers so that they do not get trapped in sunset industries.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Others take on contracts for a year or so.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But some are still having trouble landing full-time permanent jobs and are relying on internships and side projects.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is currently a global problem for all graduating cohorts, as companies worldwide scale back on headcounts.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They also face competition from other Singaporeans who are also looking for jobs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And in taking up side projects and gigs online, they may also find themselves coming up against competition from overseas.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Globalisation or its association with foreign talent flows cannot be faulted for this.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Rather, the situation arises because of the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Before the pandemic, many local students had benefited from exchange programmes and internships overseas.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is a global competition because the whole world is in the grip of this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But it will do us no good to maintain a pessimistic outlook, because that will only cause us to miss out on other opportunities that have arisen from the crisis.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Indeed, many have found themselves having to put their dream jobs on hold and taking up entirely new and unexpected career paths.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some young residents became part-time swabbers to earn an income, unexpectedly discovering their interest in healthcare and in that sector.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singaporeans across different generations have gone through different crises where they had to rechart their pathways due to the limitations of those times, for example, during the Asian Financial Crisis or even in the post-Independence days.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Today, many may find themselves sharing similar emotions of disappointment and anxiety.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But the difference is we have a lot more resources today than our parents and grandparents did, and we can afford to remain much more optimistic, as long as we manage our expectations and do our best with the opportunities that are available.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Fair employment is a subject that has always been very close to my heart.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, my next point is on PMETs working in sectors where foreign talent is perceived to be a threat.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I work in the financial sector and I do talk with those in the sector as they share their lived experiences.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I can empathise with them and their concerns.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Understandably, some sectors, especially the ICT sector, face a talent crunch too.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Employers find that, in the short term, it takes too much resources and time to hire and train a Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, they would prefer to hire an experienced and skilled foreigner.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But this does not solve the immediate problem of a skills shortage in the sector.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the financial sector, for example, in the foreign banks, the deliberations on foreign staff recruitment are done at the bank's global HQ level to fill any shortage of skilled staff and are based on specific global business needs and internal human capital movement requirements.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Therefore, to ensure that at all levels of the bank, the locals will eventually be the majority, may not be possible, given the global nature of these decisions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And, again, with the recent tightening of foreign manpower restrictions and the newly enshrined anti-discrimination laws coming, some of these anxieties can be addressed where there are wrongful practices.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think the Leader of the Opposition mentioned this, and I have mentioned this in my Adjournment Motions previously in 2019 and on various occasions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I understand that I have been very persistent in this, but I believe it will bring about several benefits.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Fewer companies are sending Singaporeans overseas for training in this climate.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, why not redeploy the funds to support the costs for employers to have their new and existing local hires receive training and mentorship under a more experienced and skilled foreign employee in the company?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the long run, this helps to build up the local talent core.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It helps to reinforce the main purpose of having foreign talent in the first place, which is to help companies, including local employees, improve as a whole, not to steal our jobs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The foreign employee would receive a boost to his CV.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is due to the complex nature of talent, the apprehension of domestic populations on attracting labour inputs from abroad and host the individual, either temporarily or permanently, near the location of the work to be performed.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For a variety of reasons, this has proven politically unpopular and nearly all countries place restrictions on migrations, Singapore included.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But ongoing trends by MNCs and companies globally, via offshoring before and still now, build-up of "digital labour markets" have the potential to radically alter the global labour market, thus overshooting in foreign talent policy responses by any country may lead to more negative outcomes and, worse, it supports xenophobic and racist behaviours that can worsen domestically.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These digital labour market platforms can connect workers worldwide with companies seeking to have tasks completed and, with technology, this can go beyond data entry and programming roles only.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Worse, if the MNCs see Singapore’s hub status eroded because of too tight foreign talent policies or any signalling thereof in that direction.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And here I would like to refer to Mr Leong Mun Wai's suggestion earlier that he intends to recommend PRs and new citizenship numbers to be reduced, going forward.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I just want to highlight that – and I think some of the previous speakers have mentioned this – the debate today is mainly about foreign manpower vis-a-vis our economic strategy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Immigration is a separate topic which covers a much broader range of imperatives.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Immigration and work passes are separate regimes with different considerations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Potential applicants know that we are very strict in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I would like to ask Mr Leong Mun Wai, does Mr Leong think that these family members of our fellow Singaporeans ought to wait longer?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There have been calls from Members of this House, including Members from the Workers' Party, for us to be more expedient in granting Permanent Residency, or PRs, and citizenships, especially for family members of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, let me give an example from the ground.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A 40-year-old resident, who is a Singaporean Citizen, works hard as a private hire car driver, has a Malaysian wife and children who want to be PRs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The question is, how long does Mr Leong want her and the children to wait before they can be granted PR status?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think most of the Members in this Chamber have, from time to time, seen residents coming to them for help in this regard.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And how long do you want their children to pay more for their school fees?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I would like to pose that question to Mr Leong.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And to go on, I urge all, in Singapore, we need to channel our efforts positively towards building back better, which begins with an understanding that our challenges are complex and cannot be resolved by narrow ideology on globalisation and foreign talent policy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Understanding the complexity of modern society, the working relationship of democracy and capitalism, and recognising the prevalence of externalities are the first steps towards genuinely healing our social, economic and financial issues amid this current crisis.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The latter, too, does not stir up racism and xenophobia and is mindful of securing Singaporean jobs and livelihoods in the long run.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: To wrap up, Mr Speaker, our success in globalisation is not something that came with the drop of a hat.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: We were faced with many challenges but, instead of crying foul, we came up with new ideas and bravely ventured ahead.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: We had to change our mindset from being an entrepot centre to looking globally.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: We were put on the path to be a Global City.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: That is what we are called to do today.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It has one of the highest proportions of PMET vacancies that employers say they are unable to fill with locals.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Consequently, the industry also employs among the highest proportion of foreign professionals.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Before continuing, I would like to declare my interest as a founder and director of a local IT solutions and consulting company.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: My conversations with people in the industry and my observations as an IT practitioner over the past 20 years inform the policy proposals that I am advancing today.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: My speech will focus on skills and employment issues surrounding this industry, although some of these issues will be similar to those faced in other industries.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I will analyse the reasons for the skills gaps and manpower shortage in the ICT sector; suggest ways in which the education system can be re-orientated to play a greater part in narrowing this gap; and propose ways the Government can address some of the imbalances that Singaporean professionals encounter in the workplace vis-à-vis foreign professionals.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We constantly hear employers complain that while there are many job opportunities in the industry, there are not enough suitable professionals, both local and foreign, who have the skills to fill those positions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: On the other hand, some Singaporean IT professionals have shared with me how they have been passed over for promotions or employment despite their best efforts to attend training and improve themselves.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singapore is an attractive work destination and often a stepping stone for foreigners.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many are willing to work longer hours at lower wages to pick up skills and experience, before moving on to countries like the US, Canada and Australia.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: When I was a senior consultant at a multinational technology consulting firm, I saw many resumes of experienced foreigners seeking junior positions just to get hired.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The admission of so many entry-level foreign ICT professionals over the past 20 years and the commoditisation of core skills, such as computer programming, has put downward pressures on wages in this industry.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Any Singaporean starting out as a software developer would be competing with many similarly skilled foreigners for jobs and promotions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This, coupled with the perception of crony hiring and discrimination against locals, prompted many Singaporeans over the past two decades to veer away from the ICT industry in favour of other sectors, leading to an even greater dearth of talent in this industry.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In the past few years, with the growth in data science, robotics and artificial intelligence, the demand for deep tech skills has increased dramatically.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Companies are now willing to pay top dollar for data scientists and cybersecurity specialists.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The NUS Graduate Employment Survey found that fresh graduates from the School of Computing have the highest gross monthly salary among all graduates, with the 75th percentile earning $6,316, higher than doctors, lawyers and business graduates.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This reflects both the high demand and the short supply of such graduates.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Yet, the supply of local tech talent is not keeping up.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is still not going to solve the manpower crunch in this industry.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: With 3,100 graduates and 20,000 new tech jobs created a year, our local graduates would not be able to fill a fifth of these roles.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will lead to a greater demand for foreigners to make up for the shortfall.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The pattern of overdependence on foreign professionals will continue.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While it is laudable that so many tech jobs are being created, how much does this benefit Singaporean workers if our people are not equipped with the skills to fill them?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It will lead to disappointment by both the companies investing in Singapore and our own people.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We should have started a bigger push to encourage and enable more students to study IT two decades ago.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Be that as it may, there is now an urgent need to reorientate our schools to prepare Singaporean students for career opportunities in technology, so as to create a stronger pipeline of local talent.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Students who are interested in working with computers should be encouraged early to pursue IT as a course of study and an eventual career.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Primary schools should introduce all students to computational thinking and basic coding as part of their core curriculum from Primary 1, although it should not be made an examination subject, as this may kill interest in it.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This could spark their early interest in tech and will help them and their parents choose suitable Secondary schools to further their interests.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We would not be alone in doing this.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Estonia, which is recognised as one of the most advanced digital societies in the world, started teaching all first graders to code almost a decade ago.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Moving forward, all Secondary schools should offer computing as an "O" level subject, and it should be extended to the "N" levels.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Computing, just like History, Geography and Literature, should be taught from Secondary 1, so that all students can try their hand at it and make an informed decision at the end of Secondary 2 if they want to pursue it further at the upper Secondary level.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Schools should develop programmes and mentorships to widen students' exposure to careers in technology, particularly those from less privileged backgrounds and also girls, given the traditionally lower female participation in the industry.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: More scholarships and grants should be awarded to students who choose to study Computing.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Tertiary institutions should connect with industries to showcase careers in tech and encourage students to pursue them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Because there are now so few Computer Science degree places in our local Universities vis-à-vis the demand, we are seeing cut-throat competition for admission and many qualified applicants are being denied places.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Take the School of Computing in the National University of Singapore, for example.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The "A" level subject prerequisites for Computer Science (CS) courses are a H2 pass in Computing, Mathematics, further Mathematics or Physics, or a good pass in H1 Mathematics.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This sounds quite achievable until we look at the indicative grade profiles of applicants offered places last year.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I doubt tech companies really need students who aced all four content subjects in Junior College.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Setting such a high bar for admission could mean missing out on many students who were initially interested in pursuing a tech career but may have decided to switch their focus to other industries after failing in their bid to study CS in local Universities.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: ITEs can also be a source of local tech talent.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Tech, after all, is not the exclusive domain of University or Polytechnic graduates.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To be sure, I am not calling for a lowering of standards just to admit more students, but an expansion of opportunities to study CS.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Minister Lawrence Wong said in his speech earlier that relying on a local pipeline is not enough and that if we increase the intake of people in ICT too sharply, there will be complaints of shortage in other sectors.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Of course, I am not advocating that everybody goes immediately into ICT, because that would be impractical.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: But if many high-growth, high-paying jobs are in the ICT sector, is it wrong to provide more educational opportunities for our fellow Singaporeans in this sector and encourage more of them to consider careers in ICT?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We should place bigger bets on tech in order to seize the burgeoning opportunities ahead of us.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Train ahead of demand, as my colleague, Mr Leon Perera proposed earlier.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This way, more Singaporeans can benefit from the thousands of well-paying tech jobs that are going to be created in the years ahead.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It will also attract more companies to set up research and development centres in Singapore because of the availability of talent.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This virtuous cycle will benefit both our economy and our people.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I would now like to address some of the imbalances that many local professionals face in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If we want to throw open our doors to global talent, our industries' demands for skilled labour can probably be met, but at what cost?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As early as 1997, when I was interning at a large local tech firm, I was surprised to discover that almost all the programmers in the IT department were foreigners.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: More than 20 years on, the situation is even more extreme in many IT firms and banks, where many management positions, especially in technology departments, are occupied by foreigners.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I am not asking the Government to mollycoddle our workers, nor are Singaporeans expecting to be "bubble wrapped" from all foreign competition.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We should remain open to foreign talent, but only those who are suitably skilled and earn their positions based on merit.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans want to be self-reliant and succeed on their own merit.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is, therefore, the responsibility of the Government to ensure that Singaporeans do not become victims of discrimination in their own country.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The world has changed and employment regulations and practices need to adapt to keep pace.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As a society, we claim to have zero tolerance for corruption and racism.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, there are other forms of corruption, like cronyism and nepotism, which have reared their ugly heads in the corporate environment.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This has sapped the morale of honest, talented and hardworking local employees who were hoping for advancement in their careers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many Members of Parliament would have heard anecdotal reports from constituents about foreign managers hiring compatriots who were less qualified than locals.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: You, Mr Speaker, were one of the first Ministers to acknowledge this disturbing phenomenon in the Committee of Supply (COS) debate in 2013, when I also raised this concern in one of my COS cuts.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Minister Tan See Leng just acknowledged that he knows these things happen.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These acts are difficult to prove and hard to catch because they can be very subtle.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is easy for the offending managers to justify that a particular candidate was the "right fit" without doing an objective, competency-based assessment against other candidates.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In Singaporean culture, hiring a less qualified candidate on account of their cultural background is considered discrimination.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, in many cultures around the world, this is the normal way society works.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While it is not my place to judge other cultures, I think Singaporeans expect that local culture and norms are adhered to while operating in our country.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This should not be difficult because most of our international friends in Singapore already do this.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Companies which operate in Singapore should adopt a zero-tolerance stance against cronyism in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This should be reflected in each company's corporate ethos and codes of conduct.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Companies should provide channels for whistleblowing and encourage reporting of such practices.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Although this is hard to prove, it could serve as a deterrent in egregious cases.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I note that Singapore Exchange Regulation is already proposing to step up efforts to enhance board diversity.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These confidential reports should be shared with the Parliamentary Standing Select Committee on foreign employment, which the Leader of the Opposition proposed earlier.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will allow MOM to objectively assess the concentration risk of foreigners from any one country before issuing them work passes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Companies must provide a reasonable justification if they cannot adhere to this threshold.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: None of what I have proposed should cause much inconvenience to companies.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They just need to run a simple query against their employee database to come up with the numbers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It will not be a deterrent to invest or set up business in Singapore, since we are not imposing any hard quotas on them or preventing them from hiring foreigners.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Yet, this level of transparency will nudge companies to relook their HR policies and expand the opportunities they provide for the hiring and advancement of local talent.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These solutions are neither easy nor cheap, but they are necessary if we are to remain a competitive economy and a cohesive society in the decades to come.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The lump of labour fallacy is the mistaken idea that there is always a fixed number of jobs.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Instead, the number of jobs in an economy is variable and determined by the interactions between the pace of job creation and the pace of job destruction.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The role of foreign direct investment recognises that in a small open economy like Singapore, with the right institutions and business-friendly policies, an increase in the size of the labour force boosts the return to capital and thus attracts multinational corporations to set up shop and create new job vacancies.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The Mozart effect recognises that if talent is randomly distributed across a given population, then the bigger the size of the population, the greater the absolute number of talented people.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The pace of job creation over the decades reflects the changing comparative advantage of the economy.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In the 1960s to the 1980s, as factories were built, the expanding manufacturing sector provided jobs to Singapore citizens even as the size of the foreign workforce expanded.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In the 1990s to the present decade, the financial sector expanded and also created new job vacancies.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, real wages were, on the whole, rising even though the economy faced adverse economic shocks that caused recessions in successive decades since 1965.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: It should be acknowledged that the Global Financial Crisis that started in 2008 most likely had lingering effects on pulling down the wage growth in the years 2009 and 2010.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: But other than that, over the decade as a whole, it is the case that as standard of living has risen, real wages, by and large, have gone up.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Certainly, from the year 2000 onwards, there came to be some divergence.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The better-skilled workers continued to see rising wages whereas in the 10 years since 2000, the low-wage workers have seen their wages somewhat decline.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: But the country has dealt with that and our focus today is on foreign talent policy.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: So, overall, with technological diffusion, because we have stayed connected to the global economy, we have been able to catch up with the US standard of living, starting from less than a third of the level of US purchasing-power-parity-adjusted GDP per capita in 1965.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: So, from 1978 to 2013, the year when I was looking at the trend, total labour force increased three times but total FDI stock increased by more than 10 times.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: So, the stock of Foreign Direct Investment per worker more than increased.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Then, from 2013 to 2017, just to check the more recent data, 2017 is the latest year that I have found publicly available data on the stock of FDI.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: That is in the Singapore Yearbook of Statistics 2019.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The latest year of the data on the stock of FDI is for 2017.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Overall then, total FDI has grown much faster than total labour force.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, you would find that the services sector share of the total FDI stock – because we have data as well of FDI stock divided across industry, manufacturing, services, and broken down – has been increasing over the years.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: So, manufacturing has been shrinking in terms of its command of the total share of FDI, even as total FDI has gone up, which means disproportionately more of it has gone into the services sector and, in particular, the financial and insurance services, where many of our PMEs find their employment.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: A direct benefit of the strong presence of multinational corporations (MNCs) that undertake the FDI in the Singapore economy comes from what is known as the employer-size wage effect.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: So, two persons who graduated from the same university, the one who works at the MNC, holding everything constant, tends to be paid more than at a smaller firm.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: That is empirical fact widely acknowledged now in the labour economics literature.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: It is true that in the early stages of recovery from a recession, small firms provide a more rapid pace of job creation than large firms in the early stage of an economic recovery.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: However, in the later stages of economic recovery, the pace of job creation tends to be more rapid at large firms and workers enjoy pay rises when they join these large firms.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: So, that is a huge advantage that we have got, that even as we have expanded our labour force, the number showed that the increase in the stock of FDI really has been huge.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: And that has been a great help in both creating good jobs and overall providing better wages.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: My final point – the Mozart effect in the face of a declining citizen workforce because of the below replacement total fertility rate.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: While MNCs still play an important part in creating new technologies, we need them both for the jobs with better pay and also their part in creating new technology because they also do R&D.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Working in an MNC might be a prelude to stepping out to launch a new business venture since moving between departments in an MNC exposes a worker to different facets of running a business.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: A shift in our own education system towards preparing students to cope with novelties and picking themselves up after failures will also help to increase the supply of entrepreneurs to boost the SME sector.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: However, as an empirical matter, SMEs exit their respective industries more frequently than large firms.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Many new business ventures end up in failure but, among the ones that survive, their growth is higher than the average growth rate.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The demographic transition, however, to a declining citizen workforce carries the implication that it will be difficult to sustain the pace of indigenous innovation necessary to maintain the trend growth.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Even as it now faces the challenges of a growth transition, a demographic transition, technological disruptions and higher worker aspirations, it will be the ability to develop political consensus and supporting social and economic institutions to continue to embrace economic openness, not only to goods and capital but also to people, that will assure it of a future with a supply of good jobs and wages.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, I support Minister Lawrence Wong's Motion to secure Singaporean jobs and livelihoods while staying open and connected to the world, in order to grow and prosper, even as we focus on the other points made in the Motion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Before I continue, I wish to declare that I am an educator at an institution of higher education, delivering courses in international trade and finance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Last month, Ministers Ong Ye Kung and Tan See Leng provided thoughtful expositions about the benefits of free trade for economic growth and prosperity, and Prof Hoon Hian Teck has just done the same.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Minister Ong has also shared with us his perspective – which I am convinced is deeply embedded in his intellectual DNA – as a trade negotiator, while simultaneously exposing us to the delicacy that is samsu.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: He also clearly articulated the Government’s position, that anxieties on jobs, while legitimate, are distinct from both FTAs, in general, and CECA, in particular.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The proposition that free trade is a net positive for national welfare has long and illustrious roots, dating back to the 18th and early 19th century.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In my courses, I teach this idea in my very first lecture: that countries are better off when they specialise and trade, instead of trying to take on the burden of producing everything within its own borders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is the case even for an advanced economy, in possession of technological capabilities to produce all manner of goods more efficiently than others can.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The conclusion is counter-intuitive, but once one embraces the logic, it is incontrovertible, and the insight deeply satisfying.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, this insight has been characterised as both non-trivial and elusive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In my second lecture, however, my students quickly learn that free trade is not an unadorned good.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even in the simplest of models, trading relationships between two countries will throw up both winners and losers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In general, for capital-rich, advanced economies, the gainers will, unsurprisingly, be industry, leaving the lot of workers worse off.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: By a similar token, higher-skilled labour in developed countries tend to benefit from trade opening, while the lower-skilled ones are often left behind.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But this unequal outcome need not be the death knell for free trade.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In the longer run, as workers displaced by trade find new jobs and reallocate to in-demand sectors, wages and employment would even out.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, since the gains outweigh the losses, it is entirely possible for winners – in this example, capitalists or higher-skilled professionals – to compensate the losers, the workers, at least, in part.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Doing so leaves everyone better off and helps ease the transition to a more liberal trading regime.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And there you have it: the case for free trade, which has survived many generations of subsequent elaborations, with bells and whistles thrown in.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Thus, as long as we keep in mind the pressing need to ease the distributional consequences, we can always build a national consensus in support of trade liberalisation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Alas, in the real world that we inhabit, many policymakers have often forgotten this important imperative.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, globally, the pursuit of trading relations has often left losing parties to fend for themselves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: When Singapore was a relatively poor, underdeveloped economy, this mattered a lot less.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, the gainers in this case were our masses of low-skilled labour, hungry for jobs and opportunities that would be ushered in by embracing globalisation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: With so many with so little to lose, it was straightforward to build a large coalition in support of free trade.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But we are no longer poor, and this complicates matters.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, this all comes down to the recognition that free trade and free trade agreements are hardly the same thing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Many of these agreements have been concluded with insufficient attention to the distributional consequences for the minority that has been hard done by the deal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As a result, we have ventured from the rules of thumb on compensation that economists have routinely advocated to secure support for free trade.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be completely fair to governments worldwide, including this one, the standard prescription for compensation has not been completely ignored.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The United States first enacted the Trade Expansion Act of 1962.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The EU created a Globalisation Adjustment Fund in 2007.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Closer to our neighbourhood, South Korea rolled out an adjustment programme targeted at SMEs that same year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But in many instances, these programmes do not do enough.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Qualification criteria for assistance tend to be stringent, and those who ultimately benefit from such programmes turn out to be only a small fraction of those who have lost jobs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Some programmes are not even specifically targeted at displacement due to trade and, as a result, underemphasise the importance of retraining and reskilling.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Other Workers’ Party colleagues have also spoken of challenges faced by our workers as they adapt to changes wrought by trade, such as Aljunied Member Sylvia Lim on underemployment and my Sengkang colleague, Louis Chua, on expanding worker protections.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But suffice to say that there is more we can do to provide an end-to-end jobs safety net that can help our workers cope with pressures from globalisation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This renewed attention to adjustment costs and distributional consequences has also come under greater re-examination even within the economics profession.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This was prompted, in no small part, by the harsh realities of the so-called “China Shock,” which accompanied the entry of China into the World Trade Organization in 2001.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The comfortable consensus in support of free trade that had existed for so long began to be seriously questioned.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Emerging evidence from the widespread displacement of workers in industrialised economies, especially in the manufacturing sector, where China has proven to be a formidable competitor, revealed that output, wages and employment losses in sectors particularly exposed to imported Chinese goods tend to be large and significant.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These effects were not limited solely to sectors confronting Chinese import competition.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The spillovers left whole regions – which used to hum with economic activity and offer respectable middle-class jobs – decimated, leaving behind armies of unemployed, disaffected workers, while also inducing declines in the wages of even those workers who worked in unrelated sectors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: With this general preamble on the merits, and demerits, of free trade agreements, it is appropriate for us to turn to a more careful examination of CECA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While the deal may, prima facie, look like a free trade agreement just like any other, it actually carries its own set of idiosyncrasies, both in practical terms and for our nation at this moment in our history.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For starters, India is much, much larger than our Little Red Dot.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is not just in geographic size, which is a given.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But it also dominates us in terms of economic size.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One important lesson that economists have learned from China’s 2001 WTO entry is that, unlike the trade liberalisation experiences of the 1970s through 1990s, gaining access to a massive market also means accepting the entry of a massive labour force.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: When there is a flood of new, lower-wage workers joining an industry that is newly open to trade, higher-wage workers that have been displaced are not easily absorbed into the rest of the economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, we should recognise that India is also at a far earlier stage of development journey than we are.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another important consequence of trade opening is that, over time, the prices paid to inputs of production – wages, rents or interest – will tend to meet somewhere in the middle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: With wages so much lower in India compared to Singapore, this could lead to a sharp downward shift in our local workers’ earnings, before some sort of convergence is achieved.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Importantly, some adjustment of this nature will occur even if foreign workers do not relocate to local shores.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is our very own version of the China Shock.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: All this is not to say that CECA is fundamentally flawed, nor that it is the main factor driving our workers’ anxieties which, as my other Workers’ Party colleagues have elaborated, are more because of our labour market and social protection policies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Doing so will bring us back to the standard remedy I mentioned earlier: that gainers compensate losers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Do we have just cause to believe that this has been the case for CECA, or for that matter, all our FTAs?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is unclear if companies that have enjoyed enhanced access to the foreign market as a result of our trade agreements necessarily pay higher taxes as a consequence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Nor is it clear that professionals recruited from foreign nations to work in Singapore systematically do, either.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: When all is said and done, it appears, from my vantage point, that the Government has been the one picking up the slack, via WSG and other adjustment schemes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As this House is well aware, Singapore is a small island bereft of natural resources, which has meant that our success has always been because of our people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As a developing country after Independence, we invested heavily in educating our workforce, producing hardworking, well-trained workers that could hold their own in competition against the rest of the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At the same time, we refined and adapted the legal institutions and civil services that we inherited as a British colony.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We imbued our people with a sense of national pride, identity and common purpose.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We had to inculcate such values, slowly, over decades, via national education, patriotic songs, a shared history and, yes, our common love for food and shopping.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Do our FTAs and labour market policies that encourage large immigration flows compromise these key contributors to our past prosperity?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While the jury is still out, there are concerns about the entry of workers with less-than-stellar educational qualifications, the presence of a sizeable but temporary expatriate labour force with a limited understanding of our unique national identity, and the dilution of the cultural capital that has hitherto been so central to our success.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The promise behind FTAs is that it will lead to increased economic opportunities, in both trade and investment, traditional strong suits for our economy, accompanied by the creation of more jobs for Singaporeans, on net, as a result.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such agreements also allow us to contribute positively, albeit indirectly, to advancing the development of our trading partners.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We need to know whether these agreements have been detrimental to the job prospects of some of our local PMETs, who are already anxious about automation-related retrenchment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We need to know whether local credentials and qualifications issued to our graduates may inadvertently become undervalued, relative to foreign ones, because of mutual recognition clauses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We need to affirm our tenuously employed workers, those who have been involuntarily forced into food delivery and private car hire jobs, that FTAs do not open up loopholes to excessive labour inflows.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such a move would permit our researchers and interested members of the public to come to their own conclusions and correct misperceptions that this Government has routinely railed against.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I am not so sure I am the right person to talk but, nevertheless, I have the duty to speak for the workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This is so, as it directly impacts workers who are at the heart of all that we do in the Labour Movement.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: While acknowledging the role of foreign talent, I would like to focus my energy more on how to help our fellow workers to seize and secure the available good-paying jobs from any big companies that offer them.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The unions and Labour Movement are constantly looking at how to help workers achieve better employment and employability outcomes in the long run.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I would, once again, like to call upon employers to be proactive in equipping your workforce with relevant skills to meet the evolving needs of your industry now and the future.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The unions will work with you to rally the workforce, allay any fears of changes and provide constant ground-up feedback.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The unions would not hesitate to deal with such companies to ensure PMEs receive fair hiring opportunities and are treated fairly when in employment.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: On the broader topic of workplace discrimination, NTUC will work closely with our tripartite partners in the Tripartite Committee on Workplace Fairness to improve workplace fairness.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: However, I am aware that not all workplace discrimination can be resolved through legislation.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The unions will continue to play an important role to work closely with employers to resolve workplace grievances.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: It has remained to be our tried and tested formula to ensure social and economic stability and success.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: As such, NTUC and the unions look forward to working together with our tripartite partners to tackle the next bound of workforce challenges and build an inclusive workforce.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Speaker, Singapore has excelled as a regional hub for businesses and talents for a number of business sectors.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: A few of Singapore's success factors are: one, public policies that prioritise the long-term interests of Singapore; two, pragmatic execution of public policies; three, open and multicultural society; four, in the face of competition, we always choose to level up by improving ourselves; and five, never wasting a crisis to emerge stronger.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has been a huge crisis for us but, through the methodical way, we have handled it.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: It is beginning to turn into a great opportunity.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: We are one of the few Asia Pacific countries that have a real plan for transiting into an endemic COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Global Investors have seen not just the resilience of the economy, but also the resilience of the society and the people of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: We can now see the conditions for Singapore to develop into an important regional or even global hub for the technology sector.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: In due course, we might become a hub for the pharma-medical and sustainability sectors as well.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: When we have the chance to develop both the breadth and depth of a desirable industry cluster, we should do so quickly and decisively.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Once we have achieved the ecosystem of companies and talents, we will likely continue to attract even more investments.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Conversely, if we were hesitant or slow to act, the ecosystem takes root somewhere else, future investments and talent will be drawn there instead.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: One of the most important considerations for businesses to locate or expand their HQ operations or R&D centres in Singapore is the availability of the right talent pool to support their growth.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: This is a genuine concern of many corporation executives, who are further unnerved by anti-foreigner public discourse.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: If our total workforce cannot meet the needs of companies, they will move out.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: We seem to take it for granted that people always want to come to Singapore to live and work.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Today, we remain attractive, but our attractiveness is relative.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: It depends as much on what we do as what our present and future competitors do.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: One critical trend to note is how digital connectivity has facilitated working from home. "Home", in this context, need not be in Singapore, it can be anywhere.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: The person competing for a job need not be physically in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: This will heighten the competition for businesses, investments and talents among cities and facilitate the emergence of new and credible competitor cities to Singapore in the future.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: To conclude, managing a complementary local and foreign workforce is a complex and emotive endeavour.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: We also need to be mindful at the cusp of emerging stronger from the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: We should try not to let great opportunities slip by.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: In the course of my work, it is always nice to meet overseas executives who had previously worked in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: They understand Singapore and still have positive regard for us.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: In a way, they continue to contribute even after they have left Singapore by helping to bridge understanding and forge business relationships for us, not unlike a school alumni.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: During my regular home visit discussions with residents at Zhenghua as well as my meetings with industry, there are employers and employees who are even concerned if newly-learned skillsets are adequate in view of continued disruptions and technological advancement.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some residents who are self-employed shared with me their concerns that “Work From Home” now means “Work From Anywhere” and clients are starting to offshore services.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The competition for jobs and opportunities is no longer confined to a geographical boundary.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We are undergoing a significant transformation, and providing national clarity on what we are doing to emerge more competitive and relevant is essential.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In my comments today I will be supporting the Motion that the Government has doubled down on our focus on workforce skills upgrading and job security; and this enables us to compete globally through strategic foreign trade agreements with greater confidence.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Government has been reviewing and enhancing several core training schemes.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, the Training Support Package and Absentee Payroll were enhanced.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Over and above that, many other schemes, such as the Professional Conversion Programme (PCP), Place and Train Programme (PnT) and so on, were put in place.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These were introduced to help support individuals and employers with skills upgrading opportunities that are directly linked to job placement.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Employers and employees will now be assured that the Government takes this issue very seriously.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the spirit of continuous review and resolving the issue from all angles and addressing concerns upstream, I would like to suggest three more areas.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The intent of these suggestions is to keep our people in jobs and create opportunities for progression.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By doing so, we reduce the probability of displacement which creates greater distress for Singaporeans and considerably more resources for assistance.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This approach is more sustainable for the Government, employers and employees.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The first is to provide a degree of longevity for those schemes that were enhanced last year, thereby giving our workers and employers confidence that the Government understands that their transition will take time.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This level of commitment will translate well to the enterprise level and workers will have assurance that help will not be pulled back too soon.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I am pleased to hear earlier from Minister Lawrence Wong that MOF is considering this.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By ensuring direct connectivity between employers' transformation and their employees' upskilling, rather than two separate activities, it maximises the return on investments for our grant schemes.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There will be many details that need to be sorted out to make this happen.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But I believe it would have a significant impact on how our workforce can see their training directly linked to their employers’ strategic direction.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This will reiterate and complement the Government’s existing and ongoing SkillsFuture initiatives, ensuring our workforce is future-ready through upskilling and reskilling.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With such a comprehensive suite of measures from skill investments to enhanced employer support and deeper legislative powers to reduce workplace discrimination, we can keep our borders open with confidence.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To further mitigate the downsides of disruptions and the "work from anywhere" phenomenon, we need to grow and anchor jobs in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To do so, we need to grow and entrench employers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Being open and connected is critical for Singapore’s competitiveness because many of our employers can only succeed if Singapore is strategically plugged into the global flow of trade, investments and people.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our FTAs are purposefully crafted and executed to ensure that our employers and workers benefit from such connectivity.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It allows employers to have access to overseas markets for their products and services; and it allows for our employers to also source for skills and technologies to accelerate their capabilities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The benefits of these agreements ensure that Singapore, with our employers and our workers, are relevant in the global movement of economic activities which lead to value creation back home.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is not about either the big picture or the small picture.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But it is about the real and practical picture of how our workers make a living by Singapore remaining open to the world because we have been strengthening ourselves.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Tunity Technologies is a home-grown employer in the business of RFID technology.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This employer benefited from many MNCs in Singapore during their inception through winning business contracts that enabled them to deepen their R&D from the revenue opportunity.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the words of Ms Lim Peck Hui, Managing Director of Tunity, and I quote: “Tunity is chosen by MNCs facing the most challenging and complex RFID projects.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such collaboration allows Tunity to develop more IPs to serve them and their clients which, in turn, strengthens our expertise, experience and capabilities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some of the collaborations bring Tunity's solutions beyond Singapore which, by ourselves, would not have been made possible.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This has helped us grow over the past 18 years.” Tunity exemplifies actually what Prof Hoon Hian Teck shared earlier on the need for SMEs to evolve from technology imitation to technology innovation and how staying open has enabled SMEs to do so.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This example of Tunity truly illustrates how participating in the global economy has helped them grow.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And as Tunity grew, they contributed further to our economy and society, hired local PMEs, creating a positive virtuous cycle.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This multi-pronged approach is important so that we can keep our borders open with confidence because our workforce is continually being prepared, ready and relevant.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore cannot live in fear of how the world is changing.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are movements which focus only on the downsides of globalisation and I believe this is not a healthy conversation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There will always be challenges and we must be sensitive to them.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, I rise in support of the Motion standing in the name of the Minister for Finance.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: He was talking about the provisions within CECA, that he would like to look at CECA and refine it.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, perhaps, can I ask him to elaborate on what he means by refining, which aspects of CECA does he want to review and change?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Just to be clear, I was saying that it was time to evaluate the agreement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And my call explicitly was for additional information for us to actually better understand what the distributional implications of the agreement had been.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We did not start the FTAs in 1965.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, I understand it is a technical distinction.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But I think it underscores the point that I was trying to raise, which is that it is important that we have policies, Government policies, to help ease this process of redistribution.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, in the interest of time, I thank you for acknowledging that the Government has been making these transfers and easing this process of redistribution, through our policy refinements and tweaking and our constant improvement in the entire situation.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In this speech, I would like to focus on two sectors that have drawn some measure of unhappiness and which the hon Member Mr Leong Mun Wai is quite fond of bringing up: financial services and technology/ICT.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I think we can safely assume that these are sectors in which he would like to see an urgent “rebalancing of the foreign PMET population” as well as a “review of the provisions in CECA”.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: At this point, I would like to declare my interest as a managing director and partner of a management consulting firm.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I do a good portion of my consulting work with banks and tech companies, and I want to share some perspectives on just how important getting the right balance in this debate around the foreign talent policy is to our competitiveness in these two sectors.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: These are both people businesses that lend themselves to being natural hubs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: These sectors do not exist merely to provide services to our domestic market.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Our strategy has been, and must unequivocally remain, to be a regional and global hub.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In the financial sector, we have banks of every colour: local banks, regional banks, multinational corporation banks.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Today, Chinese banks are actively entering the market; the fintech sector has been growing; and we are seeing the birth of the first digital banks.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Wealth management continues to grow strongly, with family offices flocking here, on whose heels highly sophisticated legal practices are also coming.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, many PMET jobs have been created, for locals and foreigners, within the sector and in adjacent sectors.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Jobs that a lot of Singaporeans want, not only for the good pay but also for a multinational corporation work environment that is seen to be more progressive, dynamic and diverse.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Today, we are, without a doubt, the place to be for financial services in Asia.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is a status that only a few global cities can claim and it is a status we cannot take for granted.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: While more recently forged, our status as a tech hub is growing by the day, with the FANG (Facebook, Amazon, Netflix and Google) companies, or the global tech giants, ramping up their Asian headquarters here.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Chinese tech giants have also come: the Bytedances, the Alibabas, the Ping Ans, the Tencents.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They bring with them high-paying jobs, stock options and a startup culture that attracts some of our brightest young Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We have unicorns like Shopee and we are also seeing more and more early stage startups or pre-unicorns.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There is also a growing phenomenon of founding teams that comprise both Singaporeans and foreigners, and that diversity is fuelling innovation and entrepreneurship.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Both these sectors are important and growing sectors for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: MNCs come for many reasons – our attractive tax laws, our business infrastructure, our skilled workforce and, yes, our open foreign talent policy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They do not only come because of our foreign talent policy, but they will not come if we curtail the flow of talent so much that they no longer feel they have access to a global talent pool.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Because they play a global game and a global game requires a global talent pool.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Global talent may also not come if they hear from their peers that they will not feel welcome.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: That explains why we have a lot of foreigners in these sectors and, in particular, a high concentration of Indian nationals, not CECA nor other FTAs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: The English Premier League (EPL) has, undoubtedly, become the most successful football league in the world.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: The EPL does not exist to bring Britons their weekly fix of soccer.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: The EPL has legions of fans around the world.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: For two of the past three seasons, the Champions League final has been an all-England affair.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: For Sunday’s match versus Leeds, the Liverpool starting 11 comprised nine nationalities, with only two Englishmen.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: But if you want to compete in the Champions League, you need the Messis, the Cristiano Ronaldos and the Mo Salahs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: They not only complement the homegrown talent, they improve them.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Local boy Trent Alexander Arnold would not be as good a right-back as he is today if he was not pinging in crosses every day to the likes of Mo Salah and Sadio Mane, without Allison and Van Dijk yelling instructions to the back four.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: This openness to talent has allowed Liverpool to bring pure joy to their fans around the world.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: It allows Liverpool kids to grow up dreaming of being the next Trent Alexandra Arnold or Curtis Jones, both academy lads.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: It also means that many local lads and academy players never break into the senior team.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Just think of Harry Wilson, the 2017/2018 Academy Player of the Year, who recently joined Fulham, unable to break the front three of Salah, Mane and Firmino.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: But with the foundation of a club like Liverpool, it is a soft landing.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: They can still make a great career for themselves.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Just think of Conor Coady who now enjoys an important role at Wolves, and even earned a call-up to the national team for Euro 2020.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Or the tireless James Milner, whose minutes get less as he pushes the old age of 36, but only a fool would question his importance to the team, on and off the pitch, for his versatility, his experience and his leadership, to talk to the younger players or in Klopp’s word, to do “his kind of a little bit dirty dressing room talks that I cannot do, these things you say in the dressing room that I am not allowed to say in public.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: I, for one, would not object if the rumours of a future role in management in Klopp’s team were to come true.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: I have spoken to residents who feel they have been displaced because there was a foreigner willing to work for lower pay.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: I have spoken to residents who see that the new expat manager is always followed by more of his countrymen.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: I have spoken to residents who have felt discriminated against at work, passed up for promotions and the plum assignments.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: I have spoken to residents who question whether their foreign colleagues really have the qualifications claimed.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: I have spoken to graduates of our tertiary institutions, who find they cannot land the sexier jobs in ICT, which seem to demand experience that they think should only be expected of people with a few years of experience, not a fresh graduate.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: And I have spoken to residents in their 30s and 50s, who have jobs, but are feeling anxious about which side they will be on in the next round of headcount cuts, or just feel a little stuck.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: The Government must be firm in enforcing this.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: It also makes sense to increase the EP and S Pass salary criteria because Singaporeans today are different from 20 or five years ago.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: We have more Singaporeans who can do these jobs and companies must recognise that.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: But it is dangerous to generalise and falsely characterise these issues as more pervasive than they are just to stoke emotions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: It is dangerous to believe that if we just had fewer foreigners, all the problems would be solved and Singaporeans would get all the jobs, because there are other issues at play.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: It is dangerous to believe that if we tell our banks and tech firms that we will not approve most of their EP applications and renewals, as I seem to hear the PSP say, that they have to get rid of the foreign talent they already have to meet some concentration ratios that the hard-earned status of being a global financial and tech hub will not be eroded.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Talk to people in the industry and they will tell you how tight the labour market is, how hard it is to fill many of the roles.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Indeed, as it has become more difficult to bring in new people, I have heard that people already in the market are able to jump to another opening, almost always with a minimum salary bump of 20% to 30% and often also with a jump in role.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: In ICT, we now have lots of well-trained IT project managers.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: But, for roles like backend developers and data scientists, often, when they put out applications for these roles, many of the Singaporean CVs they receive check off perhaps one or two of the five to six skills involved.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: And for those who check off more boxes, the competition for those who have all the skills is intense – from the tech giants, Chinese firms, even GovTech – where I have to declare I am on the board.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: On compliance in banking, we have a lot of Singaporeans in compliance.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: But for some, their knowledge is of traditional compliance frameworks while, globally, banks are adopting smart compliance, which is much more agile and aligned to business objectives, and they do not yet have that experience.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: At the leadership level, we still hear that it is still difficult to find enough Singaporeans with the leadership, communication, change management and influencing skills needed to lead in the complex multi-stakeholder environment common in most MNC organisations.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: A reason often cited is that many Singaporeans lack international work and management experience.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Minister Lawrence Wong and Minister Tan See Leng have shared the changes that have been made over time to our foreign talent policy and guidelines on employment practices.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: These have been necessary and timely, and the impact is being felt.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: But, again, does that mean that the roles will go to Singaporeans?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: The reality is that global banks are unlikely to settle because their own competition is so intense and the pressure to deliver outcomes so strong.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
