text: So, if getting an EP takes longer and is more uncertain, if they do not see the skillsets immediately available in the local market, they choose to wait or they build in flexibility for themselves, such as by "parking" the staff in London, New York, Hong Kong or Dubai temporarily, but, potentially, permanently.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: A senior bank HR executive shared that while she is supportive of the move to increase EP salary criteria, if new restrictions go too far, it will force them to reconsider their location strategies.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: By now, MNCs have gotten good at working in remote teams.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: It is not inconceivable that banks move some tech and operations roles to India or even Poland and Russia.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Indeed, it is already happening, taking along with them jobs held by Singaporeans in those teams.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Tech managers echoed these sentiments. "I could try and settle on a lower quality candidate but that really doesn’t sit well with me.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: I can wait several months but that doesn’t really work in business.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: None of these is a great option I really want to do.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: I hope to not be put in the difficult position of making these kinds of trade-offs between quality, time and location," says a hiring manager in tech.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: At the same time, many banks and tech companies are heeding the Government's call to invest in the Singaporean Core.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: At the next level, where the jobs require more specialised technical skills, there is a mix of Singaporeans and foreigners and they are trying different things to increase the proportion of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: They had tried getting hiring managers to carve out time to develop their local talent, but it did not really work – perhaps an ask too big of busy hiring managers.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: But they are now looking to start a scheme where local talent can shadow or do projects with the hiring manager one or two days a week.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: For even more senior roles, they are pushing to give internal Singaporean candidates more opportunities.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: And at all levels, screening and interviewing practices have been updated to encourage more diversity and Singaporean representation.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: For example, at least three parties, including HR, interview every candidate to address the perception that some foreign hiring managers tend to favour people from their own countries.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Similarly, in the tech sector, companies like Google are very deliberate in making sure that locals are represented in the screening and interviewing process and have also created traineeships under schemes like SG United.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Google has made a few hires from this programme and has contributed more trained talent to their ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: All these are initiatives that take effort, but they do them.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: She said, “I love what I do and I enjoy working with the diversity of colleagues.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: If Singapore were not open and Company X hadn't come here, I would never have had the opportunity to work for this great company." Another friend, who is in one of the digital banks, said, "I get to be involved in creating a new business model.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: I'm learning every day." Meanwhile, a former colleague who joined one of the unicorns has recently embarked on an exciting adventure to head up their operations as they take bold steps to expand in Brazil.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: These positive feelings persist even when there are disappointments.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Ms L shared with me how she had applied for the position of country manager, which eventually went to a foreigner. "I could feel like it was an opportunity taken from me, but you know what?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: I report to him now and I have learnt a lot from him.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: I don't begrudge him that role at all because I recognise him as a world-class talent.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: So, I learn from him and maybe one day I'll get my shot." These are intensely personal stories.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: The PSP talks about rebalancing the foreign labour force.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Based on the list of concrete proposals on how they seek to achieve that, I can only observe that they seem to be fixated on achieving this rebalancing by taking unilateral actions to reduce the number of foreigners as quickly as possible, as if that is the only way it can be done.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: It is as if the PSP has no faith in Singaporeans to get there on our own merit without risking our global hub proposition.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: We Singaporeans are much more adaptable and resilient than that.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: The Government has made significant investments in the Singaporean Core.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: The number of training and reskilling programmes for the unemployed has been impressive.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: It is still too early to tell what the overall outcomes will be, but we have some reason to be optimistic.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: We all know of mid-career PMETs who have taken courses and not landed a job, but let us not forget to celebrate those who have and let us keep working on it.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Reskilling is also relevant to two other groups of Singaporeans: first, Singaporeans who have jobs but are at risk either due to sunsetting sectors or their individual skillsets; and, second, our graduates.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: In my maiden speech, I called on companies to take accountability for their employees' learning.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: In many organisations, learning and development are still not top of mind.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Too often, conversations about skills are associated with performance management rather than professional development.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Employers sometimes say that it is difficult to get their employees to go for reskilling, even though failure to reskill will, ultimately, cost them their current jobs and their future prospects.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: As for our tertiary graduates, more can be done to equip them with industry-relevant skills, knowledge and tools.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: You may see this as an indictment of our tertiary institutions but that is not entirely fair.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: It is difficult for professors and curricula to keep up with the pace at which industry is moving, specifically when it comes to the specific tools that are used only in the industry.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: When companies recruit for backend engineers, they look not only for knowledge of backend programming languages but also knowledge of popular frameworks like Spring Framework, Spring Security or Django used in industry.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: We do not quite have this culture here yet.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: It is easy to say Singaporeans are too sheltered, passive and complacent, but I submit it is, in fact, often because they lack awareness and understanding of where and how to start, especially if there are frictions that make it difficult to, such as family commitments or side gigs to augment family incomes.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar, if you can wrap up, please.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Do not just complain that company job postings or internal job portals are just for show, even if that may be true in some cases.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: This Motion proposed by the Minister for Finance reiterates this.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: It is critical we get this balance right.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We will now call the Minister for Finance to make his reply on his Motion on Securing Singaporeans' Jobs and Livelihoods, followed by Mr Leong Mun Wai for his reply on his Motion on Foreign Talent Policy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is the reality of the globalised world we live in and this is the inevitable price of human progress.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: How Singapore capitalises on these opportunities while addressing the anxieties around jobs will determine our success and whether we remain cohesive and intact as one people.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I am glad that Members who have spoken acknowledged that this is a complex issue requiring a delicate balancing act.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We need to deliberate our options carefully and work hard to find solutions that balance the different interests and the needs of our stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If I may summarise the basic thrust of their argument: we have too many foreigners in Singapore; let us squeeze them out of Singapore; and these jobs will go to Singaporeans; even better, our wages will go up.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: First, when we squeeze foreign PMETs, the jobs will not automatically go to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Global businesses are here – international consultancies and private banks.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They are here, as Ms Mariam Jaafar said just now, to play the global game.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They are not here to serve the Singapore market.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They are here to serve the region and the world.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Here, in Singapore, they want to bring together an international team.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Imagine if you tell them, "Look, you can only be here if you fulfil 90% of your staff being locals.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is the condition." Why would they find that attractive anymore?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: To assume that by squeezing the foreigners, all these jobs will go to Singaporeans, I think that is just being very simplistic about the argument.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But Mr Leong Mun Wai goes further than that.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: He says, "Look, if foreigners go and Singaporeans cannot take the jobs, that is the failure of the education system." Really?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think that argument is completely disingenuous and does a great disservice to our educators and teachers in our schools and Institutes of Higher Learning.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Leon Perera and Mr Gerald Giam did not go as far as Mr Leong Mun Wai, but they had variations of the same argument.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If only you taught all the kids coding from a young age 20 years ago.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But I think all of these arguments miss out on the most important point.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And, that is, the stark reality that Singaporeans are great as a workforce, but there are just not enough of us.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Look at the services sector, healthcare is growing, we need more people to look after our elderly population.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Oh, by the way, low-income issues are a problem, do we not need more social workers, too?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And did some Members of the PSP not ask earlier when I was in MOE, they certainly did, let us recruit more teachers?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Where are we going to find all the Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Indeed, if you go to any of our faculties or maybe most of the faculties in our Universities, Polytechnics and ITEs, they will tell you, when they talk to industries, the industries and employers are saying, "Look, we want your graduates but produce more of them." And how are we going to produce more Singaporean graduates?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If we move to one area, the other will say that there is a shortage.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Then, there is another argument that says, "Look, so many mid-careers underemployed.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Let us train them." Yes, we are doing our best to train all the mid-career PMETs, but this does not happen overnight.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: All of us know, it is very hard for someone in his 40s and 50s to make a career change to transit from one industry that they have been working in for years to another industry.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that is why, as I have mentioned earlier, the Government is going all out to help our mid-careers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are investing more heavily in SkillsFuture, in lifelong learning, we are working with our tripartite partners, and especially with NTUC and the Labour Movement.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But individuals also do have to make the effort in order to make these transitions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is hard work getting this reskilling done and we should not just automatically assume that squeezing foreigners means jobs will go to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Second, Ms Hazel Poa also showed the chart that suggested there was an association between tight labour markets and wage growth.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Yes, perhaps there was; the data is quite clear, based on the last 10 years.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But I would say be careful about drawing simplistic policy conclusions from that data.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: After that, we waited for a while to make sure that the economy has stabilised.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And if you recall, we tightened our foreign worker policies, levies and quotas.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: At the same time, the economy bounced back very sharply, much, much more strongly than we expected.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, I remember after 2011 and entering politics, we were discussing this issue, having dialogues.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Many businesses and employers were literally scolding us for tightening foreign worker policies.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Why are you holding us back?" They were very upset with us.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But it was that combination of factors – tightening of foreign worker policies, the very strong economic growth during that period – that resulted in a wage growth.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If we make that simplistic conclusion, that tight labour markets – just tighten, just tighten – wages will automatically rise, I think we may be going down a very dangerous path, because, beyond a point, if wage increases are not matched by productivity increases, we will lose our competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: When that happens, we are not just squeezing out foreigners, we will be squeezing out investments, and jobs will go with them.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That leads me to my third point, which is that this thinking is not just simplistic or wishful; it is fatally flawed.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If we were to take such a short-sighted approach, companies will leave and jobs will leave with them.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Over time, Singapore's reputation as a business hub will surely be impacted.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Our economy will decline and Singaporeans will suffer.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There is another thing about the PSP's approach that worries me.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that is the complacent assumption in their thinking that Singapore has arrived and companies just want to be here.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, the Government can set tougher rules and the companies will have to put up with them because they had no choice.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Global competition for investments is relentless and more intense than ever.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It took many decades of hard work to get to where we are today.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Please have a care about what we say or do because things can fall apart very easily.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: At the same time, we know that there are downsides to being an open economy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we will deal with these downsides proactively.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim just now talked about the concern about an "India shock".

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And I think he also suggested that perhaps our FTA with CECA might make us more vulnerable to this India shock.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We know that the speed at which technology has developed and the way the global economy is shifting are, indeed, disorienting and difficult, especially for our older PMETs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Some have been knocked down by the winds of change and it is not simply a matter of bouncing back on your feet again, especially when you are older.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But the world will not stop and the economy will continue to change.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Government will provide the best possible support we can give to those who have been knocked back.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We cannot go back or hesitate in embracing change.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Our children now have opportunities today that we would only dream of in the past.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They get to work in the most cutting-edge industries and companies; they work alongside the world's best without having to leave Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is not just for the few as it was for an older generation, but also for the many amongst the young, and all these have been made possible because we kept ourselves open to the world, even as many other countries caved in to domestic pressures and turned inward.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There is no reason why, as fathers and mothers, we cannot walk tall, knowing that we are doing our best for our children and our next generation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Several Members have also given specific suggestions on what more we can do in various areas.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will study all suggestions carefully and continue to finetune and improve our policies.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I have also presented evidence of what we have achieved with our policies: more jobs created, incomes rising over the years and more opportunities for our children.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These are all based on published data and facts.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There is a lot of data out there – more than enough for any serious analyst to dive in, understand better what is happening in the labour market, what is happening with employment trends and unemployment trends – and Prof Hoon Hian Teck just now demonstrated that with his excellent economic exposition based on published data.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, look at the evidence and see for yourself how our policies have benefited Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But at the end of the day, I recognise that this strategy that I have set out that the Government is pursuing is not something that is easy to implement politically.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: While the vast majority benefit from an open economy, there will be some whose lived experiences are not so rosy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For everyone who suffers a negative experience, it is painful, it is very difficult and it is emotional.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In other countries, populist parties have no compunction about tapping into people's anxieties, appealing to fear, appealing to tribal instincts, pitting one group against another.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They blame immigrants and foreigners and make them scapegoats for their country's problems and this results in the countries turning inward and becoming more protectionist.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We cannot afford any of this to happen in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It will start with seemingly innocent comments and questions being raised, or dog-whistles, coded phrases.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But, over time, the comments become normalised, and racist and xenophobic sentiments become more prevalent.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: When that happens, our society will fracture and Singapore will fall apart.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Indeed, many Members have also spoken strongly against racism and xenophobia.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai himself now claims that his Motion has got nothing to do with racism or xenophobia.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But the fact is that, over the past few months, the PSP has been raging against FTAs and CECA, and for reasons that I genuinely cannot fathom.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Despite all the clarifications we have made, his Motion today continues to attribute the cause of job anxieties to FTAs and CECA.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai takes issue with the Government calling him out on this.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Others can see what the PSP is doing.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In my opening speech earlier, I read an email from someone that various Ministers received the email from.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Leong says the PSP listens to the people.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Ms Hazel Poa said, in response to my email sharing about this Singaporean who was not happy with the PSP's campaign against CECA, that we should assure him, that do not worry, the PSP's approach will give him more assurance of getting a job.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But I have already highlighted that the PSP's approach is not going to work any better.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Second, Ms Hazel Poa misses the point because this gentleman who emailed to us, his concern was not just about jobs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: He said, and I repeat what he said again: "The PSP's campaign is truly racist and it is hurting Singapore Indians and we are splitting Singaporeans along racial lines." It is not just a jobs concern, which the Member has not addressed.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The PSP's own members have expressed this concern, which my colleague, Minister Shanmugam, said just now.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: According to media reports, one senior PSP member said that focusing on CECA is, "cheap politics".

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Another member said that there are racial undertones with how the CECA issue is being raised in Parliament, and the "real problem is not about CECA".

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, these are voices that the PSP's own Members have said that Singaporeans have highlighted.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai and Ms Hazel Poa keep saying, "No, no, no, we are not racist.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But, look, if it looks like a duck, if it walks like a duck, if it quacks like a duck, it is a duck.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Whatever Mr Leong Mun Wai or Ms Hazel Poa may say, the fact is, this is how people see and perceive the PSP's campaign.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai also asked for more data.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And I cannot help but feel that the persistent data requests are red herrings to continue this campaign of casting aspersions and creating disaffection towards the Government.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I hope Mr Leong Mun Wai and Ms Hazel Poa will have the open-mindedness to look at the data and evidence again.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Listen to what Prof Hoon Hian Teck has said just now, or any other serious analyst that is looking at the data, and review the PSP's position objectively and be gracious enough to accept that the allegations are baseless and put a stop to the false claims that they have been perpetrating about CECA and FTAs, both in and out of this House.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Next, let us consider the policy issues that Mr Leong Mun Wai raised.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But as several of my colleagues have said just now, this is really a separate topic from manpower policy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And you can see for yourself in the latest census reports how we have maintained this balance over the decades.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, these are the three specific policy issues that Mr Leong Mun Wai was concerned about.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Why did PSP not raise them in the first place?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Why does his Motion harp upon the Foreign Talent Policy, Movement of Natural Persons in FTAs and, specifically, CECA?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Why is he continuing the PSP's sustained negative campaign against CECA, a move which even his own party members say is cheap politics?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Why pin the blame on Indian nationals and stir racial unhappiness in our own community?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These are questions that I doubt I will get direct answers from Mr Leong Mun Wai, but only he, Ms Hazel Poa and the PSP know the real answers to.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But I hope that, having had the benefit of this debate, Mr Leong Mun Wai, Ms Hazel Poa and the PSP will seriously reflect on their actions and conduct and abandon such irresponsible politics that will divide our society and be disastrous for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: By all means, let us talk about manpower policies; let us debate them; let us talk about the pros and cons of different settings, but they have nothing to do with CECA and FTAs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The more you persist with this line of questioning and the more you persist with your campaign, the more you obfuscate the matter and make problems worse.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Next, let me address some of the questions and points that Members from the Workers' Party have raised.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If I can summarise the Workers' Party position on my Motion, it is this: the Workers' Party agrees with the Government's overall strategy to stay open and connected to the world and deal with the downsides of an open economy, but we would like the Government to do more to help Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: First, I thank the Workers' Party for supporting our strategy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is very important, that there is alignment and common ground on this basic strategy for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As for the "do more" part, well, I have already said that the Government will do our utmost to deal with all the downsides.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Where there are specific policy suggestions – and a few were raised just now – we will consider them.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will weigh the pros and cons and consider carefully also – wearing my MOF hat – how we should pay for them.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And I am sure there will be opportunities in the future for such meaningful debates, including during the Budget next year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Workers' Party also had another line of argument, which was about information, data and communications.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Government's communication is not perfect, we will always work to improve our communication strategy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But where data is concerned, as I have said, there is already a lot of data that we have released to the public.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Data on the labour markets, data that has been requested.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have put out more than enough data for anyone looking at the matter to examine the facts carefully.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Workers' Party's line is that more data is better.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, why not go all the way and have freedom of information, a proposal which the Workers' Party has made before.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: All the external surveys will show that the trust levels are low and nowhere near where we are in Singapore today.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And this is America, but you can look at many other countries which have similar Freedom of Information provisions and that has not helped to improve public trust or public confidence in policies.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The real issue is this: when someone loses his or her job, they will be unhappy, no matter how much data you provide to them.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, when they lose their jobs, they are not interested in data.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we will do our utmost, as I have said, to help everyone who is displaced.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There are also, sometimes – from time to time – good reasons why we may want to be careful about releasing data.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Which is why I said our view on data is a lot more nuanced than the Workers' Party's position – to just release all the data and everyone will have enlightenment.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For example, people ask for more data with breakdown by nationality.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Really, do we want to let everyone know that?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, that weighs on our mind when we think about data release.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The first amendment, drops the word "support" and talks about calling for stronger actions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But this leaves it too open-ended and changes the meaning of the limb of the Motion that we originally had.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The second limb, limb (f), talks about data and information, but that is really about, as I have said, information policy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Nothing to do with the debate we are having now about jobs, and there is no shortage of data, as I have emphasised earlier.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There is a lot of data today already that allows anyone to study the facts and evidence to decide how our policies have worked and impacted Singaporeans and make an informed decision about this matter.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If the Workers' Party would like to have a separate debate on information, data provision or even what the Workers' Party has proposed, which is, to have a Freedom of Information Act, we can do so separately.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I note that the Workers' Party has tried to disassociate itself from the PSP Motion.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It suggested some amendments to the Motion, which Speaker has ruled were not acceptable, because they changed the substance of the Motion.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But it is quite clear from the speeches made by the Leader of the Opposition and Members of the Workers' Party where they stand on this matter.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And I thank Mr Pritam Singh and Workers' Party Members for your very strong stand against racism and xenophobia.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Pritam Singh himself quoted from a speech he made, I believe, at the Opening of Parliament, where he talked about "foreigners in our economy; giving Singapore vitality", that we must "maintain that openness and friendly attitude towards them." In the debate in July, he made very clear his stand again, that when it comes to racism and xenophobia, we have to reject them and there can be no "ifs and buts".

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And I believe that he also agrees that FTAs, including CECA, are fundamental to our economic survival.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Again, today, I think he was quite clear where he stood and he, I believe, also mentioned that he was concerned about the racial undertones that have entered into the present debate on FTAs and CECA.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And we should be very clear that the Workers' Party does not stand for any of this.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Those were, I believe, statements that he made earlier.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, I thank the Leader of the Opposition for making very clear where the Workers' Party stands on this important matter.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There are other viruses we should worry about: the dark forces of fear and anger of racism and xenophobia.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As a society, we need our antibodies to kick in, too, against these viruses, against these other threats, to defend against and defeat the bigots, the racists and the fear-mongers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will take all ideas and views seriously.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Often, there will be differing perspectives and it will not be possible to take on board every suggestion.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, in the end, the Government has the responsibility to govern and to make policy decisions in the best interest of all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Some decisions will not be so popular, even though we are convinced they are necessary and must proceed for the good of all.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: When that happens, we may see opposition parties finding ways to stir up disquiet and disagreement.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Sometimes, the Government decides it is an urgent matter and we need to move quickly.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Then we will be criticised for not consulting and being too high-handed.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On other occasions, we think it is better to take time to deliberate and get everyone on board.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Then, we will be criticised for moving too slowly.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But we will not be shaken from our conviction to do what is right for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will not sugar coat realities or shirk away from our responsibilities in tackling difficult issues.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will make the tough calls where necessary.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: At the end of the term, we will present our report card to Singaporeans and they will judge us on our performance.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is how our system has worked and will continue to work and that is why the PAP Government will always be on the side of Singaporeans, working with you and for you.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We know our policies are delivering results and Singaporeans are seeing improvements in their quality of life.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But we also recognise that there are segments who are more vulnerable and who struggle to keep up.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we are fully committed to do more to ensure the fruits of progress are shared by every Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is a debate about jobs and livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is also a debate, more importantly, about our values, who we are, who we want to be and the Singapore we want for ourselves and our children.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Motion that stands in my name talks about Singapore's overall economic strategy to stay open, connected to the world, and to deal with the downsides of an open economy, and to continue with all our efforts to help every Singaporean cope and adjust, and to make sure Singapore stays united and we progress together.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Motion that stands in Mr Leong Mun Wai's name is ostensibly to deal with the anxieties about jobs but, for reasons known only to the PSP, persists with a negative campaign to link this to FTAs and CECA, and to continue to stir racism and xenophobia.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: My first posting was as Minister of State in Education.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: When I visited schools, one of the questions I liked to ask our students then was: what would you like to be when you grow up?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: At that time, I received many traditional answers: to be a doctor, be a lawyer, be a soldier, be a teacher.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: When I returned to MOE last year, I went around asking the same question in my school visits.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And, this time, I heard many more diverse aspirations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Kids said that they would like to be a video game designer, data scientist, startup founder, pursuing careers in companies like Amazon and Google.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These aspirations are possible because we have defied the odds to build something special here in Singapore: a vibrant city connected to the world, brimming with life, energy and excitement, full of opportunities for our people.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: By continuing on this path, we give ourselves the best chance of helping our children realise their aspirations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is what is at stake for all of us.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We know it is not easy to thrive as a little red dot in this big ocean of globalisation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will encounter many bouts of stormy weather along the way for sure.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But we are all on the same boat together and we will get through these storms as one people.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is what we have been doing for the past 20 months, dealing with the COVID-19 crisis.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It has been difficult for all of us.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It has added to the stresses and strains felt by people who are suffering the negative experiences of trade and globalisation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But we have also seen throughout this period that we are strongest when we stand together.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have demonstrated we have the never-say-die spirit.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have the ability and drive to work as one people.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And we have the guts and gumption to meet every problem head-on.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, together, we can build our best home in Singapore and create a brighter future for ourselves and our families, and for all Singaporeans young and old.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Please if you can make a reply on your Motion.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: He has been puzzling me because it was in reference to his remarks made on a racial incident, which has nothing to do with CECA.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The very fact that he linked the incident to CECA was both disingenuous and troubling.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The Prime Minister also, in his National Day Rally speech, claimed that those who question CECA, wanting to put Singaporeans first, had a strong racial undertone.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Minister Lawrence Wong also reiterated many of those accusations throughout his two speeches today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But when I asked Minister Shanmugam for instances where I have commented about CECA prior to accepting his challenge, he cannot reply me.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: He went on to ask me a few other questions but he did not reply to me.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, these are clearly attempts by this Government to put a label on those seeking more information disclosure and more objective discussion on CECA as racist and xenophobic.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I think I will leave that issue as it is.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We have done all our explanation that we are not racist or xenophobic.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: At the end of the day, justice is in the heart of the people.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Political labels are convenient to use to discredit someone but they are not helpful for an open and objective discussion.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: By the way, I will also have to object to Minister Tan See Leng's words just now saying that PSP is attacking foreigners.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Maybe it is a slip of his tongue, but I have to correct that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: All of us here today have one common objective and, that is, to improve the job prospects and livelihoods of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And I have stayed focused on that objective.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, let me reiterate that we are neither racist nor xenophobic, and this debate is squarely about jobs and livelihoods of our PMETs, who are adversely affected by the foreign talent policy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: They play an important role in complementing, transferring skills and knowledge, as well as providing opportunities for cross-fertilisation of ideas.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: By drawing on Mr Goh Chok Tong's definition of mediocrity, a foreign talent should be one who earns more than $500,000 a year, or $40,000 a month.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: While we do need foreign talent, more importantly, we need to protect our Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It is simply our citizens, natural or new, who recite our Singapore Pledge, and whose interest the Government has the prime responsibility to look after.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The current policies have seriously hollowed out our core.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In many key industries, our PMET core is no longer the dominant force that we can rely on for long-term growth.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The very people that can ensure the future of our country are being displaced and hollowed out.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It has been a long debate and we have covered a lot of ground.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: However, as expected, the Government's stance on the causes and the severity of the problem Singaporeans are facing is very different from ours.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: As a result, probably the new policies that the Government is going to come up with will not solve the problems thoroughly and Singaporean sufferings may have to go on.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We might have to come back one year later again and debate on the same problem.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Singaporeans would note that PSP has done our best to convince this Government.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: First, the Government says displacement is due to globalised and fast-changing world.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: PSP says a large part is due to work pass holders.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Two, the displacement problem is not serious, the Government says.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Coming back to the 380,000 PME jobs that the Manpower Minister had presented to us in the 6 July Ministerial Statement, we are trying to ask him if he is sure that this number represents a net job creation for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, there were some exchanges just now with my colleague, Hazel Poa, as well.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But let me just share some numbers with you.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, the reclassification is likely to be a significant factor.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But we do not know what is the number because we do not have the number from the Government.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: On top of that, there were 400,000 University and Polytechnic graduates during that period.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, a million people seeking jobs versus 380,000 jobs created.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, I do not know how to reconcile the numbers, but maybe in other future forums, we can continue to discuss that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Third, the Government says emphasis is on training and retraining Singaporeans; PSP says better prevent job displacement first.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Let the foreigners do the skills transfer because once a person is displaced, it is difficult for him to find a new job.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It is so easy to say "train again, take up the challenge" and all that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The examples you quoted, I am sure, is a small minority of those Singaporeans who can really change to a new industry and learn new skills.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Fourth, the Government says discrimination is sporadic; PSP says probably it is structural, we have to look at it because the foreign work pass holders have been in Singapore in large numbers for the last 20 years and they are a very influential force in the job market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, if you want to rectify the discriminative situation in the job market, legislation may be too slow.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Fifth, foreign talent creates jobs, says the Government; but PSP says the work pass holders we are attracting are all average work pass holders.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Where do they have the ability to create jobs?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, they are just here to share our jobs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The jobs done by them, most of them can be done by Singaporeans as well.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In that sense, Prof Hoon Hian Teck's lump of labour fallacy may not apply.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Sixth, Member Mr Patrick Tay also mentioned this, that there is a lot of resistance from employers if you want to change the foreigners policy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Of course, that is expected because, after all, they are profit seekers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But PSP says: how long can we kick the can down the road?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: If not, our economy will continue to be stuck in a low value-add position.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Lastly, the Government says you send wrong signal to foreigners; PSP says as long as we Singaporeans are united, Government and alternative parties all united and say we have to change course, I do not think foreigners can say much because that is the way we have chosen.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And I do not think the foreigners are here just because we give them work passes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: They are here, they have made a business decision and a strategy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Work passes are just one of the factors.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In fact – afterwards I will elaborate on our policy recommendations – we are not saying that you do not allow the foreign companies to come in with the number of work passes they want initially.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We cannot allow them to continue to keep the same number of foreigners from the very day they come in.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, as long as we are united, I think we can put the message nicely to the foreigners.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: After all, we can set up a fair consideration framework for foreigners.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: That is something, as a Singaporean, I feel very puzzled about.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: An interesting point was brought up by Ms Janet Ang.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I respect Janet as a senior executive in the private sector.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: She mentioned that Singaporeans did not have the relevant skills, work knowledge and global experience.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But I would like to say that if Singaporeans continue to be uprooted from their jobs, where do we get the opportunity to accumulate the skills and know-how over time?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Like I said just now, you cannot expect the Singaporeans to pick up new skills all the time.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Are you going to say that if foreigners come in and replace the Singaporeans because it is low-cost, the Singaporeans lost the job and then he has to go and acquire a new skill again?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Skills and know-how – that comes to the capabilities of our economy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Our Singaporean Core are no longer learning over time in the same job.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Another thing I want to point out to Ms Janet Ang is that we hope the top managers in Singapore would also understand that and support Singaporeans and not keep saying "Singaporeans don't have this, don't have that", because they are now under a system that does not have the incentive to make them work hard, to make them work in the way we want them to take up the challenge and all that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Those prospects existed in our generation, Ms Janet Ang.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And, now, the leadership of the country has brought in an additional trouble for them and, that is, competition from foreigners.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But, as I have said before in my speech, the competition was not really fair, to start with.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, other than the discriminative structure that we have talked about in the job market, actually, our economy now is also in a very different operating structure, thanks to the 20 years of foreign talent policy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: If, together, we have a consensus, we can rope in a lot of initiatives, a lot of resources.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We can give each other time – employers, workers – but I think we need to make the change.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Next, what I want to comment about is from Mr Saktiandi Supaat who mentioned that Singaporeans are now very active in the global financial market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But I would also like to remind him we Singaporeans have been in the forefront of the financial market since the 1980s.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Before that, many of my seniors, not just in GIC, but seniors in the financial sector in Singapore were already pioneers in financial innovations in New York.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: They go to New York and they make the innovation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Some of the innovations were interest rate swaps and all the equity and bond derivatives.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But I set up one of the first equity derivative desks in Tokyo in 1987.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But he did not read my recommendation correctly.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Next, I would like to address the policy recommendations that I have made in reply to Minister Lawrence Wong and also Minister Tan See Leng.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: First of all, PSP is for an open economy and society.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, our policy recommendations are not meant to make Singapore a closed society or economy and our policy recommendations are meant to make a point – a point that all of us agree upon that we change course.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But after we have agreed to that, I would think that we can throw in or rope in a lot of other things and provide the leeway for us to implement those policies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And among the policies that I have recommended, only the price-related policies or what I call price-control policies, have got a timeframe.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: For the quota policies, I have purposely made it no time constraint.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And being an employer, that will go into his decision-making.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Second, in order to attract more foreign talent, the Government also agrees that the qualifying salaries should go up.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, it is just a matter of how fast.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Third, I did not put any time limit to reduce the headcount of work pass holders although I would like actually today if we can come to some conclusion as to what is the number of displaced Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, that becomes a target that we can work on.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But since the Government claims there are very few displacements, then we will not discuss that anymore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But I did not put any time limit to reducing the headcount.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I also did not put any time limit to reducing the single nationality number.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But for all these, there is an aspirational or planning target, and maybe, we should put a 10% cap on the single nationality on that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: What I am trying to say is on the policies that PSP has recommended, actually, we are very mindful of the effect that the implementation has on the job market and also, indirectly, what kind of messages we are sending to foreigners.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Next, we also have to reflect on how the problems of the foreign talent policy have been allowed to fester, develop and exist for the last 20 years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It tells us a lot about the checks and balances in our governance system.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In particular, we have to question the freedom of information, the tripartite partnership and the conduct of our Government.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Throughout this long-running saga on the foreign talent policy, accurate data has been lacking, which has contributed to the large amount of fake news and speculation floating around.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In my own experience of preparing for this debate, I cannot find the figures of intra-corporate transferees.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Of course, today, the Minister provided a few more years but the thing is: why give it out piecemeal?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: You are the one who is generating the data.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: You should be putting the data in an organised format.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Yes, we agree that some data may be sensitive but, please, put it in an organised format for people to analyse.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: There are so many people in Singapore who will be able to analyse the data if the data is presented regularly and in an organised manner.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Today, Minister Tan See Leng provided, I would say, quite a lot of new data but the new data was not actually available for us to analyse without him telling us.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, the Government is doing what I call guerilla data.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Whenever they want to prove a point, they give you a little more data.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Look at the chart that Minister Tan See Leng has given us.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Below the chart, it is stated Labour Survey Report.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: After that, "administrative data from the Research Department of MOM".

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Without the administrative data, we do not have the whole picture.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Dr Tan Cheng Bock has called for transparency, accountability and independence in matters of national governance.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The Workers' Party has always been talking about this and we thank them for that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Parliament also has a constitutional role to play in ensuring that sufficient information is provided and policies are thoroughly debated.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It is more social economic analysis but, on top of that, philosophy, history, how human beings have behaved over history, those are important things for policymaking.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The second point I want to make is tripartism.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: However, in my opinion, the weak NTUC link in the tripartite partnership has become obvious during the foreign talent policy saga.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, NTUC needs a lot of soul searching if it still wants to be relevant in representing the interests of the Singaporean worker.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We also urge Singaporean employers to stand up against discrimination.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: They will have the most to lose in the long term, if the current situation leads to a radical change of our business culture and mode of operation without a robust Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We urge employers to take the lead in rooting out discrimination in the job market so that we can build a competitive yet fair, multicultural and multinational workforce with Singaporeans at the core.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The Government needs to show more empathy rather than pay lip service in order to understand the psyche and the real experiences of the working citizen.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Even if one Singaporean is being discriminated against, we should take action.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Let us not argue about majority, widespread or not widespread.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: To every Singaporean, we have a duty to make sure he is not discriminated against in the job market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Over the years, while Singaporeans have constantly provided feedback on their predicament, the Government has insisted that all attempts in trying to curb immigration and foreign workforce growth in order to safeguard Singaporeans will end up hurting the Singaporeans themselves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I quote Dr Amy Khor from her speech at the Population White Paper debate in February 2013, "To curb immigration or foreign workforce growth in order to safeguard Singaporeans could in an ironic twist hurt the very people this reversal is intended to help." I wonder what Dr Amy Khor has to say now.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Before the ironic twist has happened, the silver bullet unleashed by the foreign talent policy has actually shot down many Singaporeans' livelihoods and may hit Singapore soon.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: When Singaporeans' anxiety has persisted for the last 10 to 20 years, I think it is difficult to justify that the current policy is not flawed.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: This has been a debate that many Singaporeans are concerned with and anxiously waiting for.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: This is not just a debate about a particular section of CECA, nor has it anything to do with racism and xenophobia.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It is a debate about alleviating the plight of our PMETs adversely affected by the foreign talent policy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It is a debate about the need to safeguard the Singaporean Core, which is a pillar of our economy and our future.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It is a debate about developing our very own talent by looking into new ideas to create opportunities for them.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We recognise the need to stay open as an economy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We are pro-trade but not "free for all" trade.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We recognise the need for real foreign talent to complement our Singaporean Core, transferring skills as well as sharing experiences but we want a healthy balance of foreign and local workforce achieved through sound immigration and employment policies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The Prime Minister has said in his National Day message that he recognises the anxieties about jobs and that his Government will make changes over time.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The changes must start now before this dire situation gets to a point of no return.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: There is nothing wrong with driving for Grab as it is an honourable job.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But this is a good illustration of underemployment, which many of our PMETs are facing.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Their skillsets could have been much better utilised.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It pains us to know that we have our own talent that are not treasured and the very Government that is supposed to look after their interests has the priority elsewhere, maybe on economic growth.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, let us not forget that it is the interest of the people that the Members of this House and this Government are elected to serve.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: There is nothing wrong in voicing out for them and championing for them.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The many Philip Wens out there deserve better.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment and Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: I did not mean to take up any more time than is necessary.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment and Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: But I think I need to address or clarify Mr Leong Mun Wai's point.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment and Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: He asked me what I have got to say about the quote from my speech.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment and Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: I think Minister Lawrence Wong has said we simply do not have enough people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment and Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: So, I would still say the same thing: that we have to be very careful in saying that we keep the foreigners out, we do not have any of these people there and we will have jobs because, indeed, if we do that, we will really hurt the very people that we are trying to help, and, that is, the Singaporeans that we care about and we want to make sure that we improve their lives, they have good jobs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, we can confirm that, from the debate today, the Government's stance is that the old policies still stand.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think there is going to be a reprise.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I have a feeling it will be, but it is okay.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, Dr Tan Cheng Bock on 2 July 2020, that PSP will call for a review of the India-Singapore Comprehensive Economic Cooperation Agreement and the canard that it allows a free movement of professionals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And others had made some statements, similar statements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Leong put up his Facebook post along similar lines in June.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: His Motion, which we debated today, is along the same lines.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: All of this is on the record and I had made it clear.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I am not quite sure what point he was making.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am not asking him to clarify, because it is past midnight.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: All I am saying is, the reason I did not respond to him was because the record is clear.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He associated himself with all these statements unless now he is saying: well, those are racist, but you know, I did not make them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think we can leave it at that.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That he concluded the Government's old policies remain.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I was flummoxed when Mr Leong said: if we do not change course, Singapore will remain a low value-add economy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Leong, have you seen the economic data?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think if we change course to adopt your policies, we will truly be a low value-add economy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I rise to clarify a point made by Minister Lawrence Wong vis-à-vis his request that we vote against the PSP Motion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We feel strongly about the amendments that we sought to amend the PSP Motion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Speaker disallowed it because it was deemed to a substantive change to the Motion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But the reason why we opined that the change was important is because we have a different view on FTAs and CECA compared to the PSP.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Similarly, I have shared with the House why I sought to move an amendment to the Minister's Motion and we feel strongly about those amendments as well.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We have a difference of opinion on that.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I do have to apologise to everybody for holding things up, but Mr Leong Mun Wai had a specific comment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: He says that the NTUC, or the Labour Movement, should do some soul-searching.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I did some soul-searching and I hope he did as well.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I am sure he also benefited from what NTUC has provided over the years through our grocery programme.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But I do want to seek some clarification from him.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Whether he also remembered the Asian Financial Crisis, when the Labour Movement worked with the Government and the people of Singapore to go through a difficult period of time?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And I want to also emphasise: we always do deep reflection and soul-searching about what is the best thing that we can do for workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The best thing that we need to do for workers is to care for them in the long term, we seek to protect workers, we care for their jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But protecting workers does not mean a zero-sum game.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We are worried that if investments go away, if companies will suffer.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: If companies suffer, then there will be no jobs for workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is something that we think about day and night.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I have it here on my phone because this is something that I look at all the time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: So, I want to seek a clarification from Mr Leong Mun Wai, after the three pointers that I have given to him, does he still agree that NTUC is the weak link?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: If he still so agrees that NTUC is the weak link, I would very much like to invite him to NTUC and share with him the work that we have done since our founding in 1961.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I appreciate all the work that NTUC has done for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In fact, NTUC was formed, no, FairPrice was formed around the time of the oil shock, the oil crisis, right?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I remember going to the Community Centre to collect rice from NTUC FairPrice.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I do not think it was called FairPrice at that time.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, yes, the things done by NTUC, we Singaporeans, we all know.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In fact, in this House, we are all for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We are just trying to say what is the right direction forward.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: There is an overall national policy called foreign talent policy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And then, there is some preference to make sure the businesses do well before the workers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Okay, I mean, that may lead to another debate.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But maybe suffice to say that, okay, we think that there is some room for improvement as far as wage policy is concerned.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Members will be glad to know that I have prepared breakfast.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: I just have one last point, just to clarify what Mr Leong Mun Wai has said.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: He said that we ought to do better.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Of course, we definitely want to do better for workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: And that, perhaps in the wages side of the house, we can do better.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: So to say that NTUC and the Labour Movement are not doing their part on wage policies, I am sure we are as confused as he is in the last eight hours of not doing homework.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Year after year, we deliberate, trying to find out what are the best wage policies for our workers across different segments.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: We have fierce exchanges with our employers, with our Government side of the house, but we need to do that because we need wage increases to be sustainable, create a pie, so that our workers can go home and come back to work tomorrow again with their job intact.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: So, I do appreciate what Mr Leong Mun Wai has done in the financial sector, but I do not want what he has said today to stand as the record for the generations of unionists before me, who have dedicated their time, their blood, their sweat, to better the lot of workers in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I want to thank PSP for sharing its survey on 700 people and sharing some of the ground sentiments.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: In healthcare, we actually have problems finding nurses, clinic assistants and radiographers for these trained jobs.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: So, I am just wondering could there be a mismatch of trained Singaporeans in getting these jobs?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: And I hear a lot of concern over foreigners and foreign talent.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: In a global economy, I would think that there will always be flow of people, crossing nations for jobs, so would our Singaporeans working overseas then be discriminated against as foreigners?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: One on the lack of manpower in certain sectors, as we have said, we are not saying that we clamp down on foreigners immediately.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We are saying that we have to chart a path.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because this path going down, does it mean that we need more and more foreigners?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because that is not something that Singaporeans want.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, we may need to chart a new path now.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But at the ground level, there are a lot of different requirements.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad
text: When Mr Leong Mun Wai spoke about NTUC, he is not doing justice; I took it very badly because I am a walking union leader.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad
text: My job is not full-time working for the union.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad
text: It is a mixture of sacrifices I have to make.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad
text: When you said that wages can be better, I would like to share with this House what you have seen and what you have heard based on just the Progressive Wage Model (PMW) is not very reflective.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad
text: We review their job scope, pay them accordingly.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad
text: So, it is not right to say that NTUC has not done our part.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad
text: We have been doing it since it was founded.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad
text: I am a beneficiary of past great union leaders.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad
text: Some might have been Nominated Members of Parliament like the late A Nithiah Nandan.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad
text: We go to the table, we quarrel over wages, even though we know at the end of the day, there would be some sacrifices to be made.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad
text: Their wages, their welfare, their work prospect will continue to be our main aim.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad
text: We are a holistic institution that upholds the belief that every worker needs to be paid due respect for what they have contributed to the company.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: I am so sorry; it is past midnight and I am 62!

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: They are real employers who are hiring and they have found the gaps they found.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: So, I am not sure what Mr Leong is disagreeing with me about.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: One is engage these employers and really, like I said in my speech, understand what those relevant skills that our people are missing are, what are the relevant experience that is missing, and then we go figure out how to get the right approach.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: But since I have managed "United Nations" employees in IBM before, I will share with Members – which is what I said in my speech – one tip that Singaporean workers need to recognise.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: We have to be brave to speak up.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: We will always have all our things in our heads: "I am so good at all these.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: Why is he taking the job?" But if you do not speak up and you do not tell anybody why you deserve that job, you will not get that job.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: Because of the competition, Mr Leong, which is my second point.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: I was going to ask you because you did say that the paradigm has shifted from our time.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: I do not know how old you are.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: So, do you not agree that competition for most jobs is not just among the talent that are onshore in Singapore, whether local or foreign, but, really, a global one?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: So, my point is, Mr Leong, you have been a private sector executive yourself.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: Do you give the job to the individual who is entitled to the job, almost like – and this one, a little bit scary to say it – Malaysia's bumiputra policy, perhaps?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: Or do you give the job to the guy who has the skills to do the job and, better yet, has the added characteristics of passion for the business, hunger for the business and a willingness to go the extra mile?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: So, Mr Leong, since you asked me those questions, if you could help me understand whether I got you wrong.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The only thing I want to confirm is that, yes, I am 62 years old.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, that is why I know we are from the same generation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But I do not think we want to go further into explaining what you just said because it will enter another debate.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I hope to have another opportunity in the near future to talk about wage policy and retirement.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I hope that is okay for Ms Janet Ang.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck
text: A reference was made to the lump of labour fallacy.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck
text: I think we all agree that, in essence, that is not a good description of labour markets.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck
text: And I will just conclude by applying that to two settings.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck
text: I think, first, with reference to what Member Desmond Choo illustrated, the understanding that the lump of labour fallacy – which is that there are only 100 jobs and, so, if you have more people than that, some other people take the jobs, the others would not have it.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck
text: In fact, that does not apply, first, in a setting when the economy is itself subject to adverse shocks, recessions.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck
text: Mr Desmond Choo pointed very well to the episode in 1984 to 1985.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck
text: In the face of a sharp recession, in fact, the number of jobs substantially decreased.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck
text: I think the remarkable thing about Singapore when you look at how it faced its challenges over the decades is the ability to demonstrate the lump of labour fallacy does not apply even in an adverse situation.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck
text: In 1984, I was an Honours year student graduating from NUS.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck
text: Prime Minister Lee was then actually directing the economic committee that came out with the report.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck
text: The remarkable thing that came out of that episode – really remarkable, because it was the sharpest recession since 1965 – was the ability to bring together union leaders, employers and the Government to convince the people that you will accept a 15-percentage-point cut in your CPF.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck
text: That amounts to 12% of your wages, really.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck
text: I had the opportunity in 2010 when Prof Paul Romer, who won the Nobel Prize in 2018, to meet him through my association with Prof Edmund Phelps who was my teacher at the University of Columbia.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck
text: Paul had, for some years before he won the Nobel, been very interested to visit various countries to talk about policy.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck
text: He was in the International Advisory Panel with the University at that time.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck
text: He came to me and said, at Prof Phelps' suggestion, "Would you like to take a trip with me to South Africa?" It was a one-day conference, where they were going to bring together their business leaders and their trade union leaders to talk about the fact that the unemployment rate among the young people was close to 50%.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck
text: I had a chance to tell them about the Singapore story, with trade union members all in the room, about how we were able to convince labour to accept the 15-percentage-point cut and, of course, with the understanding that the CPF rate will be restored.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck
text: The challenge ahead for Singapore is understanding that the lump of labour fallacy still does not apply over the long term.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck
text: The challenge for Singapore, really, is to recognise that the sources of growth going forward have to come with a continued integration into the global economy.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck
text: I think Minister Lawrence Wong has demonstrated and illustrated that very well.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck
text: The challenge for Singapore is, in the next stage, to demonstrate this.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck
text: Because we have had five decades of being able to find a new way to reinvent ourselves, I think there is a great reason to have great optimism to show that the lump of labour fallacy will not apply.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck
text: At the heart of it, I believe it is, indeed, right in that point in the Motion by Minister Lawrence Wong, which I have a deep sympathy for: that Singapore's growth must continue with economic openness.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck
text: That includes openness to trade, capital and people in the right way.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We have now finally come to the conclusion of the debate.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I shall put the necessary questions to the House for decision.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We will first deal with the Minister for Finance's Motion on "Securing Singaporeans' Jobs and Livelihoods".

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We have two substantive amendments by Mr Pritam Singh and a consequential amendment.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If this new limb is agreed to, Mr Pritam Singh's consequential amendment is to remove the word "and" at the end of part (d) and to include the word "and" at the end of part (e).

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We will deal with the first amendment by Mr Pritam Singh.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Pritam Singh's amendment number 2 is to have a new limb (f), with the words "calls on the Government to proactively release information on jobs and employment prospects of Singaporeans and the costs and benefits of Free Trade Agreements and foreign worker policies, with a view to formulating better policies to ensure Singaporeans secure good jobs in Singapore and are not disadvantaged when seeking employment", to be added at the end of the Motion.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: As a result, no consequential amendment will be made.
